updates.question_text: Regarding liver MRI contrast agents and functional sequences, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: MRI has superior lesion-to-liver contrast compared with CT.
Gadoxetic acid disodium is 90% renally excreted and has no hepatobiliary uptake.
Iron oxide agents increase liver T2 signal by lengthening T2 relaxation.
In- and out-of-phase gradient imaging can detect intracytoplasmic lipid in steatosis, HCC, and adenoma.
Gadoxetic acid disodium can help distinguish FNH from adenoma and can help evaluate hepatic metastases.
options_after: MRI has superior lesion-to-liver contrast compared with CT.
Gadoxetic acid disodium is 90% renally excreted and lacks hepatobiliary uptake.
Iron oxide agents increase liver T2 signal by lengthening T2 relaxation.
In- and out-of-phase gradient imaging can detect intracytoplasmic lipid in steatosis, HCC, and adenoma.
Gadoxetic acid disodium can help distinguish FNH from adenoma and can help evaluate hepatic metastases.
updates.explanation: The source emphasises MRI's superior lesion-to-liver contrast and lack of ionising radiation for dynamic phases. In- and out-of-phase imaging identifies intracytoplasmic lipid, which is useful in steatosis and selected masses including HCC and adenoma. Gadoxetic acid disodium is a combined extracellular/hepatobiliary agent with 50% biliary and 50% renal excretion, useful for FNH versus adenoma and metastasis assessment. Iron oxide particles are trapped by Kupffer cells and reduce T2 relaxivity, making liver or spleen dark on T2.

updates.question_text: Regarding HCC risk and surveillance, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: HCC is the most common benign liver tumour.
Cirrhosis is the major risk factor for HCC, with chronic hepatitis B and fatty liver disease also listed as risk factors.
AFP is elevated in essentially all cases of HCC.
Ultrasound is highly sensitive for detecting small HCC in end-stage cirrhotic livers.
Patients with cirrhosis or chronic viral hepatitis are screened with serum alpha-fetoprotein levels and imaging, typically ultrasound or MRI.
options_after: HCC is the most common benign liver tumour.
Cirrhosis is the major risk factor for HCC, with chronic hepatitis B and fatty liver disease also listed as risk factors.
AFP is elevated in more than 90% of cases of HCC.
Ultrasound is highly sensitive for detecting small HCC in end-stage cirrhotic livers.
Patients with cirrhosis or chronic viral hepatitis are screened with serum alpha-fetoprotein levels and imaging, typically ultrasound or MRI.
updates.explanation: HCC is described as the most common primary liver tumour, and cirrhosis is its major risk factor. Chronic viral hepatitis, particularly hepatitis B, and fatty liver disease are also listed. AFP is elevated in approximately 75% of cases, not all cases. Ultrasound is used for surveillance but is not very sensitive for small HCC in end-stage cirrhotic livers.

updates.question_text: Regarding classic imaging features of HCC, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The classic CT or MRI appearance is an encapsulated mass with arterial enhancement, portal venous washout, and an enhancing capsule.
On unenhanced MRI, HCC is characteristically slightly T2 hyperintense relative to surrounding liver and may restrict diffusion.
Noncontrast CT is the best phase for reliably detecting HCC.
The nodule-in-nodule appearance describes an enhancing nodule within a dysplastic nodule and represents early HCC.
HCC usually appears as a purely cystic mass with no vascular invasion.
options_after: The classic CT or MRI appearance is an encapsulated mass with arterial enhancement, portal venous washout, and an enhancing capsule.
On unenhanced MRI, HCC is characteristically slightly T2 hyperintense relative to surrounding liver and may restrict diffusion.
Noncontrast CT is the best phase for reliably detecting HCC.
The nodule-in-nodule appearance describes an enhancing nodule within a dysplastic nodule and represents early HCC.
HCC usually appears as a purely cystic mass without vascular invasion.
updates.explanation: Classic HCC is hypervascular on arterial phase, washes out on portal venous phase, and may show an enhancing capsule. It can be difficult to see on noncontrast or portal venous phase CT, while MRI may show slight T2 hyperintensity and diffusion restriction. The nodule-in-nodule sign is an enhancing focus within a dysplastic nodule, representing early HCC. The source also highlights local invasion rather than a purely cystic non-invasive pattern.

updates.question_text: Regarding LI-RADS major criteria for HCC, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: LI-RADS is used for every incidental liver lesion, including patients without HCC risk factors.
Ancillary findings alone assign the LI-RADS score.
Peripheral washout on portal venous phase is listed as a major HCC criterion.
A diameter increase of greater than 50% in less than 18 months is the threshold growth criterion.
Major criteria include arterial enhancement, non-peripheral washout, enhancing capsule or pseudocapsule, and threshold growth greater than 50% in less than 6 months.
options_after: LI-RADS is used for most incidental liver lesions, including patients without HCC risk factors.
Ancillary findings alone assign the LI-RADS score.
Peripheral washout on portal venous phase is listed as a major HCC criterion.
A diameter increase of greater than 50% in less than 18 months is the threshold growth criterion.
Major criteria include arterial enhancement, non-peripheral washout, enhancing capsule or pseudocapsule, and threshold growth greater than 50% in less than 6 months.
updates.explanation: The source states that LI-RADS is used only in patients with HCC risk factors such as chronic hepatitis infection or appropriate cirrhosis, and ranges from LR-1 to LR-5. Major criteria assign the score, while ancillary findings act as tie breakers. Major HCC criteria include arterial enhancement, non-peripheral washout on portal venous or delayed phases, enhancing capsule or pseudocapsule, and threshold growth defined as greater than 50% diameter increase in less than 6 months.

updates.question_text: Regarding fibrolamellar HCC, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It occurs in young patients without cirrhosis and AFP is not elevated.
It is a small encapsulated lesion that is usually detected during cirrhotic surveillance.
It has a worse prognosis than conventional HCC according to the source.
A fibrotic central scar is classic and is hypointense on both T1- and T2-weighted MRI.
It is always associated with a true tumour capsule.
options_after: It occurs in young patients without cirrhosis and AFP is not elevated.
It is a small encapsulated lesion that is usually detected during cirrhotic surveillance.
It has a worse prognosis than conventional HCC according to the source.
A fibrotic central scar is classic and is hypointense on both T1- and T2-weighted MRI.
It is characteristically associated with a true tumour capsule.
updates.explanation: Fibrolamellar HCC is described as a rare HCC subtype in young patients without cirrhosis, usually large at diagnosis, with AFP not elevated. Its prognosis is better than typical HCC. The classic fibrotic central scar is low signal on both T1- and T2-weighted images, unlike the T2 hyperintense scar of FNH. The tumour does not have a true capsule, although a pseudocapsule of compressed normal liver may be present.

updates.question_text: Regarding siderotic nodules in cirrhosis, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: They are lipid-rich HCC nodules that become hyperintense on in-phase GRE images.
They are cystic metastases that show peripheral daughter cysts.
They are iron-rich regenerative or dysplastic nodules that are hypointense on T1- and T2*-weighted images and hyperattenuating on CT.
They are premalignant by definition and should always enhance in the arterial phase.
They are caused by biliary ductules and venules within an FNH central scar.
options_after: They are lipid-rich HCC nodules that become hyperintense on in-phase GRE images.
They are cystic metastases that show peripheral daughter cysts.
They are iron-rich regenerative or dysplastic nodules that are hypointense on T1- and T2*-weighted images and hyperattenuating on CT.
They are premalignant by definition and should characteristically enhance in the arterial phase.
They are caused by biliary ductules and venules within an FNH central scar.
updates.explanation: A siderotic nodule is defined in the source as an iron-rich regenerative or dysplastic nodule. It is hypointense on T1- and T2*-weighted images, including in-phase GRE images, and hyperattenuating on CT. The source states that siderotic nodules are rarely, if ever, malignant. Daughter cysts belong to echinococcal disease, and biliary ductules with venules describe the FNH central scar.

updates.question_text: Regarding intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and hepatic metastases, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma is usually a tiny cystic lesion with no progressive enhancement.
Mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma usually presents as a large, relatively well-defined hepatic mass with lobulated margins and delayed progressive enhancement.
Metastatic disease to the liver is far more common than primary HCC.
Most metastases are best appreciated on late arterial phase because they are usually hypervascular.
Peripheral biliary dilatation may be associated with mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma.
options_after: Mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma is usually a tiny cystic lesion without progressive enhancement.
Mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma usually presents as a large, relatively well-defined hepatic mass with lobulated margins and delayed progressive enhancement.
Metastatic disease to the liver is far more common than primary HCC.
Most metastases are best appreciated on late arterial phase because they are usually hypervascular.
Peripheral biliary dilatation may be associated with mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma.
updates.explanation: Mass-forming intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is described as a large, relatively well-defined lobulated hepatic mass with delayed or progressive enhancement and often peripheral biliary dilatation. Although biliary in origin, it must be considered in the differential diagnosis of a hepatic mass. Liver metastases are far more common than primary HCC. Most metastases are hypovascular and best seen on portal venous phase, in contrast to HCC and selected hypervascular metastases.

updates.question_text: Regarding special patterns of hepatic metastatic disease, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Calcified hepatic metastases include mucinous cancers, osteosarcoma, and treated lymphoma.
Pseudocirrhosis is caused only by untreated viral hepatitis and does not have portal hypertensive consequences.
Cystic hepatic metastases include ovarian cystadenocarcinoma and gastrointestinal sarcoma.
Treated breast cancer is the most common cause of pseudocirrhosis.
Pseudocirrhosis describes a macronodular liver contour from multiple scirrhous metastases with capsular retraction.
options_after: Calcified hepatic metastases include mucinous cancers, osteosarcoma, and treated lymphoma.
Pseudocirrhosis is caused primarily by untreated viral hepatitis and does not have portal hypertensive consequences.
Cystic hepatic metastases include ovarian cystadenocarcinoma and gastrointestinal sarcoma.
Treated breast cancer is the most common cause of pseudocirrhosis.
Pseudocirrhosis describes a macronodular liver contour from multiple scirrhous metastases with capsular retraction.
updates.explanation: Calcified metastases in the source include mucinous cancers, osteosarcoma, and treated lymphoma, while cystic metastases include ovarian cystadenocarcinoma and gastrointestinal sarcoma. Pseudocirrhosis is a macronodular contour caused by multiple scirrhous hepatic metastases with capsular retraction, most commonly treated breast cancer metastases. Despite the name, patients may have portal hypertension physiology similar to cirrhosis.

updates.question_text: Regarding epithelioid haemangioendothelioma and hepatic capsular retraction, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Epithelioid haemangioendothelioma is a common benign lesion that usually forms one central cyst.
The only cause of capsular retraction listed is treated breast cancer metastases.
Epithelioid haemangioendothelioma characteristically causes multiple spherical subcapsular masses that can become confluent.
Individual lesions of epithelioid haemangioendothelioma never show halo or target appearance.
The differential diagnosis of capsular retraction includes mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma, fibrolamellar HCC, epithelioid haemangioendothelioma, pseudocirrhosis, and confluent hepatic fibrosis.
options_after: Epithelioid haemangioendothelioma is a common benign lesion that usually forms one central cyst.
The principal cause of capsular retraction listed is treated breast cancer metastases.
Epithelioid haemangioendothelioma characteristically causes multiple spherical subcapsular masses that can become confluent.
Individual lesions of epithelioid haemangioendothelioma will not show halo or target appearance.
The differential diagnosis of capsular retraction includes mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma, fibrolamellar HCC, epithelioid haemangioendothelioma, pseudocirrhosis, and confluent hepatic fibrosis.
updates.explanation: Epithelioid haemangioendothelioma is a rare vascular malignancy, not a common benign cyst. It characteristically causes multiple spherical subcapsular masses that may become confluent, with individual lesions sometimes showing a halo or target appearance. It is one of several causes of capsular retraction. The source also lists mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma, fibrolamellar HCC, pseudocirrhosis, and confluent hepatic fibrosis as causes.

updates.question_text: Regarding hepatic cavernous haemangioma on cross-sectional imaging, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: A virtually pathognomonic feature is peripheral discontinuous progressive nodular enhancement with gradual centripetal fill-in.
The peripheral enhancement should be lower than blood pool on all phases.
Haemangiomas are typically T2 hyperintense and become even more hyperintense on T2 fat-saturated images.
Giant haemangiomas may contain a non-enhancing central area representing cystic degeneration.
Noncontrast CT is highly specific because haemangioma is hyperattenuating relative to liver.
options_after: A virtually pathognomonic feature is peripheral discontinuous progressive nodular enhancement with gradual centripetal fill-in.
The peripheral enhancement should be lower than blood pool on most phases.
Haemangiomas are typically T2 hyperintense and become even more hyperintense on T2 fat-saturated images.
Giant haemangiomas may contain a non-enhancing central area representing cystic degeneration.
Noncontrast CT is highly specific because haemangioma is hyperattenuating relative to liver.
updates.explanation: The source describes peripheral discontinuous nodular enhancement matching the blood pool with progressive centripetal fill-in as virtually pathognomonic for haemangioma. On MRI, haemangiomas are typically T2 hyperintense and even brighter on T2 fat-saturated images. Giant haemangiomas may have non-enhancing central cystic degeneration. Noncontrast CT is not helpful because haemangioma appears as a nonspecific hypoattenuating mass.

updates.question_text: Regarding focal nodular hyperplasia, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: FNH is a true malignant neoplasm with high malignant potential.
FNH is a hamartoma of disorganised liver tissue with no malignant potential.
It is called a stealth lesion because it resembles background liver on most modalities except arterial phase imaging.
FNH contains no bile ductules and is therefore negative on HIDA scanning.
FNH is strongly associated with oral contraceptive use.
options_after: FNH is a true malignant neoplasm with high malignant potential.
FNH is a hamartoma of disorganised liver tissue with no malignant potential.
It is called a stealth lesion because it resembles background liver on most modalities except arterial phase imaging.
FNH lacks bile ductules and is therefore negative on HIDA scanning.
FNH is strongly associated with oral contraceptive use.
updates.explanation: The source defines FNH as a hamartoma of disorganised liver tissue with no malignant potential. It is called a stealth lesion because it resembles background liver on all modalities except arterial phase imaging. It is more common in women but is not associated with oral contraceptives. It contains Kupffer cells and bile ductules, allowing nuclear medicine confirmation with sulfur colloid or HIDA in selected cases.

updates.question_text: Regarding nuclear medicine confirmation of FNH, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: FNH is always photopenic on sulfur colloid because it lacks Kupffer cells.
HIDA is negative in FNH because FNH lacks biliary ductules.
Kupffer cells may be confirmed by sulfur colloid study and bile duct cells can be visualised on HIDA scan.
Nuclear medicine cannot be used for FNH because it is a stealth lesion on all imaging.
Sulfur colloid is positive in every FNH case.
options_after: FNH is characteristically photopenic on sulfur colloid because it lacks Kupffer cells.
HIDA is negative in FNH because FNH lacks biliary ductules.
Kupffer cells may be confirmed by sulfur colloid study and bile duct cells can be visualised on HIDA scan.
Nuclear medicine will not be used for FNH because it is a stealth lesion on the available imaging modalities.
Sulfur colloid is positive in most FNH cases.
updates.explanation: The source states that both Kupffer cells and bile ductules are present in FNH, so nuclear medicine can help confirm the diagnosis. Kupffer cells may be confirmed by sulfur colloid study one-third of the time, and bile duct cells can be visualised with HIDA. Adenoma, not FNH, lacks bile ducts and usually has reduced HIDA uptake.

updates.question_text: Regarding hepatic adenoma biology and risk groups, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Hepatic adenoma contains bile ducts and therefore is usually positive on HIDA scan.
Hepatic adenoma is a benign hepatic neoplasm containing hepatocytes and scattered Kupffer cells but no bile ducts.
It is much more common in females, especially with prolonged oral contraceptive use.
When seen in males, adenoma is never associated with anabolic steroid use.
Beta-catenin mutated adenoma is the least common subtype and has the highest risk of malignant transformation.
options_after: Hepatic adenoma contains bile ducts and therefore is usually positive on HIDA scan.
Hepatic adenoma is a benign hepatic neoplasm containing hepatocytes and scattered Kupffer cells but no bile ducts.
It is much more common in females, especially with prolonged oral contraceptive use.
When seen in males, adenoma is not associated with anabolic steroid use.
Beta-catenin mutated adenoma is the least common subtype and has the highest risk of malignant transformation.
updates.explanation: The source describes adenoma as containing hepatocytes and scattered Kupffer cells but no bile ducts, making HIDA useful for distinction from FNH. It is more common in women, particularly with prolonged oral contraceptive use, while male cases may be associated with anabolic steroids. The beta-catenin subtype is least common, occurs in men on anabolic steroids, and has the highest malignant transformation risk. The inflammatory subtype is the most common and has the highest bleeding risk.

updates.question_text: Regarding biliary cystadenoma and cystadenocarcinoma, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Biliary cystadenoma is a solid hypervascular tumour supplied by the portal vein.
Biliary cystadenoma and cystadenocarcinoma are easily differentiated on imaging by lack of septations in carcinoma.
Biliary cystadenoma is left untreated because malignant transformation cannot occur.
These lesions typically appear as multiseptated cystic masses on all imaging modalities.
Mural nodules should raise suspicion for malignant transformation to cystadenocarcinoma.
options_after: Biliary cystadenoma is a solid hypervascular tumour supplied by the portal vein.
Biliary cystadenoma and cystadenocarcinoma are easily differentiated on imaging by lack of septations in carcinoma.
Biliary cystadenoma is left untreated because malignant transformation will not occur.
These lesions typically appear as multiseptated cystic masses on all imaging modalities.
Mural nodules should raise suspicion for malignant transformation to cystadenocarcinoma.
updates.explanation: Biliary cystadenoma is a benign cystic mass lined with biliary-type epithelium, but most are surgically resected because malignant transformation to cystadenocarcinoma can occur. They typically appear as multiseptated cystic masses. Cystadenoma and cystadenocarcinoma are not easily differentiated on imaging, and mural nodules are suspicious for malignant transformation. This content is flagged for fuller discussion in the biliary neoplasia section.

updates.question_text: Regarding viral hepatitis imaging, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: The most common imaging finding is a large ring-enhancing liver abscess.
When abnormal, imaging may show periportal oedema with a starry-sky ultrasound pattern and gallbladder wall thickening or oedema.
Hepatitis B and C never cause chronic disease.
The typical CT finding is peripheral discontinuous nodular enhancement matching the aorta.
Viral hepatitis is usually caused by portal venous spread from diverticulitis.
options_after: The most common imaging finding is a large ring-enhancing liver abscess.
When abnormal, imaging may show periportal oedema with a starry-sky ultrasound pattern and gallbladder wall thickening or oedema.
Hepatitis B and C will not cause chronic disease.
The typical CT finding is peripheral discontinuous nodular enhancement matching the aorta.
Viral hepatitis is usually caused by portal venous spread from diverticulitis.
updates.explanation: The source states that the most common imaging finding in viral hepatitis is a normal liver. When abnormal, findings include periportal oedema, producing a starry-sky pattern on ultrasound or fluid around portal veins on CT/MRI, and gallbladder wall thickening or oedema. Hepatitis B and C can cause chronic disease. Ring-enhancing abscess is covered under pyogenic abscess, not uncomplicated viral hepatitis.

updates.question_text: Regarding pyogenic hepatic abscess, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Pyogenic abscess is most commonly caused by inhaled pentamidine therapy.
The most common causative organism listed is Pneumocystis jiroveci.
Common source processes include diverticulitis, appendicitis, Crohn's disease, and bowel surgery, with infectious nidus carried through the portal system.
Abscess never mimics metastasis because it lacks ring enhancement.
MRI typically shows central T2 hyperintensity and restricted diffusion, and CT/MRI may show ring enhancement with reactive perilesional hyperenhancement.
options_after: Pyogenic abscess is most commonly caused by inhaled pentamidine therapy.
The most common causative organism listed is Pneumocystis jiroveci.
Common source processes include diverticulitis, appendicitis, Crohn's disease, and bowel surgery, with infectious nidus carried through the portal system.
Abscess will not mimic metastasis because it lacks ring enhancement.
MRI typically shows central T2 hyperintensity and restricted diffusion, and CT/MRI may show ring enhancement with reactive perilesional hyperenhancement.
updates.explanation: The source links hepatic abscess to bowel processes with portal venous spread, including diverticulitis, appendicitis, Crohn's disease, and bowel surgery; E. coli is the commonest causative organism listed. Abscess can mimic metastasis by appearing as a ring-enhancing mass, sometimes with reactive perilesional hyperenhancement. MRI typically shows central T2 hyperintensity and restricted diffusion. Inhaled pentamidine relates to disseminated Pneumocystis risk, not ordinary pyogenic abscess.

updates.question_text: Regarding multicystic liver disease and common liver lesion patterns, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: Biliary hamartomas communicate freely with the biliary tree and are usually larger than simple cysts.
Autosomal dominant polycystic liver disease commonly causes hepatic failure even in severe cystic disease.
VHL-associated liver disease is characterised only by calcified metastases.
Caroli disease is listed under fat-containing hepatic lesions.
Multicystic liver disease patterns include multiple simple cysts or biliary hamartomas, Caroli disease, ADPLD associated with ADPKD, and VHL.
options_after: Biliary hamartomas communicate freely with the biliary tree and are usually larger than simple cysts.
Autosomal dominant polycystic liver disease commonly causes hepatic failure even in severe cystic disease.
VHL-associated liver disease is characterised primarily by calcified metastases.
Caroli disease is listed under fat-containing hepatic lesions.
Multicystic liver disease patterns include multiple simple cysts or biliary hamartomas, Caroli disease, ADPLD associated with ADPKD, and VHL.
updates.explanation: The pattern table lists multicystic liver causes as multiple simple cysts or biliary hamartomas, Caroli disease, ADPLD associated with ADPKD, and VHL. Biliary hamartomas are small benign cystic lesions that do not communicate with the biliary tree and are caused by embryologic bile duct formation failure. In ADPLD, hepatic failure is rare even in severe disease. VHL may have innumerable simple liver cysts, not only calcified metastases.

updates.question_text: Regarding liver transplantation candidates and post-transplant complications, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The Milan criteria allow any number of tumours if none has extrahepatic spread.
For transplant consideration, Milan criteria include a single tumour under 5 cm or up to three tumours each under 3 cm.
No extrahepatic involvement and no major vascular involvement are required by the Milan criteria.
Hepatic artery thrombosis is the most common vascular complication after liver transplantation.
Ductal stricture is the most common biliary complication after liver transplantation.
options_after: The Milan criteria allow any number of tumours provided extrahepatic spread is absent.
For transplant consideration, Milan criteria include a single tumour under 5 cm or up to three tumours each under 3 cm.
No extrahepatic involvement and no major vascular involvement are required by the Milan criteria.
Hepatic artery thrombosis is the most common vascular complication after liver transplantation.
Ductal stricture is the most common biliary complication after liver transplantation.
updates.explanation: The source lists Milan criteria for orthotopic liver transplantation as either one tumour smaller than 5 cm or up to three tumours each smaller than 3 cm, with no extrahepatic involvement and no major vascular involvement. Normal early postoperative findings can include periportal oedema, minimal ascites, right pleural effusion, and small perihepatic haematoma. Hepatic artery thrombosis is the commonest vascular complication and ductal stricture is the commonest biliary complication.

updates.question_text: Regarding PTLD after transplantation, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: PTLD is a type of lymphoma caused by Epstein-Barr virus.
PTLD is limited to the transplanted liver and cannot arise elsewhere.
PTLD has a specific imaging appearance that reliably distinguishes it from other liver masses.
Patients with renal transplants are at particular risk.
Treatment is reduction or withdrawal of immunosuppression.
options_after: PTLD is a type of lymphoma caused by Epstein-Barr virus.
PTLD is limited to the transplanted liver and will not arise elsewhere.
PTLD has a specific imaging appearance that reliably distinguishes it from other liver masses.
Patients with renal transplants are at particular risk.
Treatment is reduction or withdrawal of immunosuppression.
updates.explanation: The source defines PTLD as an Epstein-Barr virus-related lymphoma after solid organ or bone marrow transplantation. It may occur anywhere regardless of the organ transplanted, and its imaging appearance is variable and nonspecific. Renal transplant patients are noted as particularly at risk. Treatment is reduction or withdrawal of immunosuppression.

updates.question_text: Regarding intraparenchymal imaging features of Budd-Chiari syndrome, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The caudate lobe is the first region infarcted because it drains only through the hepatic veins.
Acute findings include an oedematous mottled nutmeg liver.
The caudate lobe is often spared because it drains directly into the IVC.
Flip-flop enhancement may occur, with early central enhancement and delayed peripheral enhancement.
Chronic disease is marked by absence of regenerative nodules and preserved peripheral liver volume.
options_after: The caudate lobe is the first region infarcted because it drains primarily through the hepatic veins.
Acute findings include an oedematous mottled nutmeg liver.
The caudate lobe is often spared because it drains directly into the IVC.
Flip-flop enhancement may occur, with early central enhancement and delayed peripheral enhancement.
Chronic disease is marked by absence of regenerative nodules and preserved peripheral liver volume.
updates.explanation: Acute Budd-Chiari can produce an oedematous mottled nutmeg liver with caudate sparing. The caudate is spared because it drains directly into the IVC rather than through the hepatic veins. Flip-flop enhancement is described as early central enhancement and delayed peripheral enhancement. Chronic findings include progressive liver failure, caudate hypertrophy, peripheral atrophy, and regenerative nodules.

updates.question_text: Regarding normal hepatic Doppler findings, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Normal hepatic artery flow is hepatofugal and should be below the baseline.
A typical hepatic artery resistive index is 0.20-0.35.
The normal hepatic artery waveform is pulsatile and hepatopedal, with typical RI 0.55-0.7.
Normal portal venous flow is hepatopedal and gently phasic, with velocity 16-40 cm/sec.
The normal portal vein should have no undulation and no measurable velocity.
options_after: Normal hepatic artery flow is hepatofugal and should be below the baseline.
A typical hepatic artery resistive index is 0.20-0.35.
The normal hepatic artery waveform is pulsatile and hepatopedal, with typical RI 0.55-0.7.
Normal portal venous flow is hepatopedal and gently phasic, with velocity 16-40 cm/sec.
Normal portal venous flow is non-phasic and too slow for reliable velocity measurement.
updates.explanation: Normal hepatic arterial flow is pulsatile and toward the liver, described as hepatopedal. The listed normal hepatic artery resistive index is 0.55-0.7, calculated from systolic and end-diastolic velocities. Normal portal venous flow is above the baseline, hepatopedal, and gently phasic with a velocity range of 16-40 cm/sec. Hepatofugal flow is abnormal in this context.

updates.question_text: Regarding portal vein thrombosis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Portal vein thrombosis is always tumour thrombus and never bland thrombus.
Bland portal vein thrombus may be caused by hypercoagulable states or local inflammation from pancreatitis or hepatitis.
Expansion of the portal vein excludes tumour thrombus.
Colour Doppler flow within portal venous thrombus suggests tumour thrombus.
Long-standing portal vein thrombosis can lead to cavernous transformation with multiple small periportal collateral vessels.
options_after: Portal vein thrombosis is characteristically tumour thrombus and not bland thrombus.
Bland portal vein thrombus may be caused by hypercoagulable states or local inflammation from pancreatitis or hepatitis.
Expansion of the portal vein excludes tumour thrombus.
Colour Doppler flow within portal venous thrombus suggests tumour thrombus.
Long-standing portal vein thrombosis can lead to cavernous transformation with multiple small periportal collateral vessels.
updates.explanation: Portal vein thrombosis may be bland or due to tumour invasion. Bland thrombus can follow hypercoagulability or local inflammation such as pancreatitis or hepatitis. Portal vein expansion can occur with either bland or tumour thrombus, so it does not settle the distinction. Flow inside the thrombus on colour Doppler suggests tumour thrombus, and chronic thrombosis can form cavernous periportal collaterals.

updates.question_text: Regarding secondary imaging findings of portal hypertension, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: A portal vein diameter of 13 mm is the maximal normal diameter in quiet respiration.
Splenomegaly, varices, Gamna-Gandy bodies, and portosystemic shunts are secondary findings.
An isolated portosystemic shunt always proves portal hypertension.
A recanalised paraumbilical vein is diagnostic of portal hypertension.
Splenic vein obstruction from pancreatitis-related thrombosis or neoplasm can produce an isolated shunt.
options_after: A portal vein diameter of 13 mm is the maximal normal diameter in quiet respiration.
Splenomegaly, varices, Gamna-Gandy bodies, and portosystemic shunts are secondary findings.
An isolated portosystemic shunt characteristically proves portal hypertension.
A recanalised paraumbilical vein is diagnostic of portal hypertension.
Splenic vein obstruction from pancreatitis-related thrombosis or neoplasm can produce an isolated shunt.
updates.explanation: Secondary signs of portal hypertension in the source include slow or reversed flow, dilated portal vein, splenomegaly, Gamna-Gandy bodies, varices, and portosystemic shunts. A portal vein diameter of 13 mm is the maximum normal diameter in quiet respiration. An isolated portosystemic shunt is not always from portal hypertension because splenic vein obstruction can produce a shunt. A recanalised paraumbilical vein is diagnostic.

updates.question_text: Regarding normal flow in a patent TIPS, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: Right and left portal vein branches should remain hepatopetal and flow away from the shunt.
The main portal vein should be hepatofugal in a patent TIPS.
Flow within a patent TIPS should be away from the hepatic veins.
Portal veins should show no flow after a patent TIPS is placed.
Flow in the TIPS is toward the hepatic veins, the main portal vein is hepatopetal, and the right and left portal veins are hepatofugal toward the TIPS.
options_after: Right and left portal vein branches should remain hepatopetal and flow away from the shunt.
The main portal vein should be hepatofugal in a patent TIPS.
Flow within a patent TIPS should be away from the hepatic veins.
Portal veins should fail to show flow after a patent TIPS is placed.
Flow in the TIPS is toward the hepatic veins, the main portal vein is hepatopetal, and the right and left portal veins are hepatofugal toward the TIPS.
updates.explanation: A TIPS connects portal venous flow to a systemic hepatic vein. In a patent shunt, flow goes through the TIPS toward the hepatic veins, the main portal vein remains hepatopetal toward the shunt, and the right and left portal veins reverse to hepatofugal flow toward the TIPS. This expected branch flow reversal should not be mistaken for failure.

updates.question_text: Regarding ultrasound surveillance and stenosis criteria for TIPS, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Routine follow-up is performed at 1 month, every 3 months for the first year, then every 6 to 12 months.
Ultrasound is not used for TIPS surveillance because CT is mandatory at every follow-up.
Only complete absence of TIPS flow suggests stenosis.
High intra-TIPS velocity over 190 cm/sec, low intra-TIPS velocity under 90 cm/sec, or velocity change greater than 50 cm/sec from baseline suggests stenosis.
Low main portal vein velocity under 30 cm/sec excludes TIPS stenosis.
options_after: Routine follow-up is performed at 1 month, every 3 months for the first year, then every 6 to 12 months.
Ultrasound is not used for TIPS surveillance because CT is mandatory at most follow-ups.
A low shunt velocity below 90 cm/sec is required before Doppler can suggest stenosis.
High intra-TIPS velocity over 190 cm/sec, low intra-TIPS velocity under 90 cm/sec, or velocity change greater than 50 cm/sec from baseline suggests stenosis.
Low main portal vein velocity under 30 cm/sec excludes TIPS stenosis.
updates.explanation: The source describes ultrasound surveillance starting with a post-procedure baseline, then 1 month, every 3 months for the first year, and every 6 to 12 months thereafter. Stenosis can be suggested by high intra-TIPS velocity over 190 cm/sec, low intra-TIPS velocity under 90 cm/sec, a change greater than 50 cm/sec from baseline, or low main portal vein velocity under 30 cm/sec. Complete absence of flow is instead compatible with occlusion.

updates.question_text: Regarding TIPS occlusion, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: If the TIPS becomes occluded, the right and left portal veins re-reverse and become hepatopetal.
Colour Doppler may show complete absence of flow within the TIPS.
A patent TIPS is diagnosed when there is no blood flow through the shunt.
The main portal vein remains hepatopetal toward the occluded TIPS.
Re-reversal of right and left portal venous branches means they now flow away from the TIPS.
options_after: If the TIPS becomes occluded, the right and left portal veins re-reverse and become hepatopetal.
Colour Doppler may show complete absence of flow within the TIPS.
A patent TIPS is diagnosed when there is an absence of blood flow through the shunt.
The main portal vein remains hepatopetal toward the occluded TIPS.
Re-reversal of right and left portal venous branches means they now flow away from the TIPS.
updates.explanation: In occlusion, no blood flows through the TIPS and Doppler may show complete absence of shunt flow. The right and left portal veins re-reverse from their patent-shunt hepatofugal direction and become hepatopetal, which in the source diagram means flowing away from the TIPS. The main portal vein remains hepatopetal toward the occluded shunt. A patent TIPS should have demonstrable flow through the shunt.

updates.question_text: Regarding increased hepatic vein pulsatility, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Increased hepatic vein pulsatility is caused by right-sided cardiac abnormality such as right-sided heart failure or tricuspid regurgitation.
Both right-sided heart failure and tricuspid regurgitation show accentuated A- and V-waves from increased retrograde flow during atrial systole.
Tricuspid regurgitation produces less or even reversed antegrade S-wave flow during ventricular systole.
Right-sided heart failure and tricuspid regurgitation are distinguished by absent A- and V-waves.
Right-sided heart failure always abolishes the S-wave because the tricuspid valve is incompetent.
options_after: Increased hepatic vein pulsatility is caused by right-sided cardiac abnormality such as right-sided heart failure or tricuspid regurgitation.
Both right-sided heart failure and tricuspid regurgitation show accentuated A- and V-waves from increased retrograde flow during atrial systole.
Tricuspid regurgitation produces less or even reversed antegrade S-wave flow during ventricular systole.
Right-sided heart failure and tricuspid regurgitation are distinguished by absent A- and V-waves.
Right-sided heart failure characteristically abolishes the S-wave because the tricuspid valve is incompetent.
updates.explanation: The source links increased hepatic vein pulsatility to right-sided heart failure or tricuspid regurgitation. Both have accentuated A- and V-waves due to increased right-sided pressures and retrograde flow during atrial systole. In tricuspid regurgitation, the S-wave is reduced or can become retrograde because the valve is incompetent during ventricular systole. In right-sided heart failure, the S-wave is preserved because the tricuspid valve remains competent.

updates.question_text: Regarding the Doppler implication of hepatofugal portal venous flow, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: It is normal portal venous flow toward the liver.
It is expected in the main portal vein of an occluded TIPS and excludes portal hypertension.
It means flow away from the liver and, when caused by portal hypertension, reflects reversal once portal venous pressure exceeds forward pressure.
It is the normal hepatic arterial direction in all patients.
It proves hepatic artery thrombosis after liver transplant.
options_after: It is normal portal venous flow toward the liver.
It is expected in the main portal vein of an occluded TIPS and excludes portal hypertension.
It means flow away from the liver and, when caused by portal hypertension, reflects reversal once portal venous pressure exceeds forward pressure.
It is the normal hepatic arterial direction in most patients.
It proves hepatic artery thrombosis after liver transplant.
updates.explanation: The source defines hepatofugal flow as flow away from the liver. In portal hypertension, flow may slow below 16 cm/sec or reverse once portal pressure exceeds forward pressure, and reversal is diagnostic. The main portal vein remains hepatopetal in the TIPS diagrams. Hepatic arterial flow is normally hepatopedal, and hepatic artery thrombosis after transplant is a separate vascular complication.

updates.question_text: Regarding biliary anatomic variants, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: An aberrant right posterior duct is clinically important only for left-lobe liver donors.
Low insertion of the cystic duct can lead the surgeon to misidentify the common duct as the cystic duct during cholecystectomy.
A long common channel is pancreaticobiliary maljunction, with CBD and pancreatic duct union outside the duodenal wall over 15 mm.
A long common channel may be associated with choledochal cyst, bile duct stricture, and increased biliary cancer risk.
An aberrant right posterior duct means the cystic duct runs parallel with the common hepatic duct and contains an impacted stone.
options_after: An aberrant right posterior duct is clinically important primarily for left-lobe liver donors.
Low insertion of the cystic duct can lead the surgeon to misidentify the common duct as the cystic duct during cholecystectomy.
A long common channel is pancreaticobiliary maljunction, with CBD and pancreatic duct union outside the duodenal wall over 15 mm.
A long common channel may be associated with choledochal cyst, bile duct stricture, and increased biliary cancer risk.
An aberrant right posterior duct means the cystic duct runs parallel with the common hepatic duct and contains an impacted stone.
updates.explanation: Low cystic duct insertion can cause surgical misidentification, risking inadvertent common duct ligation. A long common channel is pancreaticobiliary maljunction, with ductal union outside the duodenal wall over 15 mm, and may be linked to choledochal cyst, stricture, and biliary malignancy risk. An aberrant right posterior duct matters for right hepatic lobe donors because two right hepatic ducts need separate recipient anastomoses. A parallel cystic duct with an impacted stone belongs to Mirizzi syndrome.

updates.question_text: Regarding complicated and acalculous cholecystitis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Acalculous cholecystitis requires an obstructing gallstone impacted in the cystic duct.
Acalculous cholecystitis is typically seen in very sick patients, such as ICU patients, and is linked to bile stasis and hypoperfusion.
Emphysematous cholecystitis is caused by non-gas-forming bacteria and has no association with diabetes.
Gas in the gallbladder lumen or wall supports emphysematous cholecystitis.
Gangrenous cholecystitis can show asymmetric wall thickening or intraluminal membranes and has high perforation risk.
options_after: Acalculous cholecystitis requires an obstructing gallstone impacted in the cystic duct.
Acalculous cholecystitis is typically seen in very sick patients, such as ICU patients, and is linked to bile stasis and hypoperfusion.
Emphysematous cholecystitis is caused by non-gas-forming bacteria and lacks association with diabetes.
Gas in the gallbladder lumen or wall supports emphysematous cholecystitis.
Gangrenous cholecystitis can show asymmetric wall thickening or intraluminal membranes and has high perforation risk.
updates.explanation: Acalculous cholecystitis occurs without gallstones and is seen in very sick patients, with sepsis, prolonged TPN, and trauma listed as risk factors. Emphysematous cholecystitis is a severe gas-forming bacterial complication, especially in elderly diabetic patients, with gas in the lumen or wall. Gangrenous cholecystitis results from pressure-related ischaemia and necrosis, may show asymmetric wall thickening or membranes, and has high perforation risk.

updates.question_text: Regarding gallbladder polyps, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Most gallbladder polyps are premalignant adenomas.
Gallbladder polyps are usually incidental and asymptomatic but may cause right upper quadrant pain or cholecystitis if they obstruct the cystic duct.
Malignancy risk features include size over 10 mm or rapid growth, solitary lesion, sessile morphology, stones, primary sclerosing cholangitis, and age 60 or greater.
Typical ultrasound appearance is a mobile shadowing lesion that layers dependently after repositioning.
Adherent sludge is excluded if there is no vascular flow.
options_after: Most gallbladder polyps are premalignant adenomas.
Gallbladder polyps are usually incidental and asymptomatic but may cause right upper quadrant pain or cholecystitis if they obstruct the cystic duct.
Malignancy risk features include size over 10 mm or rapid growth, solitary lesion, sessile morphology, stones, primary sclerosing cholangitis, and age 60 or greater.
Typical ultrasound appearance is a mobile shadowing lesion that layers dependently after repositioning.
Adherent sludge is excluded if there is an absence of vascular flow.
updates.explanation: Most gallbladder polyps are benign cholesterol polyps; premalignant adenomas are rare, under 5%. The six S risk features are size or rapid growth, single, sessile, stones, primary sclerosing cholangitis, and sixty or older. Typical ultrasound shows a non-mobile, non-shadowing polypoid or sessile wall lesion, sometimes with stalk flow. Adherent sludge is a key differential and lacks vascular flow, so absence of flow does not exclude sludge.

updates.question_text: Regarding MRCP technique, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: MRCP is based on heavily T1-weighted imaging of enhancing bile.
Intermediate T2-weighting is avoided because it cannot show surrounding tissues.
MRCP uses heavily T2-weighted sequences to increase contrast between T2-hyperintense stationary biliary fluid and surrounding structures.
MRCP requires sedation and is more invasive than ERCP.
MRCP is only useful after biliary contrast agents are excreted at 1 hour.
options_after: MRCP is based on heavily T1-weighted imaging of enhancing bile.
Intermediate T2-weighting is avoided because it will not show surrounding tissues.
MRCP uses heavily T2-weighted sequences to increase contrast between T2-hyperintense stationary biliary fluid and surrounding structures.
MRCP requires sedation and is more invasive than ERCP.
MRCP is primarily useful after biliary contrast agents are excreted at 1 hour.
updates.explanation: MRCP uses specific abdominal MRI sequences, especially heavily T2-weighted sequences, to make stationary biliary fluid bright relative to adjacent structures. Intermediate T2 weighting with TE 80-100 ms can help visualise ducts and surrounding tissue. MRCP is non-invasive, avoids sedation, and can show surrounding anatomy. Contrast-enhanced MRCP with biliary-excreted agents such as Eovist is a separate approach requiring at least a 20-minute delay.

updates.question_text: Regarding choledochal cysts and the Todani classification, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Choledochal cysts represent intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation and are classified by number, distribution, and morphology.
They communicate with the biliary tree, unlike biliary hamartomas.
They are often resected because cholangiocarcinoma risk may be as high as 25%.
They are always diagnosed only in adults and never in childhood.
Type I is fusiform dilatation of the common bile duct and is the most common extrahepatic cyst.
options_after: Choledochal cysts represent intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation and are classified by number, distribution, and morphology.
They communicate with the biliary tree, unlike biliary hamartomas.
They are often resected because cholangiocarcinoma risk may be as high as 25%.
They are characteristically diagnosed primarily in adults and not in childhood.
Type I is fusiform dilatation of the common bile duct and is the most common extrahepatic cyst.
updates.explanation: Choledochal cysts are a heterogeneous group with a common endpoint of intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation, divided by Todani type I-V. They communicate with the biliary tree, unlike biliary hamartomas, and are often resected because cholangiocarcinoma risk can be up to 25%. Most are diagnosed in childhood, but adult diagnosis can occur. Type I is fusiform CBD dilatation and is the commonest extrahepatic type.

updates.question_text: Regarding Todani choledochal cyst types, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Type I is intraduodenal bile duct dilatation.
Type III is fusiform common bile duct dilatation.
Type V is extrahepatic-only dilatation and is never called Caroli disease.
Type IV involves multiple dilated segments, with type IVA involving intra- and extrahepatic dilatation and type IVB extrahepatic-only dilatation.
Type V is intrahepatic dilatation, corresponding to Caroli disease.
options_after: Type I is intraduodenal bile duct dilatation.
Type III is fusiform common bile duct dilatation.
Type V is extrahepatic-predominant dilatation and is not called Caroli disease.
Type IV involves multiple dilated segments, with type IVA involving intra- and extrahepatic dilatation and type IVB extrahepatic-only dilatation.
Type V is intrahepatic dilatation, corresponding to Caroli disease.
updates.explanation: The source diagram defines type I as fusiform common bile duct dilatation, type II as extrahepatic saccular dilatation, type III as intraduodenal bile duct dilatation, type IV as multiple dilated segments, and type V as intrahepatic dilatation or Caroli disease. Type IVA includes intra- and extrahepatic duct dilatation, while type IVB is extrahepatic only.

updates.question_text: Regarding choledocholithiasis, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: It is a stone in the cystic duct causing external compression of the common hepatic duct.
It is a stone in the common bile duct and is generally treated with ERCP.
It is treated primarily with percutaneous cholecystostomy as definitive therapy.
Patients are never symptomatic because common bile duct stones do not obstruct bile outflow.
It causes isolated gallbladder wall comet-tail artefact without biliary duct dilatation.
options_after: It is a stone in the cystic duct causing external compression of the common hepatic duct.
It is a stone in the common bile duct and is generally treated with ERCP.
It is treated primarily with percutaneous cholecystostomy as definitive therapy.
Patients are not symptomatic because common bile duct stones do not obstruct bile outflow.
It causes isolated gallbladder wall comet-tail artefact without biliary duct dilatation.
updates.explanation: Choledocholithiasis is defined as a stone in the common bile duct, generally treated with ERCP. Patients may be asymptomatic but more often present with right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, and a cholestatic LFT pattern from obstructed bile outflow. A cystic duct stone compressing the common hepatic duct describes Mirizzi syndrome. Comet-tail artefact in the gallbladder wall is adenomyomatosis.

updates.question_text: Regarding Mirizzi syndrome, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Mirizzi syndrome is caused by gas-forming bacteria within the gallbladder wall.
The cystic duct usually drains directly into the duodenum in Mirizzi syndrome.
Mirizzi syndrome is inflammation and external compression of the common hepatic duct caused by a stone in the adjacent cystic duct.
It is important preoperatively because the common hepatic duct may be mistakenly ligated instead of the cystic duct.
Mirizzi syndrome excludes biliary obstruction because the common hepatic duct is always normal calibre.
options_after: Mirizzi syndrome is caused by gas-forming bacteria within the gallbladder wall.
The cystic duct usually drains directly into the duodenum in Mirizzi syndrome.
Mirizzi syndrome is inflammation and external compression of the common hepatic duct caused by a stone in the adjacent cystic duct.
It is important preoperatively because the common hepatic duct may be mistakenly ligated instead of the cystic duct.
Mirizzi syndrome excludes biliary obstruction because the common hepatic duct is characteristically normal calibre.
updates.explanation: Mirizzi syndrome is due to inflammation and external compression of the common hepatic duct by a stone in the adjacent cystic duct. The surgeon needs to know this preoperatively because the common hepatic duct may be mistaken for and ligated as the cystic duct. Inflammation may also lead to erosion and cholecystocholedochal fistula with biliary obstruction. On ultrasound, a distal cystic duct stone and common hepatic duct dilatation are expected.

updates.question_text: Regarding gallbladder polyp risk stratification and management, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Cholecystectomy should be considered when a polyp over 10 mm has several high-risk features.
Ultrasound has limited sensitivity and specificity for small polyps under 10 mm, especially with gallstones.
Benign cholesterol polyps tend to be solitary and sessile.
Primary sclerosing cholangitis is one of the risk features for malignancy.
All gallbladder polyps under 10 mm are malignant if they are pedunculated.
options_after: Cholecystectomy should be considered when a polyp over 10 mm has several high-risk features.
Ultrasound has limited sensitivity and specificity for small polyps under 10 mm, especially with gallstones.
Benign cholesterol polyps tend to be solitary and sessile.
Primary sclerosing cholangitis is one of the risk features for malignancy.
Most gallbladder polyps under 10 mm are malignant if they are pedunculated.
updates.explanation: The source lists high-risk features using the six S framework and recommends considering cholecystectomy when several are present in a polyp greater than 10 mm. Ultrasound has limited accuracy for small polyps, especially with gallstones. PSC is one of the high-risk features. Benign cholesterol polyps tend to be multiple and polyps are more likely benign if pedunculated, while solitary sessile morphology is more suspicious.

updates.question_text: Regarding acute cholecystitis complications and treatment choices, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Complications include emphysematous cholecystitis, gangrenous cholecystitis, and gallbladder perforation.
Acalculous cholecystitis is often definitively treated with percutaneous cholecystostomy.
Uncomplicated acute calculous cholecystitis is definitively treated with long-term cholecystostomy alone in all patients.
Gangrenous cholecystitis treatment is observation because perforation risk is low.
Emphysematous cholecystitis is most often treated with emergent cholecystectomy or cholecystostomy in very high surgical risk patients.
options_after: Complications include emphysematous cholecystitis, gangrenous cholecystitis, and gallbladder perforation.
Acalculous cholecystitis is often definitively treated with percutaneous cholecystostomy.
Uncomplicated acute calculous cholecystitis is definitively treated with long-term cholecystostomy alone in most patients.
Gangrenous cholecystitis treatment is observation because perforation risk is low.
Emphysematous cholecystitis is most often treated with emergent cholecystectomy or cholecystostomy in very high surgical risk patients.
updates.explanation: The source lists emphysematous cholecystitis, gangrenous cholecystitis, and perforation as rare but serious complications. Uncomplicated acute calculous cholecystitis is treated with cholecystectomy, while cholecystostomy can temporise poor surgical candidates. Acalculous cholecystitis is often definitively managed with percutaneous cholecystostomy. Gangrenous disease and emphysematous disease require urgent treatment rather than observation.

updates.question_text: Regarding ascending cholangitis, which imaging statement is correct?
options_before: Imaging is always abnormal when the clinical triad is present
The most common cause is primary sclerosing cholangitis
The key imaging abnormality is mural calcification of the common bile duct
When abnormal, imaging may show bile duct wall thickening and hyperenhancement, with intraluminal debris or choledocholithiasis
The characteristic imaging feature is diffuse pancreatic atrophy
options_after: Imaging is characteristically abnormal when the clinical triad is present
The most common cause is primary sclerosing cholangitis
The key imaging abnormality is mural calcification of the common bile duct
When abnormal, imaging may show bile duct wall thickening and hyperenhancement, with intraluminal debris or choledocholithiasis
The characteristic imaging feature is diffuse pancreatic atrophy
updates.explanation: Ascending cholangitis is usually due to biliary obstruction, most commonly choledocholithiasis, and may present with Charcot's triad of fever, abdominal pain and jaundice. Imaging can be completely normal. When abnormal, the key features are hyperenhancement and thickening of the bile duct walls, often with intraluminal debris or choledocholithiasis. Diffuse pancreatic atrophy belongs to other pancreatic processes, not ascending cholangitis.

updates.question_text: Regarding biliary cystadenoma and cystadenocarcinoma, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Biliary cystadenoma has no malignant potential and therefore never requires resection
Malignant degeneration to biliary cystadenocarcinoma occurs in up to 15% of patients
Frank invasion into adjacent liver should raise concern for cystadenocarcinoma
A large solid component should raise concern for cystadenocarcinoma
Thick calcification should raise concern for cystadenocarcinoma
options_after: Biliary cystadenoma lacks malignant potential and therefore will not require resection
Malignant degeneration to biliary cystadenocarcinoma occurs in up to 15% of patients
Frank invasion into adjacent liver should raise concern for cystadenocarcinoma
A large solid component should raise concern for cystadenocarcinoma
Thick calcification should raise concern for cystadenocarcinoma
updates.explanation: The source states that resection is often pursued because biliary cystadenoma can undergo malignant degeneration to cystadenocarcinoma in up to 15% of patients. Imaging features raising concern for cystadenocarcinoma include frank invasion into adjacent liver, a large solid component or thick calcification. Therefore the claim that cystadenoma has no malignant potential is incorrect.

updates.question_text: Regarding primary gallbladder carcinoma, which statement is correct?
options_before: It most commonly presents as a purely intraductal biliary tumour
It has an excellent prognosis in most patients
It most commonly presents as a scirrhous infiltrating mass invading through the gallbladder wall into the liver
It usually spreads only through the pancreatic duct
It is commonly a benign mimic of a hypervascular pancreatic neoplasm
options_after: It most commonly presents as a purely intraductal biliary tumour
It has an excellent prognosis in most patients
It most commonly presents as a scirrhous infiltrating mass invading through the gallbladder wall into the liver
It usually spreads primarily through the pancreatic duct
It is commonly a benign mimic of a hypervascular pancreatic neoplasm
updates.explanation: Gallbladder carcinoma is rare and has a poor prognosis. The commonest pattern is a scirrhous infiltrating mass invading through the gallbladder wall into the liver. Less commonly it can present as a polypoid mass, and very rarely as focal mural thickening. Spread is by direct extension into liver, with lymphatic and haematogenous metastases also common.

updates.question_text: Regarding inflammatory biliary diseases and their complications, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Primary biliary cirrhosis usually affects middle-aged women and often presents with pruritus
Primary biliary cirrhosis primarily destroys the pancreatic ducts
Primary sclerosing cholangitis can lead to cirrhosis with prominent caudate lobe hypertrophy
AIDS cholangiopathy is more commonly associated with papillary stenosis than primary sclerosing cholangitis
Primary biliary cirrhosis has no relationship to cirrhosis
options_after: Primary biliary cirrhosis usually affects middle-aged women and often presents with pruritus
Primary biliary cirrhosis primarily destroys the pancreatic ducts
Primary sclerosing cholangitis can lead to cirrhosis with prominent caudate lobe hypertrophy
AIDS cholangiopathy is more commonly associated with papillary stenosis than primary sclerosing cholangitis
Primary biliary cirrhosis lacks relationship to cirrhosis
updates.explanation: Primary biliary cirrhosis is inflammation and destruction of smaller bile ducts and usually affects middle-aged women with pruritus. Chronic primary biliary cirrhosis and primary sclerosing cholangitis can both lead to hepatic cirrhosis, often with prominent caudate lobe hypertrophy. AIDS cholangiopathy can mimic primary sclerosing cholangitis, but papillary stenosis is emphasised as a distinguishing feature.

updates.question_text: Regarding normal pancreatic ductal anatomy, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The main pancreatic duct drains to the major papilla through the duct of Wirsung
The common bile duct normally drains to the minor papilla
The duct of Santorini drains to the minor papilla
The dorsal pancreatic duct normally drains the pancreatic head only
The common bile duct drains to the major papilla where it meets the duct of Wirsung
options_after: The main pancreatic duct drains to the major papilla through the duct of Wirsung
The common bile duct normally drains to the minor papilla
The duct of Santorini drains to the minor papilla
The dorsal pancreatic duct normally drains the pancreatic head in typical cases
The common bile duct drains to the major papilla where it meets the duct of Wirsung
updates.explanation: Normal anatomy has the main pancreatic duct draining to the major papilla through the duct of Wirsung, while Santorini drains to the minor papilla. The source states that the common bile duct always drains to the major papilla where it meets the duct of Wirsung. The dorsal pancreatic duct always drains the pancreatic tail, not just the head. Santorini is remembered as superior and draining to the small, or minor, papilla.

updates.question_text: Regarding CT technique in acute pancreatitis, which statement is correct?
options_before: CT is always indicated in clinically mild acute pancreatitis that is improving
Portal venous phase alone is the optimal phase for subtle necrosis
The pancreatic phase is performed at about 40 seconds after contrast injection when the pancreatic parenchyma maximally enhances
Ultrasound is the best modality for evaluating pancreatic necrosis
Subtraction MRI is mainly used to evaluate choledochal cysts
options_after: CT is characteristically indicated in clinically mild acute pancreatitis that is improving
Portal venous phase alone is the optimal phase for subtle necrosis
The pancreatic phase is performed at about 40 seconds after contrast injection when the pancreatic parenchyma maximally enhances
Ultrasound is the best modality for evaluating pancreatic necrosis
Subtraction MRI is mainly used to evaluate choledochal cysts
updates.explanation: Pancreatitis CT is ideally performed in the pancreatic phase, a late arterial phase at approximately 40 seconds after contrast injection, when pancreatic parenchymal enhancement is maximal. This phase is optimal for detecting subtle decreased enhancement suggesting necrosis. CT is not indicated for improving mild clinical pancreatitis. Ultrasound is useful initially for gallstones, choledocholithiasis or biliary obstruction, but has limited utility for necrosis and fluid collections.

updates.question_text: Regarding autoimmune pancreatitis and immunotherapy-related pancreatic change, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Autoimmune pancreatitis is the pancreatic manifestation of IgG4-related sclerosing disease
The typical appearance is a beaded distal pancreatic duct with diffuse pancreatic calcifications
Treatment of autoimmune pancreatitis is surgical resection because steroid response is not expected
Immunotherapy can lead to episodes of pancreatitis and pancreatic atrophy
Autoimmune pancreatitis cannot be focal or multifocal
options_after: Autoimmune pancreatitis is the pancreatic manifestation of IgG4-related sclerosing disease
The typical appearance is a beaded distal pancreatic duct with diffuse pancreatic calcifications
Treatment of autoimmune pancreatitis is surgical resection because steroid response is not expected
Immunotherapy can lead to episodes of pancreatitis and pancreatic atrophy
Autoimmune pancreatitis will not be focal or multifocal
updates.explanation: Autoimmune pancreatitis is described as the pancreatic manifestation of IgG4-related sclerosing disease. The typical imaging appearance is diffuse sausage-like pancreatic enlargement with loss of lobulation and sometimes a capsule-like rim, but it can also be focal or multifocal and mimic a mass. Steroid treatment can lead to complete resolution. Immunotherapy may cause clinically occult pancreatitis episodes and pancreatic atrophy.

updates.question_text: Regarding pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma resectability assessment, which statement is correct?
options_before: Limited extension to the duodenum always precludes resection
Abutment is defined as more than 180 degrees circumferential contact with a vessel
The splenic artery is not relevant to resectability assessment
Encasement is defined as more than 180 degrees circumferential contact and/or deformation of the vessel
Vascular variants are not relevant if the tumour is in the pancreatic head
options_after: Limited extension to the duodenum characteristically precludes resection
Abutment is defined as more than 180 degrees circumferential contact with a vessel
The splenic artery is not relevant to resectability assessment
Encasement is defined as more than 180 degrees circumferential contact and/or deformation of the vessel
Vascular variants are not relevant if the tumour is in the pancreatic head
updates.explanation: For pancreatic neoplasm resectability, the source emphasises assessment of vascular variants and tumour involvement of the SMA, SMV, portal vein, celiac axis, common hepatic artery and splenic artery. Abutment means less than 180 degrees circumferential contact, while encasement means more than 180 degrees contact and/or vessel deformation. Limited extension to the duodenum, distal stomach or common bile duct does not preclude resection because these are removed during a Whipple procedure.

updates.question_text: Regarding acinar cell carcinoma and solid pseudopapillary tumour, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Acinar cell carcinoma is a rare aggressive variant of pancreatic adenocarcinoma seen in elderly males
Lipase hypersecretion syndrome includes subcutaneous fat necrosis, bone infarcts causing polyarthralgias and eosinophilia
Solid pseudopapillary tumour occurs in young women and children and is nicknamed the daughter tumour
Solid pseudopapillary tumour has no capsule
Solid pseudopapillary tumour typically undergoes resection despite low malignant potential
options_after: Acinar cell carcinoma is a rare aggressive variant of pancreatic adenocarcinoma seen in elderly males
Lipase hypersecretion syndrome includes subcutaneous fat necrosis, bone infarcts causing polyarthralgias and eosinophilia
Solid pseudopapillary tumour occurs in young women and children and is nicknamed the daughter tumour
A complete fibrous capsule is atypical of a solid pseudopapillary tumour.
Solid pseudopapillary tumour typically undergoes resection despite low malignant potential
updates.explanation: Acinar cell carcinoma is rare, aggressive and described as occurring exclusively in elderly males. Its lipase hypersecretion syndrome comprises subcutaneous fat necrosis, bone infarcts causing polyarthralgias and eosinophilia. Solid pseudopapillary tumour occurs in young women and children, is nicknamed the daughter tumour, and has low malignant potential but is typically resected. The source notes that solid pseudopapillary tumour has a capsule, shared only with mucinous cystic neoplasm among pancreatic tumours.

updates.question_text: Regarding systemic diseases affecting the pancreas, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: T-cell lymphoma is the most common subtype of lymphoma to affect the pancreas
B-cell lymphoma is the most common subtype of lymphoma to affect the pancreas
von Hippel-Lindau is associated only with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma in this source
Pancreatic neoplasms seen in von Hippel-Lindau include serous cystadenoma and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours
Pancreatic lymphoma typically occurs as isolated pancreatic disease without adenopathy
options_after: T-cell lymphoma is the most common subtype of lymphoma to affect the pancreas
B-cell lymphoma is the most common subtype of lymphoma to affect the pancreas
von Hippel-Lindau is associated primarily with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma in this source
Pancreatic neoplasms seen in von Hippel-Lindau include serous cystadenoma and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours
Pancreatic lymphoma typically occurs as isolated pancreatic disease without adenopathy
updates.explanation: The source describes B-cell lymphoma as the most common subtype to affect the pancreas. The typical pancreatic lymphoma appearance is a homogeneously, diffusely enlarged gland without ductal dilatation, with associated lymphadenopathy and usually multiorgan disease; aggressive types may show necrosis. von Hippel-Lindau is a multisystem inherited disease causing cysts in multiple organs and pancreatic neoplasms including serous cystadenoma and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours.

updates.question_text: Regarding wandering spleen, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It is caused by multiple discrete splenic foci in visceral heterotaxia
It is a normal spleen with abnormal laxity or absence of fixed ligamentous attachments
It should always be accompanied by interruption of the IVC
It may present with acute abdominal pain secondary to torsion
It is diagnosed when an accessory spleen is found in the splenic hilum
options_after: It is caused by multiple discrete splenic foci in visceral heterotaxia
It is a normal spleen with abnormal laxity or absence of fixed ligamentous attachments
It should characteristically be accompanied by interruption of the IVC
It may present with acute abdominal pain secondary to torsion
It is diagnosed when an accessory spleen is found in the splenic hilum
updates.explanation: A wandering spleen is anatomically normal splenic tissue with abnormal laxity or absence of its fixed ligamentous attachments. It may be found as an abdominal mass or present acutely with pain from torsion. Polysplenia is the heterotaxy syndrome with multiple splenic foci and venous anomalies. A splenule in the splenic hilum is an accessory spleen, not a wandering spleen.

updates.question_text: Regarding inflammatory splenic lesions, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Splenic sarcoidosis most commonly presents with splenomegaly, often with hepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy
Sarcoid nodules usually show avid enhancement and high signal on all MRI sequences
Sarcoid nodules are most conspicuous on T2-weighted and early post-contrast T1-weighted images
Inflammatory pseudotumour may present as a well-circumscribed heterogeneously enhancing mass
Splenic sarcoidosis is generally easily distinguished from lymphoma on imaging
options_after: Splenic sarcoidosis most commonly presents with splenomegaly, often with hepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy
Sarcoid nodules usually show avid enhancement and high signal on routine MRI sequences
Sarcoid nodules are most conspicuous on T2-weighted and early post-contrast T1-weighted images
Inflammatory pseudotumour may present as a well-circumscribed heterogeneously enhancing mass
Splenic sarcoidosis is generally easily distinguished from lymphoma on imaging
updates.explanation: When sarcoidosis involves the spleen, splenomegaly is the commonest finding and is often associated with hepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy. Less commonly it produces multiple hypoattenuating 1-3 cm lesions that essentially do not enhance; these nodules have low signal on all MRI sequences and are most conspicuous on T2-weighted and early post-contrast T1-weighted imaging. Splenic inflammatory pseudotumour is variable but may appear as a well-circumscribed heterogeneously enhancing mass. Sarcoidosis is generally indistinguishable from splenic lymphoma on imaging.

updates.question_text: Regarding splenic metastases, which statement is correct?
options_before: Splenic metastases are present in most patients with cancer
Isolated splenic metastases account for most metastatic splenic involvement
Calcification is common regardless of the primary tumour type
The most common primary tumours include breast, lung, ovarian and melanoma
Melanoma and ovarian cancer usually produce only calcified solid metastases
options_after: Splenic metastases are present in most patients with cancer
Isolated splenic metastases account for most metastatic splenic involvement
Calcification is common despite variation in the primary tumour type
The most common primary tumours include breast, lung, ovarian and melanoma
Melanoma and ovarian cancer usually produce calcified solid splenic metastases.
updates.explanation: Splenic metastases are rare, occurring in 2-9% of cancer patients, and most patients already have widespread disease. Isolated splenic metastases occur in only 5% of patients with metastatic involvement of the spleen. The common primary tumours listed are breast, lung, ovarian and melanoma. Ovarian cancer and melanoma typically cause cystic metastases, and calcification is rare unless the primary is a mucinous adenocarcinoma.

updates.question_text: Regarding contained vascular injuries after splenic trauma, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Pseudoaneurysm and arteriovenous fistula continue to increase in size on delayed CT like active extravasation
Pseudoaneurysm is caused by injury to the intima and media with rupture contained by the adventitia
Splenic arteriography is the only way to differentiate pseudoaneurysm from traumatic arteriovenous fistula
A traumatic arteriovenous fistula is caused by injury to the splenic capsule only
Pseudoaneurysm has no important rupture risk without treatment
options_after: Pseudoaneurysm and arteriovenous fistula continue to increase in size on delayed CT like active extravasation
Pseudoaneurysm is caused by injury to the intima and media with rupture contained by the adventitia
Splenic arteriography is the only way to differentiate pseudoaneurysm from traumatic arteriovenous fistula
A traumatic arteriovenous fistula is caused by injury to the splenic capsule in typical cases
An untreated splenic pseudoaneurysm has a low rupture risk and can be managed expectantly.
updates.explanation: Pseudoaneurysm and arteriovenous fistula are contained vascular injuries that initially appear as a focal high-attenuation area but do not increase in size on delayed scanning, unlike active extravasation. A pseudoaneurysm is arterial wall injury involving the intima and media, with rupture contained by adventitia, and has a high chance of rupture without treatment. A traumatic arteriovenous fistula is due to injury of an artery and adjacent vein. CT cannot distinguish pseudoaneurysm from arteriovenous fistula; splenic arteriography is required.

updates.question_text: Regarding the 2018 AAST splenic injury scale, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Grade I includes subcapsular haematoma less than 10% of splenic surface
Grade II includes subcapsular haematoma involving 10-50% of splenic surface
Grade III includes only lacerations less than 1 cm deep
Grade IV includes extraparenchymal extension of active bleeding into the peritoneum
When multiple injuries are present, advance one grade up to grade III
options_after: Grade I includes subcapsular haematoma less than 10% of splenic surface
Grade II includes subcapsular haematoma involving 10-50% of splenic surface
Grade III includes primarily lacerations less than 1 cm deep
Grade IV includes extraparenchymal extension of active bleeding into the peritoneum
When multiple injuries are present, advance one grade up to grade III
updates.explanation: The 2018 AAST splenic injury scale incorporates CT, operative and pathologic findings, and the highest-grade assessment is the final grade. Grade I includes subcapsular haematoma less than 10% of surface or superficial laceration less than 1 cm deep. Grade II includes 10-50% subcapsular haematoma, intraparenchymal haematoma less than 5 cm or laceration 1-3 cm deep. Grade V, not grade IV, includes extraparenchymal active bleeding or shattered spleen. Multiple injuries advance one grade up to grade III.

updates.question_text: Regarding reflux oesophagitis and Barrett oesophagus, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Reflux oesophagitis is usually best demonstrated on single-contrast water-soluble swallow
Fluoroscopic findings of reflux oesophagitis are usually distal and include mucosal granularity, thickened folds, erosions and strictures
Barrett oesophagus is a precursor lesion to oesophageal adenocarcinoma
