If the prescribed velocity range is too low, faster flow may be misrepresented as aliasing
It cannot be used to assess regurgitation through a valve
It is unrelated to pressure gradients across cardiac shunts
options_after: It measures blood flow parallel to the imaging plane
Stationary tissue appears white while forward flow appears grey
If the prescribed velocity range is too low, faster flow may be misrepresented as aliasing
It will not be used to assess regurgitation through a valve
It is unrelated to pressure gradients across cardiac shunts
updates.explanation: Velocity-encoded gradient echo imaging measures flow perpendicular to the imaging plane. The source describes forward flow as white, flow in the opposite direction as black and stationary tissue as grey. Signal intensity within a region of interest reflects velocity, allowing assessment of valve regurgitation and pressure gradients across shunts. If the selected VENC is too low, high velocities are misrepresented by aliasing.

updates.question_text: Regarding myocardial tagging, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Myocardial tagging is used only for coronary artery calcium quantification
It can assess myocardial wall motion and strain
Grid tags deform as the myocardium contracts and relaxes during the cardiac cycle
Tag lines over a non-contractile mass should deform in the same way as normal myocardium
Line tags can be applied perpendicular to a myocardial, mass or pericardial interface to assess adherence or invasion
options_after: Myocardial tagging is used primarily for coronary artery calcium quantification
It can assess myocardial wall motion and strain
Grid tags deform as the myocardium contracts and relaxes during the cardiac cycle
Tag lines over a non-contractile mass should deform in the same way as normal myocardium
Line tags can be applied perpendicular to a myocardial, mass or pericardial interface to assess adherence or invasion
updates.explanation: Myocardial tagging assesses myocardial wall motion and strain using radiofrequency tag lines. Grid tags deform during myocardial contraction and relaxation, allowing strain analysis. The source also notes that line tags can be placed perpendicular to a myocardial, mass or pericardial interface to assess adherence or invasion. A non-contractile mass maintains its tag-line shape rather than deforming like contracting myocardium.

updates.question_text: Regarding non-ischaemic late gadolinium enhancement, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Non-ischaemic LGE must always follow a coronary vascular territory
Dilated cardiomyopathy can show a mesocardial LGE pattern
Sarcoidosis produces only circumferential subendocardial LGE
Cardiac sarcoidosis may show mesocardial or subepicardial LGE in a nodular or patchy pattern
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can show mesocardial LGE at right ventricular septal attachment sites
options_after: Non-ischaemic LGE must characteristically follow a coronary vascular territory
Dilated cardiomyopathy can show a mesocardial LGE pattern
Sarcoidosis produces primarily circumferential subendocardial LGE
Cardiac sarcoidosis may show mesocardial or subepicardial LGE in a nodular or patchy pattern
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can show mesocardial LGE at right ventricular septal attachment sites
updates.explanation: Delayed enhancement that does not follow a vascular territory is described as non-ischaemic. Dilated cardiomyopathy is illustrated with diffuse mesocardial LGE. Sarcoidosis may produce mesocardial or subepicardial enhancement in a nodular or patchy pattern. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy shows mesocardial LGE, particularly at the right ventricular septal attachment sites and in the most hypertrophied regions.

updates.question_text: According to the delayed enhancement MRI summary, which pairings are correct?
options_before: Mesocardial LGE - dilated cardiomyopathy
Subepicardial LGE - transmural infarct
Circumferential subendocardial LGE - amyloidosis
Transmural LGE - myocarditis only
Subendocardial LGE - subendocardial infarct
options_after: Mesocardial LGE - dilated cardiomyopathy
Subepicardial LGE - transmural infarct
Circumferential subendocardial LGE - amyloidosis
Transmural LGE - myocarditis in typical cases
Subendocardial LGE - subendocardial infarct
updates.explanation: The summary table links mesocardial enhancement with dilated cardiomyopathy and subendocardial enhancement with subendocardial infarction. Circumferential subendocardial enhancement is listed with amyloidosis, systemic sclerosis, cardiac transplantation and hypereosinophilic syndrome. Transmural enhancement is linked with transmural infarct as well as severe myocarditis and sarcoidosis, so restricting it to myocarditis alone is inaccurate. Subepicardial enhancement is listed with myocarditis, sarcoidosis and Chagas disease, not transmural infarction.

updates.question_text: Regarding chest radiography in acute myocardial infarction, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Most initial chest radiographs in acute MI show a diagnostic infarct pattern
The most common abnormality is increased pulmonary venous pressure or overt pulmonary oedema
Pulmonary oedema after MI is described as a reassuring prognostic sign
Chest radiography can suggest alternative causes of acute chest pain such as pneumothorax or pneumonia
Chest radiography cannot evaluate any complication of acute MI
options_after: Most initial chest radiographs in acute MI show a diagnostic infarct pattern
The most common abnormality is increased pulmonary venous pressure or overt pulmonary oedema
Pulmonary oedema after MI is described as a reassuring prognostic sign
Chest radiography can suggest alternative causes of acute chest pain such as pneumothorax or pneumonia
Chest radiography will not evaluate any complication of acute MI
updates.explanation: The majority of initial chest radiographs in acute MI are normal. When abnormal, the most common finding is increased pulmonary venous pressure or overt pulmonary oedema, and pulmonary oedema after MI is described as a poor prognostic indicator. Chest radiography can evaluate some complications, including pericardial effusion, LV aneurysm and papillary muscle rupture. It can also suggest alternative acute chest pain diagnoses such as pneumothorax or pneumonia.

updates.question_text: Regarding stress cardiac MRI for myocardial ischaemia, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Cardiac MRI can be used with pharmacologic stress to evaluate myocardial ischaemia
Stress perfusion MRI shows abnormality only when the epicardial layer is involved first
Cine MRI has no role in detecting wall motion abnormality in an affected coronary territory
Stress perfusion MRI demonstrates a regional first-pass perfusion deficit
The subendocardial layer is always involved in the perfusion abnormality described
options_after: Cardiac MRI can be used with pharmacologic stress to evaluate myocardial ischaemia
Stress perfusion MRI shows abnormality primarily when the epicardial layer is involved first
Cine MRI has negligible role in detecting wall motion abnormality in an affected coronary territory
Stress perfusion MRI demonstrates a regional first-pass perfusion deficit
The subendocardial layer is always involved in the perfusion abnormality described
updates.explanation: The source states that cardiac MRI can be performed with pharmacologic stress to evaluate myocardial ischaemia, similar to stress echocardiography and nuclear scintigraphy. Cine MRI can demonstrate wall motion abnormality or decreased wall thickening in the affected coronary territory. Stress first-pass perfusion MRI demonstrates regional perfusion deficits, and the subendocardial layer is always involved. The example shows a regadenoson-induced defect in the RCA territory.

updates.question_text: Regarding viability assessment after myocardial infarction on cardiac MRI, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Viable myocardium shows late gadolinium enhancement
Only chronic infarcts show LGE, while acute necrotic infarcts do not
Both acute necrotic and chronic fibrotic myocardial infarctions show LGE
The region of oedema with T2 hyperintensity is always smaller than the LGE region
Greater than 50% transmural LGE indicates low likelihood of functional recovery after revascularisation
options_after: Viable myocardium shows late gadolinium enhancement
Late gadolinium enhancement is a marker of chronic fibrosis and is absent from acute necrotic infarction.
Both acute necrotic and chronic fibrotic myocardial infarctions show LGE
The region of oedema with T2 hyperintensity is characteristically smaller than the LGE region
Greater than 50% transmural LGE indicates low likelihood of functional recovery after revascularisation
updates.explanation: Delayed contrast-enhanced MRI is used to assess myocardial viability. The source states that both acute necrotic and chronic fibrotic infarctions show LGE, while viable myocardium does not. More than 50% transmural LGE indicates low likelihood of functional recovery after revascularisation. Myocardial oedema in acute infarction is usually larger than the LGE area, representing myocardium at risk.

updates.question_text: Regarding CT findings of myocardial infarction, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Conventional CT is routinely performed as the primary test for MI and its complications
Acute myocardial ischaemia may appear as wall hypoattenuation in a coronary artery distribution
Wall hypoattenuation progresses from the subendocardial layer towards transmural involvement
Prior MI scar must always appear as a hypervascular myocardial mass
Prior MI scar can present as dense irregular myocardial calcification or thin fatty-replaced myocardium
options_after: Conventional CT is routinely performed as the primary test for MI and its complications
Acute myocardial ischaemia may appear as wall hypoattenuation in a coronary artery distribution
Wall hypoattenuation progresses from the subendocardial layer towards transmural involvement
Prior MI scar must characteristically appear as a hypervascular myocardial mass
Prior MI scar can present as dense irregular myocardial calcification or thin fatty-replaced myocardium
updates.explanation: The source states that conventional CT is not routinely performed for MI or its complications, although findings may be incidental. Acute myocardial ischaemia appears as wall hypoattenuation in a coronary artery distribution, progressing from subendocardial to transmural involvement. Subsequent myocyte death leads to decreased wall thickness. Prior myocardial scar may appear as dense irregular calcification or thin fatty-replaced myocardium in a coronary distribution.

updates.question_text: Regarding complications of myocardial infarction, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Acute complications include cardiogenic shock, pulmonary oedema and arrhythmia
Left ventricular aneurysm and heart failure are listed only as acute complications
Papillary muscle rupture, ventricular septal rupture and free-wall rupture are chronic rather than acute complications
Chronic complications include heart failure, LV aneurysm or pseudoaneurysm, and mural thrombus
Pericarditis is listed only as a chronic complication
options_after: Acute complications include cardiogenic shock, pulmonary oedema and arrhythmia
Left ventricular aneurysm and heart failure are listed primarily as acute complications
Papillary muscle rupture, ventricular septal rupture and free-wall rupture are chronic rather than acute complications
Chronic complications include heart failure, LV aneurysm or pseudoaneurysm, and mural thrombus
Pericarditis is listed primarily as a chronic complication
updates.explanation: The source lists acute MI complications as cardiogenic shock, pulmonary oedema, arrhythmia, mural thrombus, papillary muscle rupture, ventricular septal rupture, cardiac free-wall rupture and pericarditis. Chronic complications include heart failure, LV aneurysm or pseudoaneurysm, and mural thrombus. Thus rupture syndromes are acute complications, while LV aneurysm and pseudoaneurysm are discussed as chronic sequelae.

updates.question_text: Regarding the role of delayed enhancement MRI across this batch, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It helps distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic myocardial disease by enhancement pattern
Any first-pass myocardial enhancement is abnormal
It is only useful for coronary aneurysm sizing and does not assess infarct viability
It can assess myocardial viability after infarction
It can demonstrate pericardial enhancement overlying a pseudoaneurysm
options_after: It helps distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic myocardial disease by enhancement pattern
Any first-pass myocardial enhancement is abnormal
It is primarily useful for coronary aneurysm sizing and does not assess infarct viability
It can assess myocardial viability after infarction
It can demonstrate pericardial enhancement overlying a pseudoaneurysm
updates.explanation: The source uses delayed enhancement MRI to distinguish ischaemic vascular-territory patterns from several non-ischaemic patterns. Delayed enhancement also contributes to myocardial viability assessment after infarction, with viable myocardium lacking LGE and more than 50% transmural enhancement implying poor recovery after revascularisation. Pseudoaneurysm assessment may show pericardial LGE over the affected region. Normal myocardium enhances homogeneously on first-pass perfusion, so first-pass enhancement itself is not abnormal.

updates.question_text: Regarding restrictive cardiomyopathy versus constrictive physiology, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: Restrictive cardiomyopathy and constrictive physiology are the same entity
Constrictive physiology is due to intrinsic fibrofatty replacement of ventricular myocytes
Restrictive cardiomyopathy is treated surgically by pericardial stripping
Imaging has no role in differentiating these processes
A key imaging role in impaired diastolic filling is to exclude constrictive pericarditis as the cause
options_after: Restrictive cardiomyopathy and constrictive physiology are the same entity
Constrictive physiology is due to intrinsic fibrofatty replacement of ventricular myocytes
Restrictive cardiomyopathy is treated surgically by pericardial stripping
Imaging has negligible role in differentiating these processes
A key imaging role in impaired diastolic filling is to exclude constrictive pericarditis as the cause
updates.explanation: Restrictive cardiomyopathy and constrictive physiology can have identical ventricular pressure tracings, but they are different entities. Constrictive physiology is due to increased pericardial pressure from thickened, often calcified pericardium or pericardial effusion. The main role of cardiac imaging in impaired diastolic filling is to exclude constrictive pericarditis, because it can be treated surgically by pericardiectomy. Restrictive cardiomyopathy has no effective treatment and has a poor prognosis.

updates.question_text: Regarding dilated cardiomyopathy, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It is characterised by diffuse cardiac chamber enlargement with impaired systolic function
It usually involves the left ventricle only, with sparing of the right ventricle
It is the most common non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy
It may be idiopathic, alcohol-related, myocarditis-related or drug-toxicity-related
MRI and CT are not useful for determining aetiology
options_after: It is characterised by diffuse cardiac chamber enlargement with impaired systolic function
It usually involves the left ventricle primarily, with sparing of the right ventricle
It is the most common non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy
It may be idiopathic, alcohol-related, myocarditis-related or drug-toxicity-related
MRI and CT are not useful for determining aetiology
updates.explanation: Dilated cardiomyopathy is characterised by diffuse chamber enlargement with impaired systolic function and typically involves both ventricles. It may be ischaemic or non-ischaemic, and it is described as the most common non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy. Causes include idiopathic disease, alcohol abuse, myocarditis and drug toxicity. MRI or CT is useful in determining the aetiology.

updates.question_text: Regarding imaging evaluation of newly diagnosed dilated cardiomyopathy, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: An ischaemic cause is excluded if there is any delayed enhancement
Delayed enhancement in a vascular distribution suggests an ischaemic cause
Idiopathic DCM always lacks any mesocardial LGE
Coronary CT findings cannot contribute to aetiological assessment
Catheter angiography is recommended to exclude coronary artery disease in a new diagnosis
options_after: An ischaemic cause is excluded if there is any delayed enhancement
Delayed enhancement in a vascular distribution suggests an ischaemic cause
Idiopathic DCM characteristically lacks any mesocardial LGE
Coronary CT findings will not contribute to aetiological assessment
Catheter angiography is recommended to exclude coronary artery disease in a new diagnosis
updates.explanation: An ischaemic cause of DCM can be suggested by delayed enhancement in a vascular distribution on MRI or by coronary artery disease on CCTA. Up to 41% of idiopathic DCM patients may show abnormal mesocardial LGE in a non-ischaemic mid-ventricular distribution, with uncertain significance. The source recommends catheter angiography to exclude coronary artery disease when dilated cardiomyopathy is newly diagnosed.

updates.question_text: Regarding aortic regurgitation in this section, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: Long-standing aortic regurgitation causes left ventricular enlargement with cardiomegaly on radiographs
It is caused only by abnormality of the aortic valve leaflets
Pulmonary vascularity is typically severely increased
The ascending aorta is typically small in long-standing disease
It has the same chest radiograph appearance as mitral stenosis with normal heart size and isolated left atrial enlargement
options_after: Long-standing aortic regurgitation causes left ventricular enlargement with cardiomegaly on radiographs
It is caused primarily by abnormality of the aortic valve leaflets
Pulmonary vascularity is typically severely increased
The ascending aorta is typically small in long-standing disease
It has the same chest radiograph appearance as mitral stenosis with normal heart size and isolated left atrial enlargement
updates.explanation: Aortic regurgitation may arise from abnormality of the aortic valve, aortic annulus or ascending aorta. Long-standing disease causes LV enlargement, visible as cardiomegaly on radiographs, and there is typically enlargement of the ascending aorta. Similar to aortic stenosis, pulmonary vascularity is typically normal. Normal heart size with left atrial enlargement and raised pulmonary venous pressure is the mitral stenosis pattern.

updates.question_text: Regarding mitral valve disease, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The most common cause of mitral stenosis is rheumatic heart disease
Mitral stenosis appears as a normal-sized heart with left atrial enlargement
Acute mitral regurgitation after myocardial infarction always produces marked chronic cardiomegaly before pulmonary oedema
Chronic mitral regurgitation can lead to cardiac dilatation and left atrial enlargement
Mitral valve prolapse is diagnosed when valve leaflets bow more than 2 mm below the annular plane into the left atrium during systole
options_after: The most common cause of mitral stenosis is rheumatic heart disease
Mitral stenosis appears as a normal-sized heart with left atrial enlargement
Acute mitral regurgitation after myocardial infarction characteristically produces marked chronic cardiomegaly before pulmonary oedema
Chronic mitral regurgitation can lead to cardiac dilatation and left atrial enlargement
Mitral valve prolapse is diagnosed when valve leaflets bow more than 2 mm below the annular plane into the left atrium during systole
updates.explanation: Mitral stenosis is most commonly due to rheumatic heart disease and appears as a normal-sized heart with left atrial enlargement and typically elevated pulmonary venous pressures. Acute mitral regurgitation secondary to MI can present with pulmonary oedema despite a normal-sized heart. Chronic mitral regurgitation can cause cardiac dilatation and LA enlargement. Mitral valve prolapse is defined by more than 2 mm bowing of the leaflets below the annular plane into the LA during systole.

updates.question_text: Regarding normal pericardial anatomy, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The pericardium consists of visceral and parietal layers
The normal pericardial space contains no fluid
Normal pericardial thickness on CT and MRI is less than 4 mm
A pericardial thickness of at least 4 mm on imaging is considered abnormal
The pericardial apparatus normally measures more than 1 cm on cadaveric studies
options_after: The pericardium consists of visceral and parietal layers
The normal pericardial space lacks fluid
Normal pericardial thickness on CT and MRI is less than 4 mm
A pericardial thickness of at least 4 mm on imaging is considered abnormal
The pericardial apparatus normally measures more than 1 cm on cadaveric studies
updates.explanation: The pericardium consists of visceral and parietal layers separated by approximately 40 mL of pericardial fluid. The combined pericardial apparatus measures less than 1 mm on cadaveric studies and is seen on CT and MRI with normal thickness below 2 mm. A thickness of at least 4 mm is considered abnormal on imaging. A normal pericardial space therefore contains fluid, but not a large effusion.

updates.question_text: Regarding acute pericarditis, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: Tuberculosis is the only recognised cause in this section
Patients rarely respond to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Most cases are idiopathic and presumed viral
Recurrent pericardial pain is not described in this section
The expected MRI finding is absent pericardial signal with no stranding
options_after: Tuberculosis is the principal recognised cause in this section
Patients rarely respond to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Most cases are idiopathic and presumed viral
Recurrent pericardial pain is not described in this section
The expected MRI finding is absent pericardial signal without stranding
updates.explanation: Most acute pericarditis is idiopathic and presumed viral. Other causes include tuberculosis, neoplasia and autoimmune disease. Up to 30% of patients have recurrent pericardial pain, and many respond favourably to NSAIDs. The illustrated acute pericarditis case shows pericardial thickening with epicardial and pericardial stranding and increased T2 signal in the oedematous visceral and parietal layers.

updates.question_text: Regarding constrictive pericarditis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The pericardium is usually normal thickness and never calcified
It can occur after viral or tuberculous pericarditis, uraemia, radiation or cardiac surgery
Cine MRI may show paradoxical septal motion
Delayed enhancement MRI can show pericardial LGE due to fibrosis
Treatment is surgical pericardial stripping
options_after: Constrictive pericarditis usually has normal pericardial thickness without calcification.
It can occur after viral or tuberculous pericarditis, uraemia, radiation or cardiac surgery
Cine MRI may show paradoxical septal motion
Delayed enhancement MRI can show pericardial LGE due to fibrosis
Treatment is surgical pericardial stripping
updates.explanation: Constrictive pericarditis can follow multiple forms of pericarditis, uraemia, radiotherapy or cardiac surgery. The pericardium is typically thickened to at least 4 mm, and adhesions, calcification and effusion are highly suggestive. Cine MRI may show septal bounce, delayed enhancement MRI can show fibrotic pericardial LGE, and myocardial tagging can demonstrate limited motion between visceral and parietal layers. Treatment is surgical pericardial stripping.

updates.question_text: Regarding congenital absence of the pericardium, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: Total absence of the pericardium is the most common form
Right pericardial absence near the SVC is the typical form
A lucent notch between the aorta and pulmonary artery can suggest a pericardial defect
Left pericardial defects always produce rightward displacement of the heart
Partial absence carries no risk of cardiac herniation
options_after: Total absence of the pericardium is the most common form
Right pericardial absence near the SVC is the typical form
A lucent notch between the aorta and pulmonary artery can suggest a pericardial defect
Left pericardial defects characteristically produce rightward displacement of the heart
Partial absence carries negligible risk of cardiac herniation
updates.explanation: A lucent notch between the aorta and pulmonary artery can indicate interposed lung from a pericardial defect, and is usually better appreciated on CT than radiography. The most common form involves the left pericardium near the left atrial appendage and adjacent pulmonary artery. Left defects can cause leftward displacement of the heart, which may be the only imaging finding. Partial absence can allow herniation of part of the heart through the defect.

updates.question_text: Regarding pericardial masses, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Most pericardial cysts occur in the right cardiophrenic angle
Pericardial diverticula never communicate with the pericardial space
The most common primary pericardial tumour is a benign lipoma
Pericardial diverticula can change in size
The most common pericardial metastases are from lung and breast cancer
options_after: Most pericardial cysts occur in the right cardiophrenic angle
Pericardial diverticula will not communicate with the pericardial space
The most common primary pericardial tumour is a benign lipoma
Pericardial diverticula can change in size
The most common pericardial metastases are from lung and breast cancer
updates.explanation: Pericardial cysts may be congenital or post-surgical; 70% occur in the right cardiophrenic angle and 20% in the left cardiophrenic angle. Pericardial diverticula communicate with the pericardial space and can change in size. The most common primary pericardial tumour is pericardial mesothelioma. The most common pericardial metastases are from lung and breast cancer.

updates.question_text: Regarding adult cardiac masses in this section, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Primary cardiac tumours are more common than metastases to the heart or pericardium
The most common cardiac mass is a thrombus
Approximately 75% of primary cardiac tumours are benign
Metastases can reach the heart only by direct extension from lung cancer
Metastatic spread can occur by direct extension, extension through the SVC or IVC, or haematogenous spread
options_after: Primary cardiac tumours are more common than metastases to the heart or pericardium
The most common cardiac mass is a thrombus
Approximately 75% of primary cardiac tumours are benign
Metastases can reach the heart primarily by direct extension from lung cancer
Metastatic spread can occur by direct extension, extension through the SVC or IVC, or haematogenous spread
updates.explanation: The source states that the most common cardiac mass is a thrombus. Metastases to the heart or pericardium are far more common than primary cardiac tumours, and can occur by direct intrathoracic extension, extension through the SVC or IVC, or haematogenous spread. About 75% of primary cardiac tumours are benign. Lung and breast malignancy may extend directly, renal cell carcinoma can extend via the IVC, and melanoma or lymphoma may spread haematogenously.

updates.question_text: Regarding cardiac myxoma, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Myxoma is the most common benign primary cardiac tumour in adults
Most cardiac myxomas arise from the right ventricle
The usual attachment is the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis
Myxomas are uniformly T2 hypointense and never calcify
Myxomas may prolapse through a valve or patent foramen ovale
options_after: Myxoma is the most common benign primary cardiac tumour in adults
Most cardiac myxomas arise from the right ventricle
The usual attachment is the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis
Myxomas are uniformly T2 hypointense and will not calcify
Myxomas may prolapse through a valve or patent foramen ovale
updates.explanation: Myxoma is described as the most common benign primary cardiac tumour in adults. Seventy-five percent arise in the left atrium and are usually attached to the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis; 20% arise in the right atrium. The tumour can prolapse through a valve or patent foramen ovale. On MRI, myxomas are T2 hyperintense and may show calcification or haemosiderin deposition from intralesional haemorrhage.

updates.question_text: Regarding cardiac lipoma and lipomatous hypertrophy of the interatrial septum, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Cardiac lipomas are usually infiltrative malignant masses with avid enhancement
Lipomatous hypertrophy of the interatrial septum requires surgical treatment in most cases
Cardiac lipomas follow fat signal intensity on all MRI sequences and do not enhance
Lipomatous hypertrophy always has a capsule on histopathology like lipoma
Lipomatous hypertrophy spares the fossa ovalis, producing a dumbbell configuration
options_after: Cardiac lipomas are usually infiltrative malignant masses with avid enhancement
Lipomatous hypertrophy of the interatrial septum requires surgical treatment in most cases
Cardiac lipomas follow fat signal intensity on all MRI sequences and do not enhance
Lipomatous hypertrophy characteristically has a capsule on histopathology like lipoma
Lipomatous hypertrophy spares the fossa ovalis, producing a dumbbell configuration
updates.explanation: Cardiac lipomas are common benign tumours with a spherical shape, well-circumscribed margin, fat signal on all MRI sequences and no enhancement. Lipomatous hypertrophy of the interatrial septum is proliferation of fatty deposits, typically along the lateral right heart border, with sparing of the fossa ovalis and a dumbbell configuration. It is incidental, does not require treatment and should not be mistaken for a cardiac mass. Unlike lipoma, it lacks a capsule on histopathology.

updates.question_text: Regarding cardiac haemangioma, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: It is restricted to the left atrium and cannot involve the pericardium
It is T2 hypointense and non-enhancing due to fibrous content
It is the most common tumour of the cardiac valves
It can occur in any cardiac chamber and may involve the pericardium
It represents bland thrombus and therefore should not enhance
options_after: It is restricted to the left atrium and will not involve the pericardium
It is T2 hypointense and non-enhancing due to fibrous content
It is the most common tumour of the cardiac valves
It can occur in any cardiac chamber and may involve the pericardium
It represents bland thrombus and therefore should not enhance
updates.explanation: Cardiac haemangiomas can occur in any cardiac chamber and may involve the pericardium. Similar to haemangiomas elsewhere, they are T2 hyperintense and intensely enhancing because of rich vascularity, with possible flow voids and calcifications. Low T2 signal due to fibrous content belongs to papillary fibroelastoma in this section. Lack of enhancement is a feature of thrombus rather than haemangioma.

updates.question_text: Regarding adult primary cardiac sarcomas, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Adult primary cardiac sarcomas include osteosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, synovial sarcoma, liposarcoma, intimal sarcoma and undifferentiated sarcoma
Intimal sarcoma refers to sarcomas of the aorta and pulmonary artery or vein expressing the MDM2 gene
All listed sarcomas have a predilection for the right atrium
Apart from intimal sarcoma, the listed sarcomas have a predilection for the left atrium unlike angiosarcoma
Angiosarcoma is excluded from the adult primary cardiac malignancy discussion
options_after: Adult primary cardiac sarcomas include osteosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, synovial sarcoma, liposarcoma, intimal sarcoma and undifferentiated sarcoma
Intimal sarcoma refers to sarcomas of the aorta and pulmonary artery or vein expressing the MDM2 gene
Most listed sarcomas have a predilection for the right atrium
Apart from intimal sarcoma, the listed sarcomas have a predilection for the left atrium unlike angiosarcoma
Angiosarcoma is excluded from the adult primary cardiac malignancy discussion
updates.explanation: The source lists adult primary cardiac sarcomas as osteosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, synovial sarcoma, liposarcoma, intimal (spindle cell) and undifferentiated sarcoma. Intimal sarcoma is described as a relatively new WHO classification for sarcomas of the aorta and pulmonary artery or vein expressing MDM2. Apart from intimal sarcoma, these sarcomas have a predilection for the left atrium, unlike angiosarcoma. Angiosarcoma is then discussed separately as the most common primary cardiac malignancy in adults.

updates.question_text: According to the common-location table, which location is matched correctly?
options_before: Myxoma - right atrium
Angiosarcoma - left atrium
Fibroelastoma - valvular
Pericardial cyst - myocardium
Thrombus - pericardium only
options_after: Myxoma - right atrium
Angiosarcoma - left atrium
Fibroelastoma - valvular
Pericardial cyst - myocardium
Thrombus - pericardium in typical cases
updates.explanation: The common-location table places fibroelastoma and vegetations in the valvular category. Myxoma is listed under the left atrium, while angiosarcoma and lymphoma are listed under the right atrium. Pericardial cyst, metastases and mesothelioma are listed under pericardium. Thrombus, metastases, lipoma and haemangioma are listed as possible in any chamber.

updates.question_text: When evaluating an adult cardiac mass, which of the following source-grounded patterns support malignancy rather than a benign or non-neoplastic mimic?
options_before: No gadolinium enhancement with adjacent myocardial scar
Involvement of more than one cardiac chamber
Intralesional necrosis and invasion of epicardial fat
Fat signal on all MRI sequences without enhancement
Hemorrhagic pericardial effusion or metastases
options_after: Absent gadolinium enhancement with adjacent myocardial scar
Involvement of more than one cardiac chamber
Intralesional necrosis and invasion of epicardial fat
Fat signal on routine MRI sequences without enhancement
Hemorrhagic pericardial effusion or metastases
updates.explanation: Common malignant features in the source include involvement of more than one cardiac chamber, intralesional necrosis, invasion of the pericardium and epicardial fat, extracardiac extension, haemorrhagic pericardial effusion and metastases. Lack of enhancement with adjacent myocardial scar supports thrombus, a non-neoplastic mimic. Fat signal on all sequences without enhancement supports lipoma, while septal fat with fossa ovalis sparing supports lipomatous hypertrophy.

updates.question_text: Regarding accessory pulmonary fissures, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The inferior accessory fissure is present in approximately 12% of patients and is more commonly seen in the right lung.
The azygos fissure is present in less than 1% of patients.
The azygos lobe is encased in its own visceral pleura only.
The left minor fissure separates the lingula from the left upper lobe and is present in approximately 8% of patients.
The superior accessory fissure is present in approximately 12% of patients.
options_after: The inferior accessory fissure is present in approximately 12% of patients and is more commonly seen in the right lung.
The azygos fissure is present in less than 1% of patients.
The azygos lobe is encased in its own visceral pleura in typical cases.
The left minor fissure separates the lingula from the left upper lobe and is present in approximately 8% of patients.
The superior accessory fissure is present in approximately 12% of patients.
updates.explanation: The inferior accessory fissure divides the medial basal segment from the remaining basal segments and is present in approximately 12% of patients, with a right-sided predominance. The azygos fissure is an uncommon anatomical variant, found in fewer than 1% of patients, in which a portion of the apical right upper lobe is encased in its own parietal and visceral pleura — not visceral pleura alone. The left minor fissure, present in approximately 8% of patients, separates the lingula from the left upper lobe. The superior accessory fissure, which separates the superior and basal segments of the right lower lobe, is present in approximately 5% — not 12% — of patients.

updates.question_text: Regarding the differential diagnosis of acute pulmonary consolidation, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Pneumonia is by far the most common cause of acute pulmonary consolidation.
Adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is caused by decreased capillary permeability in critically ill patients.
Aspiration may produce heterogeneous consolidation due to mucus plugging.
Pulmonary oedema causes consolidation only when mild.
Pulmonary haemorrhage is a recognised cause of acute consolidation.
options_after: Pneumonia is by far the most common cause of acute pulmonary consolidation.
Adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is caused by decreased capillary permeability in critically ill patients.
Aspiration may produce heterogeneous consolidation due to mucus plugging.
Pulmonary oedema causes consolidation primarily when mild.
Pulmonary haemorrhage is a recognised cause of acute consolidation.
updates.explanation: Pneumonia is by far the most common cause of acute consolidation. Aspiration produces heterogeneous consolidation because mucus plugging from aspirated secretions creates uneven airspace opacification. Pulmonary haemorrhage — whether primary or from aspiration of blood — fills alveoli with blood and is a recognised acute cause. ARDS results from increased — not decreased — capillary permeability leading to non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Severe pulmonary oedema may cause frank consolidation — not only mild oedema.

updates.question_text: Regarding perilymphatic nodules and sarcoidosis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: They are usually distributed randomly because of haematogenous spread.
They follow lymphatics in subpleural, peribronchovascular, and septal locations.
Sarcoidosis is the most common cause of perilymphatic nodules.
The galaxy sign is produced by confluent tiny nodules surrounding a central lesion.
They never involve the bronchovascular bundles.
options_after: They are usually distributed randomly because of haematogenous spread.
They follow lymphatics in subpleural, peribronchovascular, and septal locations.
Sarcoidosis is the most common cause of perilymphatic nodules.
The galaxy sign is produced by confluent tiny nodules surrounding a central lesion.
They will not involve the bronchovascular bundles.
updates.explanation: Perilymphatic nodules track the anatomic locations of pulmonary lymphatics: subpleural, peribronchovascular, and within the interlobular septa. Sarcoidosis is the commonest cause and may produce the galaxy sign when tiny nodules become confluent around a central lesion. Random haematogenous spread is the mechanism for random nodules, and bronchovascular bundle involvement is part of the perilymphatic pattern.

updates.question_text: Regarding diffuse cystic lung disease, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis causes uniformly distributed thin-walled cysts and may be associated with chylous effusion.
Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis features irregular cysts and nodules predominantly in the upper lungs.
Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome is associated with renal tumours and pulmonary cysts.
Emphysema classically contains no central vessels and is therefore indistinguishable from cysts.
Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia can feature cysts in late-stage disease.
options_after: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis causes uniformly distributed thin-walled cysts and may be associated with chylous effusion.
Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis features irregular cysts and nodules predominantly in the upper lungs.
Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome is associated with renal tumours and pulmonary cysts.
Emphysema classically lacks central vessels and is therefore indistinguishable from cysts.
Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia can feature cysts in late-stage disease.
updates.explanation: The source lists LAM, pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis, LIP, amyloid, Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, and late Pneumocystis pneumonia among causes of multiple lung cysts. LAM is diffuse and uniform and may have a chylous effusion; Langerhans disease is upper-lung predominant with irregular cysts and nodules; Birt-Hogg-Dube is associated with renal tumours and cysts. Emphysema is distinguished because it typically lacks walls and may contain central vessels.

updates.question_text: Regarding primary pulmonary tuberculosis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It must always occur in the lung apices.
It may involve the pulmonary parenchyma, airways, and pleura.
It always produces radiographic abnormalities.
The typical imaging manifestation is lobar consolidation with or without pleural effusion and lymphadenopathy.
Adenopathy may show central low attenuation and peripheral enhancement, especially in children.
options_after: It must characteristically occur in the lung apices.
It may involve the pulmonary parenchyma, airways, and pleura.
It characteristically produces radiographic abnormalities.
The typical imaging manifestation is lobar consolidation with or without pleural effusion and lymphadenopathy.
Adenopathy may show central low attenuation and peripheral enhancement, especially in children.
updates.explanation: Primary TB can affect parenchyma, airways, and pleura and may occur in any lobe. The typical imaging pattern is lobar consolidation with possible effusion and lymphadenopathy, but not all elements have to be present. Up to 15% of primary TB infections have no radiographic change. Low-attenuation adenopathy with peripheral enhancement is common, particularly in children.

updates.question_text: Regarding healed and miliary tuberculosis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Healed tuberculosis usually presents as diffuse lower-lobe consolidation.
Healed tuberculosis may show apical scarring, upper-lobe volume loss, and superior hilar retraction.
Miliary tuberculosis produces a centrilobular pattern with pleural sparing.
Miliary tuberculosis consists of innumerable tiny random nodules reflecting haematogenous seeding.
Miliary tuberculosis can occur only in reactivation disease.
options_after: Healed tuberculosis usually presents as diffuse lower-lobe consolidation.
Healed tuberculosis may show apical scarring, upper-lobe volume loss, and superior hilar retraction.
Miliary tuberculosis produces a centrilobular pattern with pleural sparing.
Miliary tuberculosis consists of innumerable tiny random nodules reflecting haematogenous seeding.
Miliary tuberculosis can occur primarily in reactivation disease.
updates.explanation: Healed TB is described as apical scarring with upper-lobe volume loss and superior hilar retraction, with possible calcified granulomas. Miliary TB is a random distribution of innumerable tiny nodules caused by haematogenous dissemination. It can occur in either primary or reactivation TB, and the random distribution may include nodules at the pleural surface rather than centrilobular sparing.

updates.question_text: Regarding the spectrum of pulmonary Aspergillus disease, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Aspergillus manifests as distinct patterns including ABPA, aspergilloma, semi-invasive disease, airway-invasive disease, and angioinvasive disease.
ABPA requires a pre-existing pulmonary cavity as the key predisposing abnormality.
Aspergillus affects patients with abnormal immunity or pre-existing pulmonary disease.
Angioinvasive aspergillosis is the expected pattern in otherwise healthy patients with no immune abnormality.
The predisposing abnormality varies by manifestation and may include asthma, immunocompromise, prior infection, or structural/congenital lung abnormality.
options_after: Aspergillus manifests as distinct patterns including ABPA, aspergilloma, semi-invasive disease, airway-invasive disease, and angioinvasive disease.
ABPA requires a pre-existing pulmonary cavity as the key predisposing abnormality.
Aspergillus affects patients with abnormal immunity or pre-existing pulmonary disease.
Angioinvasive aspergillosis is the expected pattern in otherwise healthy patients without immune abnormality.
The predisposing abnormality varies by manifestation and may include asthma, immunocompromise, prior infection, or structural/congenital lung abnormality.
updates.explanation: The source organises pulmonary Aspergillus into ABPA, aspergilloma, semi-invasive, airway-invasive, and angioinvasive forms. Aspergillus affects abnormal hosts or abnormal lungs, with the predisposing factor depending on manifestation. ABPA is linked to asthma or cystic fibrosis rather than a pre-existing cavity, while aspergilloma develops in a pre-existing cavity. Angioinvasive disease is seen in immunocompromised, especially neutropenic, patients.

updates.question_text: Regarding allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It is an invasive aspergillus infection seen almost exclusively in neutropenic patients.
It is a hypersensitivity reaction to aspergillus seen most commonly in patients with longstanding asthma.
Serum testing for aspergillus IgE can be used in diagnosis.
Central bronchiectasis with mucoid impaction produces the finger-in-glove sign.
High-attenuation mucus is a specific finding, even though the finger-in-glove sign is not specific to ABPA.
options_after: It is an invasive aspergillus infection seen predominantly in neutropenic patients.
It is a hypersensitivity reaction to aspergillus seen most commonly in patients with longstanding asthma.
Serum testing for aspergillus IgE can be used in diagnosis.
Central bronchiectasis with mucoid impaction produces the finger-in-glove sign.
High-attenuation mucus is a specific finding, even though the finger-in-glove sign is not specific to ABPA.
updates.explanation: ABPA is a hypersensitivity reaction to aspergillus, most common in longstanding asthma, and it is not an infection. Serum aspergillus IgE may support the diagnosis. CT shows central bronchiectasis and mucoid impaction, creating the finger-in-glove sign. The sign itself is not specific, but high-attenuation mucus is described as specific.

updates.question_text: Regarding semi-invasive and airway-invasive aspergillosis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Semi-invasive aspergillosis is most typical in young otherwise healthy patients after hot-tub exposure.
Semi-invasive aspergillosis resolves over days and does not cavitate.
Semi-invasive aspergillosis is seen in debilitated, diabetic, alcoholic, and COPD patients.
Airway-invasive aspergillosis is seen only in immunocompetent asthmatic patients.
Airway-invasive aspergillosis may range from bronchiolitis to bronchopneumonia and shows centrilobular and tree-in-bud nodules.
options_after: Semi-invasive aspergillosis is most typical in young otherwise healthy patients after hot-tub exposure.
Semi-invasive aspergillosis resolves over days and does not cavitate.
Semi-invasive aspergillosis is seen in debilitated, diabetic, alcoholic, and COPD patients.
Airway-invasive aspergillosis is seen primarily in immunocompetent asthmatic patients.
Airway-invasive aspergillosis may range from bronchiolitis to bronchopneumonia and shows centrilobular and tree-in-bud nodules.
updates.explanation: Semi-invasive aspergillosis is chronic necrotising granulomatous inflammation in debilitated, diabetic, alcoholic, or COPD patients, with slowly progressive consolidation, often cavitation, and pleural thickening. Airway-invasive aspergillosis is seen only in immunocompromised patients and ranges from bronchiolitis to bronchopneumonia. Its main CT features are centrilobular and tree-in-bud nodules.

updates.question_text: Regarding lung cancer epidemiology and risk factors, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States.
Tobacco smoking is thought to cause 80-90% of lung cancers.
Asbestos exposure reduces the risk of lung cancer in smokers.
Pulmonary fibrosis increases the risk of lung cancer by a factor of ten.
Pulmonary scarring, such as from prior tuberculosis, has no association with lung cancer risk.
options_after: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States.
Tobacco smoking is thought to cause 80-90% of lung cancers.
Asbestos exposure reduces the risk of lung cancer in smokers.
Pulmonary fibrosis increases the risk of lung cancer by a factor of ten.
Pulmonary scarring, such as from prior tuberculosis, lacks association with lung cancer risk.
updates.explanation: The source states that lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States and has a 5-year survival of 15% across all stages and subtypes. Smoking causes 80-90% of lung cancers and pulmonary fibrosis increases risk tenfold. Asbestos increases lung-cancer risk by a factor of five and acts synergistically with smoking. Prior pulmonary scarring such as TB increases risk rather than having no association.

updates.question_text: Which statement is correct regarding histologic subtype and smoking association in the source?
options_before: Lifelong non-smokers without secondhand exposure almost always develop small cell carcinoma if they develop primary bronchogenic carcinoma.
Almost all squamous cell and small cell carcinomas are seen in smokers.
Adenocarcinoma is unrelated to tobacco smoking.
Large cell carcinoma is the classic tumour arising from asbestos plaques.
Carcinoid tumour is the most common smoking-related lung cancer subtype.
options_after: Lifelong non-smokers without secondhand exposure typically develop small cell carcinoma if they develop primary bronchogenic carcinoma.
Almost all squamous cell and small cell carcinomas are seen in smokers.
Adenocarcinoma is unrelated to tobacco smoking.
Large cell carcinoma is the classic tumour arising from asbestos plaques.
Carcinoid tumour is the most common smoking-related lung cancer subtype.
updates.explanation: The source states that almost all squamous cell and small cell carcinomas occur in smokers. Adenocarcinoma is also associated with smoking, but a primary bronchogenic carcinoma in a lifelong non-smoker without secondhand exposure is almost always adenocarcinoma. The section does not identify large cell carcinoma or carcinoid tumour as the classic smoking-linked subtype in that way.

updates.question_text: Regarding solitary pulmonary nodules, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: A solitary pulmonary nodule is a well-defined round or oval parenchymal lesion measuring 30 mm or less.
A lesion larger than 30 mm is classified as a mass.
Nipple shadow, rib lesion, and summation of markings are common radiographic mimics.
The differential diagnosis is limited to bronchogenic carcinoma.
Central, laminar, and diffuse calcification patterns are almost always malignant.
options_after: A solitary pulmonary nodule is a well-defined round or oval parenchymal lesion measuring 30 mm or less.
A lesion larger than 30 mm is classified as a mass.
Nipple shadow, rib lesion, and summation of markings are common radiographic mimics.
The differential diagnosis is limited to bronchogenic carcinoma.
Central, laminar, and diffuse calcification patterns are typically malignant.
updates.explanation: A solitary pulmonary nodule is defined as a well-defined round or oval lung-parenchymal lesion measuring 30 mm or less; lesions larger than 30 mm are masses. Common radiographic mimics include nipple shadows, rib lesions, and summation of markings. The differential includes neoplastic, inflammatory, and congenital causes. Central, laminar, and diffuse calcifications are described as almost always benign.

updates.question_text: Regarding CT morphology of solid pulmonary nodules, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Intra-lesional fat suggests an invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma rather than a benign lesion.
Popcorn calcification is suggestive of pulmonary hamartoma.
Amorphous calcification is associated with malignancy, usually mucinous tumours.
Small size is the single most important risk factor for malignancy regardless of morphology.
Clustered nodules strongly suggest haematogenous metastases rather than infection.
options_after: Intra-lesional fat suggests an invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma rather than a benign lesion.
Popcorn calcification is suggestive of pulmonary hamartoma.
Amorphous calcification is associated with malignancy, usually mucinous tumours.
Small size is the single most important risk factor for malignancy despite variation in morphology.
Clustered nodules strongly suggest haematogenous metastases rather than infection.
updates.explanation: Popcorn calcification supports pulmonary hamartoma, while amorphous calcification is associated with malignancy, usually mucinous tumours. Intra-lesional fat suggests benign hamartoma or lipoid granuloma rather than invasive adenocarcinoma. Large size, not small size, is the single most important malignancy risk factor. Clustering of nodules suggests infection rather than haematogenous metastases.

updates.question_text: Regarding pulmonary nodule follow-up, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The 2017 Fleischner recommendations apply to noncalcified nodules in patients older than 35 without a history of malignancy.
Follow-up is recommended for every low-risk patient with solitary or multiple nodules smaller than 6 mm.
A 26% increase in diameter corresponds to doubling in nodule volume.
A decrease in size on a single follow-up study is sufficient to prove benignity.
Longer follow-up is recommended for subsolid nodules because they often represent indolent adenocarcinomas.
options_after: The 2017 Fleischner recommendations apply to noncalcified nodules in patients older than 35 without a history of malignancy.
Follow-up is recommended for most low-risk patients with solitary or multiple nodules smaller than 6 mm.
A 26% increase in diameter corresponds to doubling in nodule volume.
A decrease in size on a single follow-up study is sufficient to prove benignity.
Longer follow-up is recommended for subsolid nodules because they often represent indolent adenocarcinomas.
updates.explanation: The source limits the 2017 Fleischner recommendations to noncalcified nodules in patients over 35 without malignancy history. Low-risk patients with nodules under 6 mm do not require routine follow-up, so mandatory follow-up for every such patient is incorrect. A 26% diameter increase doubles volume, and subsolid nodules require longer follow-up because they may represent indolent adenocarcinoma. A single decrease in size does not establish benignity.

updates.question_text: Which statement is correct regarding pleural effusion in lung cancer?
options_before: All effusions associated with lung cancer contain malignant cells.
Pleural effusion in lung cancer is staged as T1 regardless of cytology.
Cytology is unnecessary because imaging can distinguish sterile and malignant effusions reliably.
A malignant effusion is an M1a lesion and precludes curative resection.
Pleural effusion excludes lymphatic obstruction.
options_after: Most effusions associated with lung cancer contain malignant cells.
Pleural effusion in lung cancer is staged as T1 despite variation in cytology.
Cytology is unnecessary because imaging can distinguish sterile and malignant effusions reliably.
A malignant effusion is an M1a lesion and precludes curative resection.
Pleural effusion excludes lymphatic obstruction.
updates.explanation: The source states that malignant pleural effusion means malignant cells are present in the effusion. This is staged as M1a and precludes curative resection. Not all effusions in lung cancer are malignant, so cytological evaluation is necessary. Effusions may result from lymphatic obstruction or pleural metastases.

updates.question_text: Regarding the eighth-edition TNM staging principles described in the source, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Stage IV disease is generally treated surgically unless there are multiple brain metastases.
Early stages up to IIB and sometimes IIIA are unresectable and are generally not treated surgically.
Extrathoracic metastases are no longer subdivided in the eighth edition.
Tumour-size T classifiers were upstaged to reflect that survival is inversely proportional to each centimetre increase until 7 cm.
Stage IIIB disease with N3 nodes or T4/N2 disease is unresectable.
options_after: Stage IV disease is generally treated surgically unless there are multiple brain metastases.
Early stages up to IIB and sometimes IIIA are unresectable and are generally not treated surgically.
Extrathoracic metastases are not currently subdivided in the eighth edition.
Tumour-size T classifiers were upstaged to reflect that survival is inversely proportional to each centimetre increase until 7 cm.
Stage IIIB disease with N3 nodes or T4/N2 disease is unresectable.
updates.explanation: The eighth edition uses tumour size more granularly because prognosis worsens with each centimetre up to 7 cm, after which prognosis resembles T4 disease. Extrathoracic metastases are split into M1b oligometastatic and M1c multiple-metastasis categories, so stating that they are no longer subdivided is incorrect. Stage IIIB disease with N3 nodes or T4/N2 disease is unresectable. Surgery is usually performed for early stages up to IIB and sometimes IIIA, while stage IV is generally non-surgical unless there is a solitary adrenal or brain metastasis.

updates.question_text: Regarding nodal staging in lung cancer, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: N1 includes contralateral mediastinal nodes.
N2 includes supraclavicular nodes on either side.
Subcarinal lymph nodes are N1 for all primary lung tumours.
For level 2 and 4 nodes, the boundary between right and left is the left lateral border of the trachea.
N3 includes contralateral mediastinal or hilar nodes, or supraclavicular nodes on either side.
options_after: N1 includes contralateral mediastinal nodes.
N2 includes supraclavicular nodes on either side.
Subcarinal lymph nodes are N1 for most primary lung tumours.
For level 2 and 4 nodes, the boundary between right and left is the left lateral border of the trachea.
N3 includes contralateral mediastinal or hilar nodes, or supraclavicular nodes on either side.
updates.explanation: The source defines N1 as ipsilateral hilar or intrapulmonary nodes and N2 as ipsilateral mediastinal nodes. N3 is contralateral mediastinal or hilar disease, or supraclavicular nodes on either side. The right-left boundary for levels 2 and 4 is the left lateral tracheal border because of lymphatic drainage. Subcarinal station 7 is listed among mediastinal nodes rather than the N1 hilar/intrapulmonary group.

updates.question_text: Regarding M staging in lung cancer, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: M0 indicates local thoracic metastatic disease only.
A separate tumour nodule in the contralateral lung is staged as T4.
M1a includes malignant pleural or pericardial effusion.
M1b is malignant pleural effusion without extrathoracic metastasis.
M1c is multiple extrathoracic metastases in one or more organs.
options_after: M0 indicates local thoracic metastatic disease in typical cases.
A separate tumour nodule in the contralateral lung is staged as T4.
M1a includes malignant pleural or pericardial effusion.
M1b is malignant pleural effusion without extrathoracic metastasis.
M1c is multiple extrathoracic metastases in one or more organs.
updates.explanation: The source defines M0 as no metastatic disease. M1a is local thoracic metastatic disease, including contralateral lung tumour nodule and malignant pleural or pericardial effusion. M1b is a single extrathoracic metastasis or single non-regional node, not malignant pleural effusion. M1c is multiple extrathoracic metastases in one or more organs.

updates.question_text: Which statement is correct regarding a left-sided lung primary with right paratracheal nodal disease?
options_before: The right paratracheal nodes are always N1 because they are hilar nodes.
The right paratracheal nodes are ignored because only ipsilateral mediastinal nodes matter.
The finding is M1b because paratracheal nodes are extrathoracic.
The right-sided nodes would be N3 because they are contralateral for a left-sided primary.
The nodal stage is N0 if no supraclavicular nodes are present.
options_after: The right paratracheal nodes are characteristically N1 because they are hilar nodes.
Right paratracheal nodes are ignored because contralateral mediastinal disease does not affect nodal stage.
The finding is M1b because paratracheal nodes are extrathoracic.
The right-sided nodes would be N3 because they are contralateral for a left-sided primary.
The nodal stage is N0 if supraclavicular nodes are absent.
updates.explanation: For the left-sided primary example in the source, right-sided mediastinal nodes are contralateral and therefore N3. Paratracheal nodes are mediastinal, not extrathoracic metastases. N1 refers to ipsilateral hilar or intrapulmonary nodes, and N0 requires no nodal metastases.

updates.question_text: Regarding acute pulmonary embolism management categories, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Low-risk non-massive PE is managed with anticoagulation only or surveillance in selected isolated subsegmental PE.
Intermediate-risk submassive PE should never receive intervention even when RV strain or acute distress is moderate to severe.
High-risk massive PE is managed with anticoagulation plus intervention.
Intervention options exclude systemic IV thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy.
Anticoagulation is contraindicated in all patients with massive PE.
options_after: Low-risk non-massive PE is managed with anticoagulation only or surveillance in selected isolated subsegmental PE.
Intermediate-risk submassive PE should not receive intervention even when RV strain or acute distress is moderate to severe.
High-risk massive PE is managed with anticoagulation plus intervention.
Intervention options exclude systemic IV thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy.
Anticoagulation is contraindicated in most patients with massive PE.
updates.explanation: The source stratifies acute PE management by risk. Low-risk PE receives anticoagulation alone or surveillance for selected isolated subsegmental PE without proximal lower-extremity DVT and low recurrence risk. Massive PE requires anticoagulation plus intervention. Submassive PE may receive intervention if RV strain or acute distress is more moderate to severe, and the intervention list includes systemic IV thrombolysis, mechanical thrombectomy, and catheter-directed therapy, with surgical embolectomy listed for massive PE.

updates.question_text: Regarding chronic pulmonary embolism and CTEPH, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Chronic PE may present with exertional shortness of breath, fatigue, and chest pressure or pain.
Chronic PE may appear as eccentric filling defects, webs, or pruning of pulmonary artery branches.
Mosaic attenuation and occasional scarring are parenchymal signs of chronic PE.
All patients with chronic PE develop pulmonary hypertension.
CTEPH is chronic pulmonary embolism without pulmonary hypertension.
options_after: Chronic PE may present with exertional shortness of breath, fatigue, and chest pressure or pain.
Chronic PE may appear as eccentric filling defects, webs, or pruning of pulmonary artery branches.
Mosaic attenuation and occasional scarring are parenchymal signs of chronic PE.
Most patients with chronic PE develop pulmonary hypertension.
CTEPH is chronic pulmonary embolism without pulmonary hypertension.
updates.explanation: Chronic PE produces symptoms of pulmonary hypertension such as exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, and chest pressure or pain. Imaging may show eccentric defects, webs, pruning, mosaic attenuation, and scarring. CTEPH is the constellation of chronic PE with pulmonary hypertension, not chronic PE without pulmonary hypertension. The source explicitly notes that not all chronic PE patients develop pulmonary hypertension.

updates.question_text: Regarding CTEPH workup and CT pulmonary angiogram pitfalls, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Patients with suspected CTEPH are often evaluated with both V/Q scan and CT PE because each can miss defects.
V/Q scan is expected to be normal in CTEPH because only CT can show perfusion defects.
Hilar lymph nodes and mucus-impacted bronchi cannot simulate pulmonary embolism.
Unopacified pulmonary veins can simulate PE on a single CT slice, but tracing the vessel to the heart can distinguish artery from vein.
Valsalva-related contrast disruption is best recognised by dense contrast in the pulmonary artery with no contrast in the aorta.
options_after: Patients with suspected CTEPH are often evaluated with both V/Q scan and CT PE because each can miss defects.
A normal V/Q scan excludes CTEPH because CTA is sufficient to demonstrate chronic perfusion defects.
Hilar lymph nodes and mucus-impacted bronchi will not simulate pulmonary embolism.
Unopacified pulmonary veins can simulate PE on a single CT slice, but tracing the vessel to the heart can distinguish artery from vein.
Valsalva-related contrast disruption is best recognised by dense contrast in the pulmonary artery without contrast in the aorta.
updates.explanation: The source states that V/Q and CT PE may both be used because each can miss CTEPH defects, and V/Q shows segmental perfusion defects rather than being normal. Hilar nodes and mucus-impacted bronchi can simulate PE. Unopacified veins can also mimic PE on a single slice, but tracing the vessel back to the heart distinguishes artery from vein. Valsalva causes dense contrast in the SVC, no contrast in the pulmonary artery, and dense contrast in the aorta; late timing has less dense contrast in the SVC.

updates.question_text: Regarding the WHO pulmonary hypertension groups in this section, which of the following pairings are correct?
options_before: Group 1 - pulmonary arterial hypertension including idiopathic/familial PPH and shunt-related PAH.
Group 2 - pulmonary venous hypertension from left-sided heart disease.
Group 3 - pulmonary hypertension caused by chronic thromboembolic disease.
Group 4 - pulmonary hypertension due to chronic thromboembolic disease.
Group 5 - pulmonary hypertension only from congenital left-to-right shunts.
options_after: Group 1 - pulmonary arterial hypertension including idiopathic/familial PPH and shunt-related PAH.
Group 2 - pulmonary venous hypertension from left-sided heart disease.
Group 3 - pulmonary hypertension caused by chronic thromboembolic disease.
Group 4 - pulmonary hypertension due to chronic thromboembolic disease.
Group 5 - pulmonary hypertension primarily from congenital left-to-right shunts.
updates.explanation: The source classifies group 1 as pulmonary arterial hypertension, including idiopathic/familial PPH and shunt-related PAH; group 2 as pulmonary venous hypertension from left-sided heart disease; and group 4 as chronic thromboembolic disease. Group 3 is chronic hypoxaemia-related disease from COPD, interstitial lung disease, or sleep apnoea, not chronic thromboembolic disease. Group 5 includes miscellaneous disorders, such as sarcoidosis or pulmonary-vessel compression from neoplasm or fibrosing mediastinitis.

updates.question_text: Regarding fibrosing mediastinitis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It is progressive proliferation of fibrous tissue within the mediastinum that may encase and compress mediastinal structures.
The most common causes listed are histoplasmosis and tuberculosis.
Fibrous encasement of pulmonary veins does not alter endothelial cells.
Encasement of pulmonary arteries cannot create pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension.
Imaging typically shows no mediastinal soft tissue and excludes calcified lymph nodes.
options_after: It is progressive proliferation of fibrous tissue within the mediastinum that may encase and compress mediastinal structures.
The most common causes listed are histoplasmosis and tuberculosis.
Fibrous encasement of pulmonary veins does not alter endothelial cells.
Encasement of pulmonary arteries will not create pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension.
Imaging typically fails to show mediastinal soft tissue and excludes calcified lymph nodes.
updates.explanation: Fibrosing mediastinitis is fibrous proliferation in the mediastinum that can encase and compress vessels and other structures. Histoplasmosis and tuberculosis are the commonest causes listed. Venous encasement can produce permanent endothelial changes, and pulmonary arterial encasement can cause pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension. Imaging features include increased mediastinal soft tissue, often with calcified nodes from prior granulomatous infection.

updates.question_text: Regarding hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It is caused by hypersensitivity reaction to inhaled organic antigens.
A history of antigen exposure is always elicited.
Acute or subacute disease is defined by established fibrosis without recurrence.
Acute or subacute disease may show ground glass, consolidation, small ill-defined centrilobular nodules, and mosaic attenuation.
Chronic disease has fibrosis as its key feature, often with peribronchovascular fibrosis.
options_after: It is caused by hypersensitivity reaction to inhaled organic antigens.
A history of antigen exposure is characteristically elicited.
Acute or subacute disease is defined by established fibrosis without recurrence.
Acute or subacute disease may show ground glass, consolidation, small ill-defined centrilobular nodules, and mosaic attenuation.
Chronic disease has fibrosis as its key feature, often with peribronchovascular fibrosis.
updates.explanation: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is due to inhaled organic antigens such as bird proteins or thermophilic actinomycetes, though exposure history is not found in about one third of patients. Acute or subacute disease may recur but does not have fibrosis and can show ground glass, consolidation, centrilobular nodules, and mosaic attenuation. Chronic HP is defined by fibrosis, typically peribronchovascular and often upper-lobe predominant.

updates.question_text: Regarding the head-cheese sign and chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The head-cheese sign is central opacity with peripheral ground glass haemorrhage.
Honeycombing is more common in HP than in IPF and is always basal.
The head-cheese sign combines patchy ground glass and lucent areas due to air trapping.
Chronic HP always lacks findings of acute or subacute disease.
When honeycombing occurs in HP, it may involve the upper lobes.
options_after: The head-cheese sign is central opacity with peripheral ground glass haemorrhage.
Honeycombing is more common in HP than in IPF and is characteristically basal.
The head-cheese sign combines patchy ground glass and lucent areas due to air trapping.
Chronic HP characteristically lacks findings of acute or subacute disease.
When honeycombing occurs in HP, it may involve the upper lobes.
updates.explanation: The head-cheese sign combines patchy ground glass with lucent areas caused by air trapping. Chronic HP may have superimposed centrilobular nodules, ground glass, and mosaic attenuation from acute or subacute disease. Honeycombing is not common in HP, unlike IPF, but if present it may involve the upper lobes. Central opacity with peripheral ground glass is the halo sign pattern described for angioinvasive aspergillosis.

updates.question_text: Regarding pneumoconioses, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Pneumoconiosis is caused by organic dust inhalation, whereas hypersensitivity pneumonitis is caused by inorganic dust.
Silicosis and coal workers pneumoconiosis are the two most common pneumoconioses.
Uncomplicated silicosis and coal workers pneumoconiosis most characteristically show upper-lobe predominant perilymphatic nodules.
Silicosis and coal workers pneumoconiosis both increase the risk of tuberculosis.
Their imaging findings are entirely distinct from sarcoidosis.
options_after: Pneumoconiosis is caused by organic dust inhalation, whereas hypersensitivity pneumonitis is caused by inorganic dust.
Silicosis and coal workers pneumoconiosis are the two most common pneumoconioses.
Uncomplicated silicosis and coal workers pneumoconiosis most characteristically show upper-lobe predominant perilymphatic nodules.
Silicosis and coal workers pneumoconiosis both increase the risk of tuberculosis.
Their imaging findings are predominantly distinct from sarcoidosis.
updates.explanation: Pneumoconiosis is inorganic dust disease, while HP is caused by organic antigens. Silicosis and coal workers pneumoconiosis are the two most common pneumoconioses and have indistinguishable imaging features, overlapping with sarcoidosis. The characteristic uncomplicated pattern is upper-lobe predominant perilymphatic nodules. Both silicosis and CWP confer increased TB risk.

updates.question_text: Regarding pulmonary vasculitis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Pulmonary vasculitis may manifest as alveolar haemorrhage or nodular foci with cavitation.
Microscopic polyangiitis is the most common cause of pulmonary haemorrhage with rapidly progressive renal failure in pulmonary-renal syndrome.
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis usually has P-ANCA positivity and never affects the upper airways.
Alveolar haemorrhage in microscopic polyangiitis occurs in all patients.
Microscopic polyangiitis may show diffuse central-predominant ground-glass opacity due to haemorrhage.
options_after: Pulmonary vasculitis may manifest as alveolar haemorrhage or nodular foci with cavitation.
Microscopic polyangiitis is the most common cause of pulmonary haemorrhage with rapidly progressive renal failure in pulmonary-renal syndrome.
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis usually has P-ANCA positivity and will not affect the upper airways.
Alveolar haemorrhage in microscopic polyangiitis occurs in most patients.
Microscopic polyangiitis may show diffuse central-predominant ground-glass opacity due to haemorrhage.
updates.explanation: Pulmonary vasculitis can appear as alveolar haemorrhage or cavitating nodular foci. Microscopic polyangiitis is highlighted as the most common cause of pulmonary haemorrhage with rapidly progressive renal failure, is P-ANCA positive, and shows central-predominant ground glass from haemorrhage. Alveolar haemorrhage occurs in only 20-30% of patients. GPA is C-ANCA positive and affects the upper airways as part of its classic triad.

updates.question_text: Which statement is correct regarding granulomatosis with polyangiitis in the source?
options_before: It is a large-vessel vasculitis that spares the kidneys.
It is characterised by pulmonary oedema and pleural effusion without nodules.
It is P-ANCA positive and causes pulmonary haemorrhage in all patients.
It is a systemic small-vessel vasculitis with sinusitis, lung involvement, renal insufficiency, and C-ANCA positivity.
It causes only diffuse miliary nodules without cavitation.
options_after: It is a large-vessel vasculitis that spares the kidneys.
It is characterised by pulmonary oedema and pleural effusion without nodules.
It is P-ANCA positive and causes pulmonary haemorrhage in most patients.
It is a systemic small-vessel vasculitis with sinusitis, lung involvement, renal insufficiency, and C-ANCA positivity.
It causes primarily diffuse miliary nodules without cavitation.
updates.explanation: The source describes GPA as a systemic small-vessel vasculitis with the classic triad of sinusitis, lung involvement, and renal insufficiency, with C-ANCA positivity. Lung disease may show multiple nodules with a ground-glass halo in the acute setting and cavitation. P-ANCA positivity and pulmonary-renal haemorrhage are used in the microscopic polyangiitis discussion.

updates.question_text: Regarding drug toxicity and radiation lung injury, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Pulmonary drug reaction has only one imaging response: UIP.
Pulmonary drug reaction is most commonly due to cytotoxic drugs and can elicit a finite range of injury responses.
Radiographic abnormalities occur after external radiotherapy in up to 40% of patients, although most are asymptomatic.
Radiation-associated abnormalities are always anatomically limited to one lobe.
Radiation changes often have non-anatomic linear margins and may cross fissures.
options_after: Pulmonary drug reaction has a single imaging response: UIP.
Pulmonary drug reaction is most commonly due to cytotoxic drugs and can elicit a finite range of injury responses.
Radiographic abnormalities occur after external radiotherapy in up to 40% of patients, although most are asymptomatic.
Radiation-associated abnormalities are characteristically anatomically limited to one lobe.
Radiation changes often have non-anatomic linear margins and may cross fissures.
updates.explanation: The source lists several finite lung responses to injury, including oedema, ARDS, organising pneumonia, eosinophilic pneumonia, bronchiolitis obliterans, haemorrhage, NSIP, and UIP, and says cytotoxic drugs are common causes. Up to 40% of patients develop radiographic abnormalities after external radiotherapy, most asymptomatic. The abnormality is often but not always confined to the radiation port and usually has non-anatomic linear margins; radiation-associated findings may cross fissures.

updates.question_text: Regarding sarcoidosis staging on radiographs, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Stage 0 is end-stage fibrosis.
Stage 1 is hilar or mediastinal adenopathy only, without lung changes.
Stage 4 is hilar or mediastinal adenopathy only without lung changes.
Patients necessarily progress through stages 0 to 4 in order.
The historical staging system applies to radiographic findings rather than CT.
