options_after: Obliteration or infiltration of pterygopalatine fossa fat by soft tissue is the earliest imaging sign of pathological involvement.
The pterygopalatine fossa can primarily be involved by benign congenital cysts, not malignancy or inflammation.
Contrast enhancement and enlargement of neural foramina or canals leading to the fossa indicate perineural tumour spread.
Later signs include spontaneous restoration of fat and narrowing of most bony walls.
Primary sites that can spread to the fossa are limited to pituitary macroadenoma and Rathke cleft cyst.
updates.explanation: The source describes the pterygopalatine fossa as a hub for direct invasion and perineural spread. The earliest imaging sign is loss or infiltration of its normal fat by soft tissue. Later signs are widening or erosion of bony walls. Enhancement and enlargement of the connected neural foramina or canals indicate perineural tumour spread. Potential primary sites include cheek, maxillary sinus, nasal cavity/nasopharynx, palate, masticator space and orbit, not primarily sellar lesions such as pituitary macroadenoma or Rathke cleft cyst.

updates.question_text:
A contrast-enhanced temporal bone MRI shows a heterogeneously enhancing middle ear lesion with internal flow voids.

Which of the following statements are correct regarding this image?
options_before: The lesion should demonstrate no enhancement because it is keratin rather than tumour
The finding is most specific for congenital cholesteatoma medial to the ossicles
A glomus tympanicum tumour is typically centred at the cochlear promontory along Jacobson nerve
Intratumoral flow voids in larger tumours produce the classic salt-and-pepper MRI pattern
Ga-68 DOTATATE PET-CT is described as the most sensitive modality for detecting these tumours
options_after: The lesion should lack enhancement because it is keratin rather than tumour
The finding is most specific for congenital cholesteatoma medial to the ossicles
A glomus tympanicum tumour is typically centred at the cochlear promontory along Jacobson nerve
Intratumoral flow voids in larger tumours produce the classic salt-and-pepper MRI pattern
Ga-68 DOTATATE PET-CT is described as the most sensitive modality for detecting these tumours
updates.explanation: The image and caption describe a glomus tympanicum paraganglioma. Glomus tympanicum is isolated to the middle ear and centred at the cochlear promontory along Jacobson nerve, with the jugular plate preserved. Paragangliomas are highly vascular and avidly enhancing; larger lesions may show the salt-and-pepper pattern from flow voids. Their SSTR2 expression explains the role of Ga-68 DOTATATE PET-CT.

updates.question_text: Regarding the classification and typical location of middle ear cholesteatoma, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Congenital cholesteatoma is the vast majority of all cholesteatomas
Primary acquired cholesteatoma occurs in the setting of a tympanic membrane retraction pocket
Secondary acquired cholesteatoma is unrelated to tympanic membrane perforation, trauma, or surgery
Acquired cholesteatomas most commonly arise in Prussak space
Acquired pars tensa and congenital middle ear cholesteatomas are typically medial to the ossicles
options_after: Congenital cholesteatoma is the vast majority of most cholesteatomas
Primary acquired cholesteatoma occurs in the setting of a tympanic membrane retraction pocket
Secondary acquired cholesteatoma is unrelated to tympanic membrane perforation, trauma, or surgery
Acquired cholesteatomas most commonly arise in Prussak space
Acquired pars tensa and congenital middle ear cholesteatomas are typically medial to the ossicles
updates.explanation: Acquired cholesteatoma represents the vast majority and may be primary or secondary. Primary acquired lesions occur with tympanic membrane retraction pockets, often related to Eustachian tube dysfunction. Secondary acquired lesions occur with tympanic membrane perforation from chronic otitis media, trauma, or surgery. Prussak space is the common site of acquired pars flaccida cholesteatoma, whereas pars tensa and congenital middle ear lesions are usually medial to the ossicles.

updates.question_text: Regarding CT assessment of cholesteatoma before surgery, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: CT is sensitive for detecting even small cholesteatomas
Middle ear opacification on CT is specific for cholesteatoma and needs no assessment for bony erosion
Pars flaccida cholesteatoma can show early erosion of the scutum
The long process of the incus is the ossicular site most commonly eroded
Erosion involving the lateral semicircular canal, facial nerve canal, tegmen tympani, or sigmoid plate is surgically important
options_after: CT is sensitive for detecting even small cholesteatomas
Middle ear opacification on CT is specific for cholesteatoma and does not need assessment for bony erosion
Pars flaccida cholesteatoma can show early erosion of the scutum
The long process of the incus is the ossicular site most commonly eroded
Erosion involving the lateral semicircular canal, facial nerve canal, tegmen tympani, or sigmoid plate is surgically important
updates.explanation: CT is sensitive for small cholesteatoma but middle ear opacification is non-specific and can reflect effusion, granulation tissue, or fibrosis. Bony erosion is therefore crucial, especially scutum erosion in pars flaccida lesions and ossicular erosion, most commonly of the long process of the incus. Erosion of the lateral semicircular canal, facial nerve canal, tegmen, or sigmoid plate must be identified to protect these structures during surgery.

updates.question_text: Regarding otomastoiditis and mastoid complications, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Fluid in the middle ear and mastoid on imaging is specific for clinically significant otomastoiditis
Coalescent mastoiditis is defined on CT by resorption of bony septae with merging of adjacent opacified mastoid air cells
A subperiosteal abscess results when coalescent mastoiditis erodes through the external mastoid cortex but remains contained by periosteum
Bezold abscess tracks along the sternocleidomastoid muscle after erosion through the mastoid tip
Imaging is routinely required to diagnose uncomplicated otitis media in every patient
options_after: Fluid in the middle ear and mastoid on imaging is specific for clinically significant otomastoiditis
Coalescent mastoiditis is defined on CT by resorption of bony septae with merging of adjacent opacified mastoid air cells
A subperiosteal abscess results when coalescent mastoiditis erodes through the external mastoid cortex but remains contained by periosteum
Bezold abscess tracks along the sternocleidomastoid muscle after erosion through the mastoid tip
Imaging is routinely required to diagnose uncomplicated otitis media in most patients
updates.explanation: Otomastoiditis is primarily a clinical diagnosis, and middle ear or mastoid fluid on imaging is common and non-specific. Imaging is used to detect complications. Coalescent mastoiditis is defined by CT resorption of bony septae, allowing opacified mastoid air cells to merge. External cortical erosion contained by periosteum creates a subperiosteal abscess, while mastoid tip erosion can track along the sternocleidomastoid as a Bezold abscess.

updates.question_text: Regarding intracranial and intratemporal complications of otomastoiditis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Intracranial complications include meningitis, epidural abscess, subdural empyema, cerebritis, brain abscess, and dural venous sinus thrombosis
Labyrinthitis and petrous apicitis are excluded from the temporal bone complication spectrum
Otomastoiditis mortality is mainly due to external auditory canal exostosis
Chronic otitis media sequelae never affect the ossicles
Intratympanic sequelae of chronic otitis media include cholesteatoma, cholesterol granuloma, tympanosclerosis, and ossicular erosion
options_after: Intracranial complications include meningitis, epidural abscess, subdural empyema, cerebritis, brain abscess, and dural venous sinus thrombosis
Labyrinthitis and petrous apicitis are excluded from the temporal bone complication spectrum
Otomastoiditis mortality is mainly due to external auditory canal exostosis
Chronic otitis media sequelae will not affect the ossicles
Intratympanic sequelae of chronic otitis media include cholesteatoma, cholesterol granuloma, tympanosclerosis, and ossicular erosion
updates.explanation: The source identifies intracranial complications as the main cause of mortality in acute and chronic otomastoiditis, including meningitis, empyema, abscess, cerebritis, and dural venous sinus thrombosis. Chronic otitis media can leave intratympanic sequelae such as effusion, granulation tissue, cholesteatoma, cholesterol granuloma, tympanosclerosis, and ossicular erosion. Labyrinthitis and petrous apicitis are part of the temporal bone discussion rather than excluded entities.

updates.question_text:
A temporal bone CT in a child shows subtle enlargement of the tympanic segment of the facial nerve canal.

Which of the following statements is correct regarding this image?
options_before: The lesion should contain intralesional bone spicules and is therefore diagnostic of facial nerve venous malformation
Calcification is the typical CT finding in facial nerve schwannoma
Facial nerve schwannoma can present as enlargement of the bony canal containing the involved nerve segment
The most common location of facial nerve schwannoma is the posterior genu
Facial nerve schwannoma never presents without facial nerve symptoms
options_after: The lesion should contain intralesional bone spicules and is therefore diagnostic of facial nerve venous malformation
Calcification is the typical CT finding in facial nerve schwannoma
Facial nerve schwannoma can present as enlargement of the bony canal containing the involved nerve segment
The most common location of facial nerve schwannoma is the posterior genu
Facial nerve schwannoma will not present without facial nerve symptoms
updates.explanation: The captioned CT demonstrates subtle enlargement of the tympanic segment of the facial nerve canal, which is the typical CT finding of facial nerve schwannoma. These tumours most commonly involve the geniculate ganglion, followed by labyrinthine and tympanic segments, and usually enhance briskly on MRI without calcification. Up to 30% of patients may present without facial nerve symptoms. Honeycomb intralesional spicules are instead characteristic of facial nerve venous malformation.

updates.question_text:
A temporal bone CT demonstrates absence of the cochlea, a dysplastic vestibule, hypoplastic semicircular canals, and a small stenotic internal auditory canal.

Which of the following statements is correct regarding this image?
options_before: The expected diagnosis is incomplete partition type II
This is the most common form of cochlear deformity
The appearance is compatible with complete labyrinthine aplasia
The contralateral side is always normal when the abnormality is unilateral
The internal auditory canal is expected to be enlarged with a normal CN VIII
options_after: The expected diagnosis is incomplete partition type II
This is the most common form of cochlear deformity
The appearance is compatible with complete labyrinthine aplasia
The contralateral side is characteristically normal when the abnormality is unilateral
The internal auditory canal is expected to be enlarged with a normal CN VIII
updates.explanation: Complete labyrinthine aplasia, also called Michel aplasia, is the most severe inner ear deformity and is defined by absence of inner ear structures. CT shows an atretic or stenotic IAC without visualisation of CN VIII. It is extremely rare and accounts for about 1% of inner ear malformations. When unilateral, the contralateral ear is frequently also dysplastic rather than reliably normal.

updates.question_text: Regarding retrofenestral otospongiosis and cochlear demineralisation, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Retrofenestral otospongiosis is always limited to the external auditory canal
Retrofenestral otospongiosis is thought to represent a more severe form of disease
The only differential diagnosis for cochlear demineralisation is cholesteatoma
Involvement of the cochlear promontory can produce a red-tinged otologic appearance called the Schwartze sign
Differential diagnoses include osteogenesis imperfecta in a child, fibrous dysplasia in a young adult, and Paget disease in an older adult
options_after: Retrofenestral otospongiosis is characteristically limited to the external auditory canal
Retrofenestral otospongiosis is thought to represent a more severe form of disease
The principal differential diagnosis for cochlear demineralisation is cholesteatoma
Involvement of the cochlear promontory can produce a red-tinged otologic appearance called the Schwartze sign
Differential diagnoses include osteogenesis imperfecta in a child, fibrous dysplasia in a young adult, and Paget disease in an older adult
updates.explanation: Retrofenestral otospongiosis is a more severe form involving the otic capsule separate from the oval window, typically the cochlear capsule, with possible extension to the vestibule, semicircular canals, and IAC. Cochlear promontory involvement can produce the Schwartze sign. The source lists osteogenesis imperfecta, fibrous dysplasia, and Paget disease as differential diagnoses for cochlear demineralisation. Cholesteatoma is not given as the differential for this demineralisation pattern.

updates.question_text: Regarding less common CPA/IAC and intra-axial lesions extending to the CPA, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Lipomas and dermoids are less frequent benign lesions seen in the IAC/CPA
Ependymoma cannot extend into the CPA because the foramina of Luschka block tumour spread
Posterior fossa intra-axial neoplasms such as hemangioblastoma or glioma may invade laterally into the CPA
Ependymoma may extend into the CPA through the lateral fourth ventricular foramina
Petrous bone tumours such as chondrosarcoma or endolymphatic sac tumour may extend to the CPA
options_after: Lipomas and dermoids are less frequent benign lesions seen in the IAC/CPA
Ependymoma will not extend into the CPA because the foramina of Luschka block tumour spread
Posterior fossa intra-axial neoplasms such as hemangioblastoma or glioma may invade laterally into the CPA
Ependymoma may extend into the CPA through the lateral fourth ventricular foramina
Petrous bone tumours such as chondrosarcoma or endolymphatic sac tumour may extend to the CPA
updates.explanation: The source lists lipomas and dermoids as less frequent benign IAC/CPA lesions. Posterior fossa intra-axial neoplasms can extend laterally into the CPA, including hemangioblastoma or glioma. Ependymoma can squeeze through the lateral fourth ventricular foramina of Luschka into the CPA. Petrous bone tumours, including chondrosarcoma and endolymphatic sac tumours, may also extend to the CPA.

updates.question_text: Regarding complications of temporal bone fractures, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Delayed incomplete facial paralysis always requires immediate surgical exploration
Facial nerve transection results in immediate facial paralysis
CSF leak is seen in fractures involving the tegmen
Carotid canal fracture is unrelated to internal carotid artery injury
CT venography should be performed when the fracture line traverses the venous sinuses
options_after: Delayed incomplete facial paralysis characteristically requires immediate surgical exploration
Facial nerve transection results in immediate facial paralysis
CSF leak is seen in fractures involving the tegmen
Carotid canal fracture is unrelated to internal carotid artery injury
CT venography should be performed when the fracture line traverses the venous sinuses
updates.explanation: Facial nerve transection produces immediate facial paralysis, while delayed injury may result from contusion, oedema, or haematoma. CSF leak occurs with tegmen involvement and is more frequent in otic capsule-violating fractures. Carotid canal fracture is highly suggestive of internal carotid artery injury and should be evaluated with CTA. Venous sinus fracture traversal warrants CT venography.

updates.question_text: Regarding the petrous apex, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The petrous apex is the most medial portion of the temporal bone
It is normally composed entirely of air cells in nearly all individuals
Dorello canal contains the trigeminal ganglion
Pneumatisation of the petrous apex occurs in approximately 10% of the population and increases risk of cholesterol cyst or apical petrositis
Meckel's cave is the site of the facial nerve geniculate ganglion
options_after: The petrous apex is the most medial portion of the temporal bone
It is normally composed predominantly of air cells in the large majority of individuals
Dorello canal contains the trigeminal ganglion
Pneumatisation of the petrous apex occurs in approximately 10% of the population and increases risk of cholesterol cyst or apical petrositis
Meckel's cave is the site of the facial nerve geniculate ganglion
updates.explanation: The petrous apex is the most medial temporal bone segment and bridges the suprahyoid neck and intracranial compartment. It is normally composed of marrow and dense bone, but is pneumatised in about 10% of the population, increasing the risk of cholesterol cyst and apical petrositis. Cranial nerve VI passes through Dorello canal. Meckel's cave contains the trigeminal ganglion.

updates.question_text: Regarding posterior skull base anatomy, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The foramen magnum transmits the medulla oblongata, vertebral arteries, spinal arteries, and spinal accessory nerve
The jugular foramen and hypoglossal canal are separated by the foramen spinosum
Pars nervosa transmits cranial nerve IX, Jacobson nerve, and the inferior petrosal sinus
Pars vascularis is the smaller anteromedial compartment containing only cranial nerve XII
The hypoglossal canal transmits cranial nerve XII
options_after: The foramen magnum transmits the medulla oblongata, vertebral arteries, spinal arteries, and spinal accessory nerve
The jugular foramen and hypoglossal canal are separated by the foramen spinosum
Pars nervosa transmits cranial nerve IX, Jacobson nerve, and the inferior petrosal sinus
Pars vascularis is the smaller anteromedial compartment containing primarily cranial nerve XII
The hypoglossal canal transmits cranial nerve XII
updates.explanation: The foramen magnum transmits the medulla, vertebral arteries, anterior and posterior spinal arteries, and spinal accessory nerve. The jugular foramen and hypoglossal canal are separated by the jugular tubercle. Pars nervosa transmits cranial nerve IX with Jacobson nerve and the inferior petrosal sinus, while pars vascularis is larger and transmits the internal jugular vein, posterior meningeal artery, cranial nerves X and XI, and Arnold nerve. The hypoglossal canal transmits cranial nerve XII.

updates.question_text:
A CT through the mastoid air cells shows permeative moth-eaten bony destruction centred on the jugular foramen.

Which of the following statements are correct regarding this image?
options_before: The image is typical of smooth remodelling from a jugular foramen schwannoma
The appearance supports glomus jugulare tumour
Glomus jugulare tumours make up 80% of primary neoplasms arising from the jugular foramen
Meningiomas classically cause permeative erosion while glomus tumours cause hyperostosis
The typical patient is a young child with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and no pulsatile tinnitus
options_after: The image is typical of smooth remodelling from a jugular foramen schwannoma
The appearance supports glomus jugulare tumour
Glomus jugulare tumours make up 80% of primary neoplasms arising from the jugular foramen
Meningiomas classically cause permeative erosion while glomus tumours cause hyperostosis
The typical patient is a young child with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss without pulsatile tinnitus
updates.explanation: The captioned CT shows permeative moth-eaten destruction centred on the jugular foramen, supporting glomus jugulare tumour. The source states that glomus jugulare tumours account for 80% of primary jugular foramen neoplasms and classically present in late middle-aged women with pulsatile tinnitus and conductive hearing loss. CT bony change helps differentiate lesions: glomus tumours cause permeative erosion, schwannomas smooth remodelling, and meningiomas hyperostosis.

updates.question_text: Regarding the mucosal spaces of the oral cavity, pharynx, and larynx, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The oral cavity includes the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
The pharynx extends only from the soft palate to the hyoid bone
The nasopharynx is the top of the pharynx behind the nasal cavity
The hypopharynx extends from the palate to the hyoid and includes the posterior one-third of the tongue
Mucosal squamous cell carcinoma arises from the squamous lining of the pharynx, larynx, and sinonasal cavity
options_after: The oral cavity includes the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
The pharynx extends primarily from the soft palate to the hyoid bone
The nasopharynx is the top of the pharynx behind the nasal cavity
The hypopharynx extends from the palate to the hyoid and includes the posterior one-third of the tongue
Mucosal squamous cell carcinoma arises from the squamous lining of the pharynx, larynx, and sinonasal cavity
updates.explanation: The oral cavity is defined by the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, palate superiorly, and floor of mouth inferiorly. The nasopharynx lies posterior to the nasal cavity at the top of the pharynx. Mucosal SCC arises from the squamous lining of the pharynx, larynx, and sinonasal cavity. The pharynx extends from skull base to thoracic inlet; the oropharynx, not the hypopharynx, contains the posterior one-third of the tongue.

updates.question_text: Regarding TNM staging of mucosal squamous cell carcinoma in the head and neck, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The T and N criteria are identical across nasopharynx, oropharynx, hypopharynx, and all laryngeal subsites
T stage refers to primary tumour extent
Lymph node measurements are reported using short-axis diameter in contrast to other parts of the body
Tumour size and lymph nodes are reported using the longest diameter
M stage is used for parapharyngeal space invasion rather than distant metastases
options_after: The T and N criteria are closely comparable across nasopharynx, oropharynx, hypopharynx, and most laryngeal subsites
T stage refers to primary tumour extent
Lymph node measurements are reported using short-axis diameter in contrast to other parts of the body
Tumour size and lymph nodes are reported using the longest diameter
M stage is used for parapharyngeal space invasion rather than distant metastases
updates.explanation: TNM staging classifies primary tumour extent, regional lymph nodes, and distant metastases. In head and neck mucosal SCC, tumour size and lymph nodes are reported using longest diameter, unlike lymph node measurements in many other body sites. The T and N criteria are site-specific, and laryngeal staging also varies by supraglottic, glottic, and subglottic subsites. M stage refers to distant metastases.

updates.question_text: Regarding imaging and treatment considerations for nasopharyngeal SCC, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: T staging is primarily determined by lesion size alone
CT is preferred over MRI when skull base infiltration and intracranial extension are the key staging concerns
Extension to the parapharyngeal space, surrounding muscles, skull base, or intracranial compartment increases T stage
Treatment is most frequently surgical resection with neck dissection regardless of stage
Treatment is most frequently non-surgical, using chemotherapy and/or radiation depending on TNM stage
options_after: T staging is primarily determined by lesion size alone
CT is preferred over MRI when skull base infiltration and intracranial extension are the key staging concerns
Extension to the parapharyngeal space, surrounding muscles, skull base, or intracranial compartment increases T stage
Treatment is most frequently surgical resection with neck dissection despite variation in stage
Treatment is most frequently non-surgical, using chemotherapy and/or radiation depending on TNM stage
updates.explanation: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma T stage is primarily defined by tumour extent and invasion rather than size alone. Extension to parapharyngeal spaces, surrounding muscles, bony skull base, or intracranial compartment raises stage. MRI is preferred for staging because skull base infiltration and intracranial extension are crucial to detect. Treatment is usually non-surgical with chemotherapy and/or radiation according to TNM stage.

updates.question_text: Regarding dermoid and epidermoid lesions of the floor of mouth, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: A sack-of-marbles appearance from floating fat globules is pathognomonic for dermoid
A dermoid contains only ectoderm and an epidermoid contains at least two germ cell layers
Both lesions usually appear as avidly enhancing solid masses on CT
Dermoid lesions arise from the sublingual gland as a sequela of inflammation
The usual location is eccentric in the submandibular space rather than midline floor of mouth
options_after: A sack-of-marbles appearance from floating fat globules is pathognomonic for dermoid
A dermoid contains primarily ectoderm and an epidermoid contains at least two germ cell layers
Both lesions usually appear as avidly enhancing solid masses on CT
Dermoid lesions arise from the sublingual gland as a sequela of inflammation
The usual location is eccentric in the submandibular space rather than midline floor of mouth
updates.explanation: Dermoid is a teratomatous lesion containing at least two germ cell layers, whereas epidermoid contains only ectoderm. Both appear as fluid-attenuation lesions on CT, most commonly in the midline floor of mouth. The sack-of-marbles MRI appearance from floating fat globules is pathognomonic for dermoid. Ranula, not dermoid, arises from the sublingual gland as a mucous retention cyst.

updates.question_text:
A cystic lesion arises in the left sublingual space on contrast-enhanced CT at the level of the mandible.

Which of the following statements are correct regarding this image?
options_before: The lesion is most likely a Thornwaldt cyst because it is midline nasopharyngeal
A ranula is a mucous retention cyst arising from the sublingual gland or adjacent minor salivary glands
All ranulas begin in the submandibular space and secondarily extend into the sublingual space
A plunging ranula reaches the submandibular space by passing posteriorly over the mylohyoid free edge or directly through a mylohyoid defect
A dermoid cyst below the mandible is typically midline rather than eccentric
options_after: The lesion is most likely a Thornwaldt cyst because it is midline nasopharyngeal
A ranula is a mucous retention cyst arising from the sublingual gland or adjacent minor salivary glands
Most ranulas begin in the submandibular space and secondarily extend into the sublingual space
A plunging ranula reaches the submandibular space by passing posteriorly over the mylohyoid free edge or directly through a mylohyoid defect
A dermoid cyst below the mandible is typically midline rather than eccentric
updates.explanation: The captioned CT demonstrates a ranula in the sublingual space. Ranulas are mucous retention cysts arising from the sublingual gland or adjacent minor salivary glands and therefore begin in the sublingual space. Plunging ranulas extend into the submandibular space by passing posteriorly over the free edge of the mylohyoid or directly through a defect. A dermoid below the mandible is usually midline, unlike the eccentric plunging ranula pattern.

updates.question_text: Regarding thyroglossal duct cyst, lingual thyroid, and lymphatic malformation, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Approximately 65% of thyroglossal duct cysts are infrahyoid
Thyroglossal duct cysts are strictly always midline and cannot occur slightly off midline
Lingual thyroid is often the only functioning thyroid tissue, so the neck should be evaluated for a normal gland
Cystic hygroma is the least common lymphatic malformation and usually presents in late adulthood
Cystic hygroma has large lymphatic spaces and is most commonly located in the posterior triangle of the neck
options_after: Approximately 65% of thyroglossal duct cysts are infrahyoid
Thyroglossal duct cysts are strictly characteristically midline and will not occur slightly off midline
Lingual thyroid is often the only functioning thyroid tissue, so the neck should be evaluated for a normal gland
Cystic hygroma is the least common lymphatic malformation and usually presents in late adulthood
Cystic hygroma has large lymphatic spaces and is most commonly located in the posterior triangle of the neck
updates.explanation: Most thyroglossal duct cysts are infrahyoid and usually midline, although they may be slightly off midline, especially below the hyoid. Lingual thyroid is incompletely descended thyroid tissue at the floor of mouth and is often the only functioning thyroid, so the neck must be checked for a normal gland. Cystic hygroma is the commonest lymphatic malformation, usually present at birth, with large lymphatic spaces and posterior triangle predilection. Cavernous and capillary lymphangiomas have smaller spaces.

updates.question_text: Regarding radicular cysts, ameloblastoma, and odontogenic keratocyst, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Radicular cyst is the rarest odontogenic lytic lesion and is unrelated to dental infection
Radicular cyst cannot progress beyond the tooth apex into adjacent soft tissues
Ameloblastoma most commonly occurs in the anterior maxilla
Odontogenic keratocyst is frequently seen in the body and ramus of the mandible
Odontogenic keratocyst is more likely than ameloblastoma to be heterogeneous on T2 and not associated with mandibular buccolingual expansion
options_after: Radicular cyst is the rarest odontogenic lytic lesion and is unrelated to dental infection
Radicular cyst will not progress beyond the tooth apex into adjacent soft tissues
Ameloblastoma most commonly occurs in the anterior maxilla
Odontogenic keratocyst is frequently seen in the body and ramus of the mandible
Odontogenic keratocyst is more likely than ameloblastoma to be heterogeneous on T2 and not associated with mandibular buccolingual expansion
updates.explanation: Odontogenic keratocyst is a benign unilocular expansile lucent lesion most often in the body and ramus of the mandible. Compared with ameloblastoma, it is more likely to be heterogeneous on T2 and not associated with buccolingual expansion in the mandible. Radicular cyst is actually the most common odontogenic lytic lesion and is associated with an infected tooth; it may progress to dehiscence and soft tissue abscess. Ameloblastoma most often affects the ramus and posterior mandibular body.

updates.question_text:
A CT shows an expansile mixed-density peripherally calcified mass associated with the root of an anterior maxillary molar, with biopsy showing ameloblastoma.

Which of the following statements is correct regarding ameloblastoma?
options_before: It is a malignant lymphoma of the nasopharyngeal adenoids
It never appears unilocular on imaging
It is a benign epithelial neoplasm with locally aggressive behaviour
It is usually centred around the apex of an infected tooth
It is defined by absence of buccolingual expansion in all mandibular cases
options_after: It is a malignant lymphoma of the nasopharyngeal adenoids
It will not appear unilocular on imaging
It is a benign epithelial neoplasm with locally aggressive behaviour
It is usually centred around the apex of an infected tooth
It is defined by absence of buccolingual expansion in most mandibular cases
updates.explanation: Ameloblastoma is a benign epithelial neoplasm with locally aggressive behaviour. It most commonly occurs in the ramus and posterior body of the mandible, and classically appears as a multilocular lytic lesion with mixed cystic and solid regions. It can be unilocular 40% of the time and then may be indistinguishable from odontogenic keratocyst or dentigerous cyst. Radicular cyst is the lesion centred around an infected tooth apex.

updates.question_text: Regarding hypopharyngeal anatomy and SCC staging, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The hypopharynx is the superior continuation of the nasopharynx above the soft palate
Most hypopharyngeal SCCs arise in the piriform sinus
Aryepiglottic fold tumours are staged as hypopharyngeal tumours
Hypopharyngeal SCC staging ignores lesion size and depends only on nodal status
Imaging should assess hemilarynx fixation, local invasion, carotid encasement, and mediastinal involvement
options_after: The hypopharynx is the superior continuation of the nasopharynx above the soft palate
Most hypopharyngeal SCCs arise in the piriform sinus
Aryepiglottic fold tumours are staged as hypopharyngeal tumours
Hypopharyngeal SCC staging ignores lesion size and depends primarily on nodal status
Imaging should assess hemilarynx fixation, local invasion, carotid encasement, and mediastinal involvement
updates.explanation: The hypopharynx is the inferior continuation of the oropharynx, surrounding the larynx on three sides and extending to the inferior laryngeal border before becoming cervical oesophagus. Most hypopharyngeal SCCs arise in the piriform sinus. Staging depends on lesion size and invasion of adjacent structures, with imaging assessment of hemilarynx fixation, oesophageal mucosa, thyroid/cricoid cartilage, hyoid, prevertebral fascia, carotid artery, and mediastinal structures. Aryepiglottic fold tumours are staged as supraglottic laryngeal tumours.

updates.question_text: Regarding vocal cord paralysis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The most common cause is iatrogenic trauma from neck surgery
A mediastinal or thoracic mass is the most common mass cause of left vocal cord paralysis
CT shows thickening and medialisation of the aryepiglottic fold with enlargement of the piriform sinus on the affected side
Imaging should extend from the skull base to the level of the left pulmonary artery
The superior laryngeal nerve innervates all laryngeal musculature except cricothyroid
options_after: The most common cause is iatrogenic trauma from neck surgery
A mediastinal or thoracic mass is the most common mass cause of left vocal cord paralysis
CT shows thickening and medialisation of the aryepiglottic fold with enlargement of the piriform sinus on the affected side
Imaging should extend from the skull base to the level of the left pulmonary artery
The superior laryngeal nerve innervates most laryngeal musculature except cricothyroid
updates.explanation: Vocal cord paralysis is most often due to iatrogenic trauma from neck surgery, but masses along the vagus or recurrent laryngeal nerves are important causes. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is most often affected, and mediastinal or thoracic mass is the commonest mass cause on the left. Imaging should cover skull base to the left pulmonary artery. CT signs include medialised thickened aryepiglottic fold and enlarged ipsilateral piriform sinus. The recurrent laryngeal nerve innervates all laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid.

updates.question_text: Regarding supraglottic SCC staging and surgical management, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The number of involved supraglottic subsites is irrelevant to staging
Staging depends on involved supraglottic subsites, vocal cord mobility, and adjacent structure involvement
Involvement of bilateral arytenoid cartilage is a contraindication to supraglottic laryngectomy
Paraglottic space spread has no relevance in supraglottic tumours
Treatment is always total laryngectomy regardless of tumour extent
options_after: The number of involved supraglottic subsites is irrelevant to staging
Staging depends on involved supraglottic subsites, vocal cord mobility, and adjacent structure involvement
Involvement of bilateral arytenoid cartilage is a contraindication to supraglottic laryngectomy
Paraglottic space spread lacks relevance in supraglottic tumours
Treatment is characteristically total laryngectomy despite variation in tumour extent
updates.explanation: Supraglottic SCC staging depends on the number of involved supraglottic subsites, vocal cord mobility, and invasion of adjacent structures. Treatment can range from laser epiglottectomy to supraglottic or total laryngectomy. Several structures influence surgical planning, including laryngeal ventricle, thyroid cartilage, posterior cricoid, anterior commissure, and bilateral arytenoid involvement. Local paraglottic spread is particularly relevant in supraglottic tumours.

updates.question_text: Regarding glottic and subglottic SCC, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Glottic SCC staging depends on vocal cord mobility, cartilaginous involvement, and extension to relevant adjacent structures
Patients with glottic SCC usually present late because voice change is uncommon
Contralateral involvement is irrelevant because it never affects surgical planning
Transglottic tumours cross the laryngeal ventricle to involve both false and true vocal cords and have worse prognosis
Subglottic SCC constitutes less than 5% of laryngeal carcinomas
options_after: Glottic SCC staging depends on vocal cord mobility, cartilaginous involvement, and extension to relevant adjacent structures
Patients with glottic SCC usually present late because voice change is uncommon
Contralateral involvement is irrelevant because it will not affect surgical planning
Transglottic tumours cross the laryngeal ventricle to involve both false and true vocal cords and have worse prognosis
Subglottic SCC constitutes less than 5% of laryngeal carcinomas
updates.explanation: Glottic SCC staging depends on vocal cord mobility, cartilage involvement, and spread to relevant structures. Glottic lesions present early with voice change, so late presentation due to absent voice symptoms is incorrect. Contralateral involvement is a key consideration because it affects whether the opposite side can be spared. Transglottic tumours cross the ventricle to involve false and true cords and have worse prognosis. Subglottic SCC accounts for less than 5% of laryngeal carcinomas and often presents late.

updates.question_text: Regarding laryngeal haemangiomas, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: They most commonly occur in the supraglottic larynx in elderly adults
They are never associated with cutaneous lesions
Infantile lesions do not regress and are always surgically resected
They most commonly occur in the subglottic larynx in infants and may compromise the airway
Adult laryngeal haemangiomas are common and usually regress spontaneously
options_after: They most commonly occur in the supraglottic larynx in elderly adults
They are not associated with cutaneous lesions
Infantile lesions do not regress and are characteristically surgically resected
They most commonly occur in the subglottic larynx in infants and may compromise the airway
Adult laryngeal haemangiomas are common and usually regress spontaneously
updates.explanation: Laryngeal haemangiomas occur most commonly in the subglottic larynx in infants and are frequently associated with cutaneous lesions. They often regress in infants, but airway compromise may require laser therapy. Adult laryngeal haemangiomas are very rare, described only in case reports in the source, and do not regress spontaneously, so they are surgically treated.

updates.question_text:
A CT in bone windows shows a minimally displaced thyroid cartilage fracture after blunt neck trauma.

Which of the following statements are correct regarding laryngeal trauma?
options_before: Blunt trauma can compress the larynx against the cervical spine with posterior soft tissue injury from a sandwich effect
Thyroid and cricoid cartilage fractures are always easy to detect in young patients because the cartilage is fully ossified
Iatrogenic trauma from intubation cannot affect the arytenoid cartilages
Laryngeal trauma is staged using the nasopharyngeal carcinoma T classification
CT can demonstrate thyroid cartilage fracture
options_after: Blunt trauma can compress the larynx against the cervical spine with posterior soft tissue injury from a sandwich effect
Thyroid and cricoid cartilage fractures are characteristically easy to detect in young patients because the cartilage is fully ossified
Iatrogenic trauma from intubation will not affect the arytenoid cartilages
Laryngeal trauma is staged using the nasopharyngeal carcinoma T classification
CT can demonstrate thyroid cartilage fracture
updates.explanation: The captioned image demonstrates a thyroid cartilage fracture on CT bone windows. Blunt trauma may compress the larynx against the cervical spine, causing posterior soft tissue injury through a sandwich effect. Thyroid and cricoid fractures may be difficult to detect in young patients because ossification is incomplete. Intubation can cause arytenoid cartilage dislocation, so stating that it cannot affect the arytenoids is incorrect.

updates.question_text: Regarding other malignant neoplasms of the mucosal spaces, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Lymphoma can arise from the adenoids of the nasopharynx
Nasopharyngeal lymphoma is usually papillary thyroid carcinoma arising in a thyroglossal duct cyst
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma of the adenoids affects a younger population
Sarcomas are excluded from the larynx because it contains no cartilage
Chondrosarcomas are generally centred in cricoid or thyroid cartilage and have popcorn-like calcifications best seen on CT
options_after: Lymphoma can arise from the adenoids of the nasopharynx
Nasopharyngeal lymphoma is usually papillary thyroid carcinoma arising in a thyroglossal duct cyst
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma of the adenoids affects a younger population
Sarcomas are excluded from the larynx because it lacks cartilage
Chondrosarcomas are generally centred in cricoid or thyroid cartilage and have popcorn-like calcifications best seen on CT
updates.explanation: Lymphoma can arise from nasopharyngeal adenoids, most often non-Hodgkin lymphoma affecting a younger population. Sarcomas can occur in the larynx, including synovial sarcoma, chondrosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, and liposarcoma. Chondrosarcomas are usually centred in cricoid or thyroid cartilage and show characteristic popcorn-like calcifications on CT. Papillary carcinoma is the rare malignancy associated with thyroglossal duct cyst, not nasopharyngeal lymphoma.

updates.question_text: Regarding radiology reporting priorities across mucosal SCC subsites in this batch, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: For all subsites, reporting should focus only on the visible mucosal thickness and ignore deep space extension

The relevant imaging targets differ by subsite: skull base/intracranial spread for nasopharynx, pre-epiglottic and pterygopalatine/perineural risk for oropharynx, mandibular/retromolar routes for oral cavity, and laryngeal mobility/cartilage/deep-space involvement for larynx
Nasopharyngeal SCC staging is primarily size based, while oropharyngeal SCC staging is primarily defined by skull base invasion
Oral cavity SCC has separate HPV-dependent staging schemes identical to oropharyngeal SCC
Hypopharyngeal SCC staging excludes carotid artery and mediastinal assessment
options_after: For most subsites, reporting should focus primarily on the visible mucosal thickness and ignore deep space extension

The relevant imaging targets differ by subsite: skull base/intracranial spread for nasopharynx, pre-epiglottic and pterygopalatine/perineural risk for oropharynx, mandibular/retromolar routes for oral cavity, and laryngeal mobility/cartilage/deep-space involvement for larynx
Nasopharyngeal SCC staging is primarily size based, while oropharyngeal SCC staging is primarily defined by skull base invasion
Oral cavity SCC has separate HPV-dependent staging schemes closely comparable to oropharyngeal SCC
Hypopharyngeal SCC staging excludes carotid artery and mediastinal assessment
updates.explanation: The source repeatedly ties reporting priorities to the specific subsite. Nasopharynx requires attention to skull base and intracranial extension, while oropharynx requires assessment of pre-epiglottic fat, pterygopalatine fossa/perineural risk, resectability, and nodes. Oral cavity reporting emphasises bone invasion, retromolar trigone, routes through the pterygomandibular raphe, and tongue midline/intrinsic muscle involvement. Hypopharynx and larynx require attention to local invasion, mobility, cartilage, carotid encasement, mediastinal structures, and surgical contraindications.

updates.question_text: Regarding the extramucosal suprahyoid neck spaces, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Cervical fascial layers create spaces that help localise neck masses
Specific lesions arise randomly, so space localisation is not useful diagnostically
Knowledge of the space of origin helps generate a focused differential diagnosis
All extramucosal spaces have identical contents and routes of spread
Adjacent-space mass displacement patterns can help infer lesion origin
options_after: Cervical fascial layers create spaces that help localise neck masses
Specific lesions arise randomly, so space localisation is not useful diagnostically
Knowledge of the space of origin helps generate a focused differential diagnosis
Most extramucosal spaces have closely comparable contents and routes of spread
Adjacent-space mass displacement patterns can help infer lesion origin
updates.explanation: The source emphasises that complex cervical fascial layers create several suprahyoid neck spaces. Lesions tend to arise in characteristic locations, so localisation to a space is a practical way to narrow the differential diagnosis. Displacement of adjacent fat or vascular structures is repeatedly used in this batch to infer the compartment of origin. Treating the spaces as diagnostically identical would defeat the main radiological purpose of this anatomy.

updates.question_text: Regarding carotid space anatomy, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The carotid space is identical to the prestyloid parapharyngeal fat space
The carotid space contains the carotid artery, carotid body, jugular vein, and several cranial nerves
The vagus nerve remains within the carotid space all the way into the thorax
Lymph nodes are contained within the carotid space sheath
Cranial nerves IX, XI, and XII pass transiently through the carotid space
options_after: The carotid space is closely comparable to the prestyloid parapharyngeal fat space
The carotid space contains the carotid artery, carotid body, jugular vein, and several cranial nerves
The vagus nerve remains within the carotid space all the way into the thorax
Lymph nodes are contained within the carotid space sheath
Cranial nerves IX, XI, and XII pass transiently through the carotid space
updates.explanation: The carotid space, or post-styloid parapharyngeal space, is an incomplete fascial ring around the carotid artery and jugular vein extending from skull base to aortic arch. It contains the carotid artery, carotid body, jugular vein, and cranial nerves, with the vagus nerve remaining in the space into the thorax. Cranial nerves IX, XI, and XII pass through it transiently. There are lymph nodes around, but not contained within, the carotid space.

updates.question_text: Regarding differentiating carotid space masses by vascular displacement and vascularity, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Carotid body tumour displaces both carotid arteries anteromedially without bifurcation splaying
Glomus vagale tumour and vagal schwannoma both displace the carotid arteries anteromedially
Schwannoma is less vascular than paraganglioma and lacks internal flow voids
Internal flow voids and marked vascularity support paraganglioma over schwannoma
Neurofibroma and schwannoma are always reliably distinguished by MRI
options_after: Carotid body tumour displaces both carotid arteries anteromedially without bifurcation splaying
Glomus vagale tumour and vagal schwannoma both displace the carotid arteries anteromedially
Schwannoma is less vascular than paraganglioma and lacks internal flow voids
Internal flow voids and marked vascularity support paraganglioma over schwannoma
Neurofibroma and schwannoma are characteristically reliably distinguished by MRI
updates.explanation: The source uses displacement and vascularity as the key imaging logic for carotid space masses. Carotid body tumour splays the internal and external carotid arteries at the bifurcation. Glomus vagale tumour and vagal schwannoma both displace the carotid arteries anteromedially, but schwannoma is less vascular and lacks the internal flow voids typical of paraganglioma. Neurofibroma and schwannoma are indistinguishable by MRI in the source.

updates.question_text: Regarding the prestyloid parapharyngeal space, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: It is a muscular space containing the longus colli-capitis complex
It is a vascular sheath containing no fat and no lymphatics
It is a triangular fat-filled space containing lymphatics, arterial branches, and V3
It extends from the carotid bifurcation to the aortic arch
It is directly posterior to the vertebral body and separated from the pharynx by alar fascia
options_after: It is a muscular space containing the longus colli-capitis complex
The carotid space is a vascular sheath devoid of both fat and lymphatics.
It is a triangular fat-filled space containing lymphatics, arterial branches, and V3
It extends from the carotid bifurcation to the aortic arch
It is directly posterior to the vertebral body and separated from the pharynx by alar fascia
updates.explanation: The prestyloid parapharyngeal space is described as a triangular fat-filled space. Its contents include lymphatics, branches of the internal maxillary artery, the ascending pharyngeal artery, and the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. The longus colli-capitis complex is perivertebral, while carotid artery and jugular vein define the carotid space. The retropharyngeal/danger/prevertebral relationships are separate.

updates.question_text: Regarding benign and malignant prestyloid parapharyngeal space lesions, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Second branchial cleft cysts cannot present in the parapharyngeal space
Malignant tumours in this space are rare and most often salivary gland in origin
Schwannomas in this space usually arise from the optic nerve
Skull base chordoma and chondrosarcoma are excluded from secondary invasion of the parapharyngeal space
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, and acinic cell carcinoma are examples of salivary malignancies
options_after: Second branchial cleft cysts will not present in the parapharyngeal space
Malignant tumours in this space are rare and most often salivary gland in origin
Schwannomas in this space usually arise from the optic nerve
Skull base chordoma and chondrosarcoma are excluded from secondary invasion of the parapharyngeal space
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, and acinic cell carcinoma are examples of salivary malignancies
updates.explanation: The source lists second branchial cleft cyst as a possible parapharyngeal space presentation, and rare schwannomas usually arise from the sympathetic plexus or mandibular nerve. Malignant lesions are uncommon and most frequently salivary in origin, including mucoepidermoid carcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, and acinic cell carcinoma. Secondary invasion may arise from pharyngeal, salivary, lymphomatous, or skull base tumours, including chordoma and chondrosarcoma, so excluding skull base spread is incorrect.

updates.question_text: Regarding the perivertebral space, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The perivertebral space is formed by the superficial cervical fascia and contains only fat
The deep layer of the deep cervical fascia wraps around the prevertebral and paraspinal muscles to form it
The anterior perivertebral space is synonymous with the prevertebral space
It includes longus colli-capitis, paraspinal muscles, vertebral bodies, spinal canal neurovascular structures, vertebral arteries, and brachial plexus
The prestyloid parapharyngeal space is the analogous region in the thoracolumbar spine
options_after: The perivertebral space is formed by the superficial cervical fascia and contains primarily fat
The deep layer of the deep cervical fascia wraps around the prevertebral and paraspinal muscles to form it
The anterior perivertebral space is synonymous with the prevertebral space
It includes longus colli-capitis, paraspinal muscles, vertebral bodies, spinal canal neurovascular structures, vertebral arteries, and brachial plexus
The prestyloid parapharyngeal space is the analogous region in the thoracolumbar spine
updates.explanation: The perivertebral space is formed by the deep layer of deep cervical fascia around the prevertebral and paraspinal musculature. The anterior perivertebral space is the prevertebral space. Its contents include muscles, vertebral bodies, spinal canal structures, exiting nerves, vertebral arteries, and brachial plexus. The source distinguishes the suprahyoid perivertebral space from the analogous thoracolumbar paravertebral space; the prestyloid parapharyngeal space is not that analogue.

updates.question_text: Regarding tumour and non-neoplastic masses in the masticator space, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: Masticator space masses can only arise from the muscles of mastication
V3 schwannoma can smoothly expand foramen ovale and present as a well-defined masticator space mass
Venous malformations are confined to the sublingual gland and cannot involve masseter
Mandibular odontogenic lesions are excluded from the masticator space differential
Rhabdomyosarcoma, lymphoma, and metastases are impossible within masticator muscles
options_after: Masticator space masses can primarily arise from the muscles of mastication
V3 schwannoma can smoothly expand foramen ovale and present as a well-defined masticator space mass
Venous malformations are confined to the sublingual gland and will not involve masseter
Mandibular odontogenic lesions are excluded from the masticator space differential
Rhabdomyosarcoma, lymphoma, and metastases are not considered a realistic possibility within masticator muscles
updates.explanation: The source organises masticator space masses by origin from mandible, V3 branches, or muscles of mastication. V3 travels along the medial margin of the lateral pterygoid after exiting foramen ovale, and V3 schwannoma can smoothly expand the foramen ovale and appear as a well-defined masticator space mass. Mandibular bone tumours and odontogenic lesions are relevant. Venous malformations may involve masseter, and muscle malignancies include rhabdomyosarcoma, lymphoma, and metastases.

updates.question_text: Regarding lymph node and malignant spread patterns involving these extramucosal spaces, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: Retropharyngeal malignant lymphadenopathy is most often associated with oral cavity dermoid
There are lymph nodes contained within the carotid space fascial ring
Second branchial cleft cyst is the most common malignant lesion of the retropharyngeal space
Nasopharyngeal SCC is a key tumour associated with retropharyngeal lymphadenopathy and contiguous retropharyngeal extension
Parapharyngeal malignant lesions are always primary vertebral body metastases
options_after: Retropharyngeal malignant lymphadenopathy is most often associated with oral cavity dermoid
There are lymph nodes contained within the carotid space fascial ring
Second branchial cleft cyst is the most common malignant lesion of the retropharyngeal space
Nasopharyngeal SCC is a key tumour associated with retropharyngeal lymphadenopathy and contiguous retropharyngeal extension
Parapharyngeal malignant lesions are characteristically primary vertebral body metastases
updates.explanation: The source links retropharyngeal malignant lymphadenopathy most strongly with nasopharyngeal SCC and also describes contiguous nasopharyngeal SCC spread into the retropharyngeal space. Lymph nodes surround but are not contained within the carotid space. Second branchial cleft cyst is a congenital lesion, not the most common retropharyngeal malignancy. Parapharyngeal malignancies are rare and most often salivary in origin, though secondary invasion can occur.

updates.question_text: Regarding avoiding common localisation traps in extramucosal neck imaging, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: A medially deviated internal carotid artery can mimic a retropharyngeal mass and can be injured during spine surgery
A cystic mass at the mandibular angle in an older adult should not automatically be assumed to be a benign branchial cleft cyst
The direction of parapharyngeal fat displacement can help distinguish adjacent compartment origin
All cystic neck lesions with wall enhancement are odontogenic abscesses
All carotid space masses should be biopsied before vascular displacement and enhancement pattern are assessed
options_after: A medially deviated internal carotid artery can mimic a retropharyngeal mass and can be injured during spine surgery
A cystic mass at the mandibular angle in an older adult should not automatically be assumed to be a benign branchial cleft cyst
The direction of parapharyngeal fat displacement can help distinguish adjacent compartment origin
Most cystic neck lesions with wall enhancement are odontogenic abscesses
Most carotid space masses should be biopsied before vascular displacement and enhancement pattern are assessed
updates.explanation: The source highlights several practical traps. A medially deviated internal carotid artery may mimic a retropharyngeal mass and creates surgical risk. In older adults, a cystic mass in a branchial cleft location should prompt consideration of cystic metastasis, especially if irregular or mural nodular. Parapharyngeal fat displacement helps infer the compartment of origin. Wall enhancement can indicate superinfection, and carotid space masses require vascular pattern assessment before any invasive assumption.

updates.question_text:
A lateral neck radiograph shows marked prevertebral soft tissue thickening, and contrast CT shows a peripherally enhancing retropharyngeal fluid collection effacing the oropharynx.

Which of the following statements are correct regarding this image?
options_before: The imaging findings support retropharyngeal abscess
Retropharyngeal infection cannot cause airway compromise
In children, spread from upper respiratory tract infection can cause suppuration and rupture of retropharyngeal lymph nodes
In adults, penetrating injury such as fish bone ingestion or instrumentation is a common cause
The collection should be localised to the carotid bifurcation because it splays the carotid arteries
options_after: The imaging findings support retropharyngeal abscess
Retropharyngeal infection will not cause airway compromise
In children, spread from upper respiratory tract infection can cause suppuration and rupture of retropharyngeal lymph nodes
In adults, penetrating injury such as fish bone ingestion or instrumentation is a common cause
The collection should be localised to the carotid bifurcation because it splays the carotid arteries
updates.explanation: The image caption describes retropharyngeal abscess, with prevertebral soft tissue thickening on radiograph and a rim-enhancing retropharyngeal collection on CT. Retropharyngeal infection can compromise the airway. In children, the typical route is spread from an upper respiratory tract infection such as pharyngitis, with suppuration and rupture of retropharyngeal nodes. In adults, penetrating injury including fish bone ingestion or instrumentation is the commoner mechanism.

updates.question_text: Regarding Hashimoto thyroiditis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It is the most common cause of hypothyroidism
It is usually diagnosed by identifying a solitary taller-than-wide thyroid nodule on ultrasound
It is thought to be autoimmune with autoantibodies to thyroglobulins
Patients are always frankly hypothyroid at first presentation and never euthyroid early
Patients have increased risk of thyroid lymphoma
options_after: It is the most common cause of hypothyroidism
It is usually diagnosed by identifying a solitary taller-than-wide thyroid nodule on ultrasound
It is thought to be autoimmune with autoantibodies to thyroglobulins
A euthyroid presentation argues against early Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Patients have increased risk of thyroid lymphoma
updates.explanation: Hashimoto thyroiditis is chronic lymphocytic autoimmune thyroiditis and is the most common cause of hypothyroidism. Patients may be euthyroid early but eventually become hypothyroid as functional thyroid tissue is replaced. Ultrasound may show a diffusely micronodular gland or heterogeneous coarsened gland without a measurable nodule, with thickened isthmus and eventual atrophy. The source also notes increased risk of thyroid lymphoma.

updates.question_text: Regarding multinodular thyroid gland and initial thyroid nodule risk stratification, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The term multinodular gland is preferred because goitre is a generic term for an enlarged gland with many possible causes
A multinodular gland appears as an atrophic thyroid with no measurable nodules
There are no definitive ultrasound features that distinguish benign from malignant thyroid nodules
ATA ultrasound guidelines use sonographic pattern and size for risk stratification and FNA decision-making
All nodules found on CT require biopsy regardless of size or suspicious features
options_after: The term multinodular gland is preferred because goitre is a generic term for an enlarged gland with many possible causes
A multinodular gland appears as an atrophic thyroid without measurable nodules
There are no definitive ultrasound features that distinguish benign from malignant thyroid nodules
ATA ultrasound guidelines use sonographic pattern and size for risk stratification and FNA decision-making
Most nodules found on CT require biopsy despite variation in size or suspicious features
updates.explanation: The source prefers multinodular gland over multinodular goitre because goitre is a generic enlargement term. A multinodular gland appears enlarged with innumerable mixed cystic and solid nodules. No ultrasound features definitively separate benign from malignant nodules, so ATA guidelines combine sonographic pattern and size for risk stratification and FNA decisions. Incidental CT/MRI nodules have separate size thresholds when no suspicious features are present.

updates.question_text: Regarding incidental thyroid nodules detected on CT or MRI, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: ACR guidance recommends ultrasound in the absence of suspicious CT/MRI features for nodules at least 1 cm in patients younger than 35 years
ACR guidance recommends ultrasound in the absence of suspicious CT/MRI features for nodules greater than 1.5 cm in patients older than 35 years
Nodules that do not meet size criteria do not require further evaluation when suspicious CT/MRI features are absent
Suspicious features on CT or MRI override the simple size-threshold logic
Every incidental thyroid nodule seen on CT or MRI needs ultrasound regardless of age, size, or suspicious features
options_after: ACR guidance recommends ultrasound in the absence of suspicious CT/MRI features for nodules at least 1 cm in patients younger than 35 years
ACR guidance recommends ultrasound in the absence of suspicious CT/MRI features for nodules greater than 1.5 cm in patients older than 35 years
Nodules that do not meet size criteria do not require further evaluation when suspicious CT/MRI features are absent
Suspicious features on CT or MRI override the simple size-threshold logic
Most incidental thyroid nodules seen on CT or MRI needs ultrasound despite variation in age, size, or suspicious features
updates.explanation: The source summarises ACR incidental thyroid nodule guidance for CT/MRI. If suspicious CT/MRI features are absent, ultrasound is recommended for nodules at least 1 cm in patients younger than 35 years and greater than 1.5 cm in patients older than 35 years. Nodules below these size thresholds require no further evaluation. The rule applies in the absence of suspicious features; suspicious CT/MRI findings change the decision-making.

updates.question_text: Regarding non-papillary thyroid malignancies, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Follicular carcinoma tends to spread haematogenously and has the next best prognosis after papillary carcinoma
Medullary carcinoma is the commonest subtype and has the best prognosis
Medullary carcinoma is associated with MEN II syndrome
Anaplastic carcinoma is the commonest thyroid cancer subtype and has the best prognosis
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma cannot occur in the thyroid
options_after: Follicular carcinoma tends to spread haematogenously and has the next best prognosis after papillary carcinoma
Medullary carcinoma is the commonest subtype and has the best prognosis
Medullary carcinoma is associated with MEN II syndrome
Anaplastic carcinoma is the commonest thyroid cancer subtype and has the best prognosis
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma will not occur in the thyroid
updates.explanation: The source states that follicular carcinomas spread haematogenously and have the next best prognosis after papillary carcinoma. Medullary carcinoma is less common and more aggressive than papillary carcinoma, and is associated with MEN II syndrome. Anaplastic carcinoma is very rare and has the worst prognosis, not the best prognosis. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma can occur in the thyroid and usually presents as a solid nodule.

updates.question_text: Regarding 4DCT for parathyroid adenoma, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: 4DCT uses noncontrast, arterial, and delayed phases to exploit adenoma perfusion kinetics
Classic adenomas are hyperdense to thyroid on noncontrast images and never enhance arterially
Classic adenomas are hyperdense to thyroid on noncontrast images, hypoenhance in the arterial phase, and retain contrast on delayed phase
Nearly all parathyroid adenomas follow the classic enhancement pattern
The greatest limitation of 4DCT is high radiation exposure
options_after: 4DCT uses noncontrast, arterial, and delayed phases to exploit adenoma perfusion kinetics
Classic adenomas are hyperdense to thyroid on noncontrast images and will not enhance arterially
Classic adenomas are hyperdense to thyroid on noncontrast images, hypoenhance in the arterial phase, and retain contrast on delayed phase
The large majority of parathyroid adenomas follow the classic enhancement pattern
The greatest limitation of 4DCT is high radiation exposure
updates.explanation: 4DCT consists of noncontrast, arterial, and delayed phases to use adenoma perfusion kinetics. The classic pattern is hypodensity relative to thyroid on noncontrast images, arterial hyperenhancement greater than thyroid at about 35 seconds, and greater washout than thyroid on delayed images. Less than half of adenomas follow the classic pattern, and large adenomas may enhance heterogeneously. The major limitation is high radiation exposure.

updates.question_text: Regarding imaging strategy in acute aortic pathology, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: First-line CT includes noncontrast chest CT and ECG-gated CTA of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
MR angiography can be considered in stable patients who cannot undergo CTA
Imaging should usually be limited to the symptomatic thoracic segment only
Fast noncontrast MR techniques such as SSFP and post-contrast MRA may be used in the MR approach
The unenhanced phase is irrelevant when intramural haematoma is a consideration
options_after: First-line CT includes noncontrast chest CT and ECG-gated CTA of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
MR angiography can be considered in stable patients who cannot undergo CTA
Imaging should usually be limited to the symptomatic thoracic segment in typical cases
Fast noncontrast MR techniques such as SSFP and post-contrast MRA may be used in the MR approach
The unenhanced phase is irrelevant when intramural haematoma is a consideration
updates.explanation: The source describes first-line CT as noncontrast chest CT plus ECG-gated CTA of the chest, abdomen and pelvis. If the patient is stable and cannot undergo CTA, MRA can be considered with fast noncontrast techniques such as SSFP and post-contrast MRA of the chest, abdomen and pelvis. The full aorta is generally imaged in acute aortic pathology. The unenhanced phase is important for evaluating intramural haematoma.

updates.question_text: Regarding aortic dissection pathophysiology, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The key feature is disruption of the intima allowing high-pressure blood to infiltrate and expand the media
The false lumen has faster flow than the true lumen and therefore never thromboses
A re-entry tear may obstruct outflow and increase pressure in the false lumen
Pressure difference between lumina can compress the true lumen and alter contrast opacification
The adventitia is the primary layer expanded by false-lumen blood flow
options_after: The key feature is disruption of the intima allowing high-pressure blood to infiltrate and expand the media
The false lumen has faster flow than the true lumen and therefore will not thrombose
A re-entry tear may obstruct outflow and increase pressure in the false lumen
Pressure difference between lumina can compress the true lumen and alter contrast opacification
The adventitia is the primary layer expanded by false-lumen blood flow
updates.explanation: Aortic dissection begins with an intimal disruption that lets high-pressure blood enter and expand the media. The false lumen has slower flow, which can lead to thrombosis. A re-entry tear may obstruct outflow, raising false-lumen pressure. This pressure differential can compress the true lumen and create differences in contrast opacification between the two lumina. The adventitia is not described as the primary dissected layer.

updates.question_text: Regarding penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It is a focal intimal defect at the site of an atherosclerotic plaque
It tends to be caused by hypertension rather than atherosclerosis
It can lead to saccular aneurysm formation
On imaging it appears as a contrast-filled outpouching extending beyond the expected aortic wall contour
It is identical to a simple ulcerated atherosclerotic plaque because both extend beyond the expected aortic contour
options_after: It is a focal intimal defect at the site of an atherosclerotic plaque
It tends to be caused by hypertension rather than atherosclerosis
It can lead to saccular aneurysm formation
On imaging it appears as a contrast-filled outpouching extending beyond the expected aortic wall contour
It is closely comparable to a simple ulcerated atherosclerotic plaque because both extend beyond the expected aortic contour
updates.explanation: Penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer is a focal intimal defect occurring at an atherosclerotic plaque and may cause saccular aneurysm formation. Its key imaging feature is a contrast-filled outpouching beyond the expected contour of the aortic wall. Unlike dissection and IMH, PAU tends to be caused by atherosclerosis rather than hypertension. A simple ulcerated plaque does not extend beyond the expected wall contour and represents chronic atherosclerotic disease rather than acute aortic syndrome.

updates.question_text: Regarding traumatic aortic injury, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The relatively fixed injury-prone levels are the aortic root, isthmus and hiatus
The aortic isthmus is the most common location for traumatic aortic injury
CTA is the gold standard for suspected traumatic aortic injury
Associated injuries to origins of the brachiocephalic, left carotid or left subclavian arteries are never seen
Traumatic aortic injury may result in minimal aortic injury, laceration, transection or pseudoaneurysm
options_after: The relatively fixed injury-prone levels are the aortic root, isthmus and hiatus
The aortic isthmus is the most common location for traumatic aortic injury
CTA is the gold standard for suspected traumatic aortic injury
Associated injuries to origins of the brachiocephalic, left carotid or left subclavian arteries are not seen
Traumatic aortic injury may result in minimal aortic injury, laceration, transection or pseudoaneurysm
updates.explanation: Traumatic aortic injury occurs at relatively fixed levels, specifically the root, isthmus and hiatus, with the isthmus the commonest site. CTA is the gold standard in suspected traumatic injury. The source lists possible results as minimal aortic injury, laceration, transection or pseudoaneurysm. Injuries to the origins of the brachiocephalic, left carotid or left subclavian arteries are frequently present, not absent.

updates.question_text: Regarding CT signs and mediastinal haemorrhage in traumatic aortic injury, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Mediastinal haemorrhage has no value in deciding whether aortic injury is present
Traumatic mediastinal haemorrhage is always arterial and therefore confirms aortic injury
Mediastinal haemorrhage separated from an intact aorta by a fat plane mandates surgical treatment
Haemorrhage in contact with the aortic wall suggests aortic injury and requires surgical treatment
Direct CT signs include intimal irregularity, dissection flap, pseudoaneurysm and intramural haematoma
options_after: Mediastinal haemorrhage lacks value in deciding whether aortic injury is present
Traumatic mediastinal haemorrhage is characteristically arterial and therefore confirms aortic injury
Mediastinal haemorrhage separated from an intact aorta by a fat plane mandates surgical treatment
Haemorrhage in contact with the aortic wall suggests aortic injury and requires surgical treatment
Direct CT signs include intimal irregularity, dissection flap, pseudoaneurysm and intramural haematoma
updates.explanation: Direct CT signs of traumatic aortic injury include intimal irregularity, dissection flap, pseudoaneurysm and intramural haematoma. Mediastinal haemorrhage is often venous, although aortic injury remains the key concern. If haemorrhage is separated from an intact aorta by a fat plane it may be treated conservatively as venous bleeding. Haemorrhage contacting the aortic wall suggests aortic injury and requires surgical treatment.

updates.question_text: Regarding minimal aortic injury, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It accounts for approximately 10-30% of blunt traumatic aortic injuries
It involves all layers of the aortic wall with complete transection
It involves only the intima
Mechanisms are unrelated to rapid deceleration or shearing forces
Typical CT findings require a large intimal flap greater than 3 cm with extensive periaortic haematoma
options_after: It accounts for approximately 10-30% of blunt traumatic aortic injuries
It involves most layers of the aortic wall with complete transection
It involves only the intima
Mechanisms are unrelated to rapid deceleration or shearing forces
Typical CT findings require a large intimal flap greater than 3 cm with extensive periaortic haematoma
updates.explanation: Minimal aortic injury lesions make up about 10-30% of blunt traumatic aortic injuries and involve only the intima. Mechanisms listed include rapid deceleration, shearing forces, water-hammer effect and osseous pinch against the thoracic spine. Common CT findings include intimal irregularity, a small intimal flap under 1 cm with little or no periaortic haematoma, intraluminal aortic thrombus or intramural haematoma. A large flap with extensive haematoma suggests more severe injury.

updates.question_text: Regarding management logic across acute aortic syndromes in this batch, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: Descending aortic involvement is always treated surgically regardless of clinical context
Ascending aortic involvement is most commonly treated surgically
PAU is never imaged beyond the single visible ulcer
Type B dissection is treated surgically because it always causes organ ischaemia
MR angiography is preferred first-line in all unstable patients
options_after: Descending aortic involvement is characteristically treated surgically despite variation in clinical context
Ascending aortic involvement is most commonly treated surgically
PAU is not imaged beyond the single visible ulcer
Type B dissection is treated surgically because it characteristically causes organ ischaemia
MR angiography is preferred first-line in most unstable patients
updates.explanation: Across acute aortic syndrome, the source emphasises that treatment depends primarily on location. Ascending aortic involvement is most commonly surgical, whereas descending aortic pathology is most commonly managed medically with blood pressure control. Type B dissection is described as typically treated medically. Full-aorta imaging is generally recommended, including when PAU is seen, because multiple ulcers may be present. CTA is first-line, while MRA is reserved for stable patients who cannot undergo CTA.

updates.question_text: Regarding causes, associations and treatment thresholds for thoracic aortic aneurysm, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms are more commonly atherosclerotic than descending aneurysms
Almost one-third of patients with atherosclerotic thoracic aortic aneurysm have an associated abdominal aortic aneurysm
Bicuspid aortic valve-associated aortopathy is listed as a non-atherosclerotic cause
The surgical threshold for all ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms is 4.5 cm regardless of cause
Annual growth greater than 1 cm per year is an indication for surgical repair
options_after: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms are more commonly atherosclerotic than descending aneurysms
Almost one-third of patients with atherosclerotic thoracic aortic aneurysm have an associated abdominal aortic aneurysm
Bicuspid aortic valve-associated aortopathy is listed as a non-atherosclerotic cause
