Weight-bearing radiographs are most sensitive for subtle Lisfranc malalignment, CT demonstrates the true extent of Chopart fracture-dislocation, and traumatic calcaneal fracture is associated with serious lumbar spine and abdominal vascular injuries that may require further imaging. MRI can distinguish acute sesamoid fracture from bipartite sesamoid by showing non-corticated margins, distraction, capsular tear, and oedema. Normal initial radiographs do not exclude metatarsal stress fracture.

updates.question_text: Regarding the radiographic implications of a supination-external rotation stage IV ankle fracture, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Medial clear-space widening implies an intact deltoid ligament.
Medial clear-space widening indicates deltoid ligament disruption.
The pattern is stable because the injury is confined to the lateral malleolus.
Posterior syndesmotic involvement is excluded if no posterior malleolus fracture is visible.
Anterior and posterior syndesmotic ligament tears can be presumed in the illustrated stage IV injury pattern.
options_after: Medial clear-space widening implies an intact deltoid ligament.
Medial clear-space widening indicates deltoid ligament disruption.
The pattern is stable because the injury is confined to the lateral malleolus.
Posterior syndesmotic involvement is excluded if posterior malleolus fracture is absent.
Anterior and posterior syndesmotic ligament tears can be presumed in the illustrated stage IV injury pattern.
updates.explanation: The source describes medial clear-space widening as evidence of deltoid ligament disruption, defining a stage IV injury. In the illustrated stage IV example, the anterior and posterior syndesmotic ligaments can be presumed torn, making the pattern unstable. A posterior malleolus fracture is one route to stage III injury, but posterior syndesmotic tear is the alternative, so absence of one does not exclude posterior syndesmotic involvement.

updates.question_text: Regarding anterior tibialis tendon injury, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Anterior tibialis injury is much less common than posterior tibialis tendon injury.
Anterior tibialis rupture is always traumatic and is not associated with tendon degeneration.
Anterior tibialis rupture classically presents as posterior ankle swelling in Kager's fat pad.
Anterior tibialis tears usually preserve tendon continuity without retraction.
An anterior ankle mass is a classic clinical presentation of anterior tibialis rupture.
options_after: Anterior tibialis injury is much less common than posterior tibialis tendon injury.
Anterior tibialis rupture is characteristically traumatic and is not associated with tendon degeneration.
Anterior tibialis rupture classically presents as posterior ankle swelling in Kager's fat pad.
Anterior tibialis tears usually preserve tendon continuity without retraction.
An anterior ankle mass is a classic clinical presentation of anterior tibialis rupture.
updates.explanation: The source states that anterior tibialis injury is much less common than posterior tibialis injury. Rupture may be traumatic or atraumatic in the setting of tendon degeneration, and an anterior ankle mass is a classic presentation. The illustrated full-thickness tear shows proximal retraction, so preserved continuity is not the typical message of this passage.

updates.question_text: Which single imaging action is most directly supported when ankle radiographs show subtle mortise widening concerning for a Maisonneuve pattern?
options_before: Obtain contralateral ankle stress radiographs only.
Image the ipsilateral leg more proximally to assess the proximal fibula.
Stop imaging because isolated ankle radiographs fully exclude a proximal fibular fracture.
Proceed directly to MR arthrography of the subtalar joint.
Perform ultrasound of the peroneal tendons as the next diagnostic step.
options_after: Obtain contralateral ankle stress radiographs in typical cases.
Image the ipsilateral leg more proximally to assess the proximal fibula.
Stop imaging because isolated ankle radiographs fully exclude a proximal fibular fracture.
Proceed directly to MR arthrography of the subtalar joint.
Perform ultrasound of the peroneal tendons as the next diagnostic step.
updates.explanation: Maisonneuve injury may be missed if only the ankle is imaged, because the proximal fibular fracture lies outside the field of view. The source states that subtle ankle mortise widening should prompt a more proximal radiograph. The purpose is to detect the associated high proximal fibular fracture and interosseous membrane or medial ankle injury pattern.

updates.question_text: Regarding knee dislocation and vascular injury, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The knee can dislocate in any direction, with anterior dislocation being the most common.
Normal distal pulses exclude clinically important popliteal artery injury.
CT angiography is typically recommended for all knee dislocations.
Posterior knee dislocation is the only direction associated with popliteal artery injury.
Marked widening of the knee joint space on radiography should raise suspicion for dislocation.
options_after: The knee can dislocate in any direction, with anterior dislocation being the most common.
Normal distal pulses exclude clinically important popliteal artery injury.
CT angiography is typically recommended for all knee dislocations.
Posterior knee dislocation is the principal direction associated with popliteal artery injury.
Marked widening of the knee joint space on radiography should raise suspicion for dislocation.
updates.explanation: The source states that the knee may dislocate in any direction, although anterior dislocation is most common. Popliteal artery injury is a major risk and may be present even when distal pulses remain intact, so CT angiography is typically recommended for all knee dislocations. The illustrated radiograph shows marked joint-space widening, a radiographic clue to dislocation, with angiographic popliteal artery occlusion.

updates.question_text: Regarding oblique and horizontal meniscal tears, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The terms oblique and horizontal are never used interchangeably.
A true horizontal tear cleaves the meniscus parallel to the tibial plateau.
Oblique or horizontal tear is the most common meniscal tear pattern.
Oblique and horizontal tears are more often acute traumatic tears than degenerative tears.
Oblique or horizontal tear typically occurs in the posterior horn of the medial meniscus.
options_after: The terms oblique and horizontal are not used interchangeably.
A true horizontal tear cleaves the meniscus parallel to the tibial plateau.
Oblique or horizontal tear is the most common meniscal tear pattern.
Oblique and horizontal tears are more often acute traumatic tears than degenerative tears.
Oblique or horizontal tear typically occurs in the posterior horn of the medial meniscus.
updates.explanation: The source notes that oblique and horizontal are sometimes used interchangeably, although strictly a horizontal tear remains parallel to the tibial plateau and an oblique tear is at a slight angle. Oblique/horizontal tear is described as the most common meniscal tear, typically in the posterior horn of the medial meniscus. These tears are more often degenerative rather than traumatic. Parameniscal cysts may accompany horizontal cleavage tears.

updates.question_text: Regarding vertical or longitudinal meniscal tears, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: A vertical or longitudinal tear follows the contour of the meniscus.
On serial sagittal images, a vertical tear changes position relative to the meniscal edge.
A vertical tear is synonymous with a radial tear.
A vertical tear is parallel to the tibial plateau and therefore identical to a horizontal tear.
On serial sagittal images, a vertical tear remains a fixed distance from the edge of the meniscus.
options_after: A vertical or longitudinal tear follows the contour of the meniscus.
On serial sagittal images, a vertical tear changes position relative to the meniscal edge.
A vertical tear is synonymous with a radial tear.
A vertical tear is parallel to the tibial plateau and therefore closely comparable to a horizontal tear.
On serial sagittal images, a vertical tear remains a fixed distance from the edge of the meniscus.
updates.explanation: The vertical tear is synonymous with a longitudinal tear and follows the curved contour of the meniscus. On serial sagittal imaging, it remains a fixed distance from the edge of the meniscus. That behaviour contrasts with a radial tear, which changes position relative to the meniscal edge. Horizontal tears cleave parallel to the tibial plateau and are a different pattern.

updates.question_text: Regarding the ghost meniscus sign and parameniscal cysts, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The ghost meniscus sign is specific for bucket-handle tear with anterior displacement.
A radial tear may produce the ghost meniscus sign when the scan plane passes directly through the tear.
Parameniscal cysts are most commonly associated with vertical longitudinal tears.
A parameniscal cyst is loculated fluid adjacent to the meniscus, thought to result from joint fluid extending through a tear.
Parameniscal cysts should be ignored because they always resolve after meniscectomy.
options_after: The ghost meniscus sign is specific for bucket-handle tear with anterior displacement.
A radial tear may produce the ghost meniscus sign when the scan plane passes directly through the tear.
Parameniscal cysts are most commonly associated with vertical longitudinal tears.
A parameniscal cyst is loculated fluid adjacent to the meniscus, thought to result from joint fluid extending through a tear.
Parameniscal cysts should be ignored because they characteristically resolve after meniscectomy.
updates.explanation: The ghost meniscus sign can occur with radial tears when the imaging plane passes through the tear, classically producing apparent absence of the posterior horn near the intercondylar notch. A parameniscal cyst is loculated fluid adjacent to the meniscus from joint fluid extending through a meniscal tear. Such cysts are most commonly associated with horizontal cleavage tears and should be mentioned because symptoms may persist even after meniscal resection.

updates.question_text: Regarding discoid meniscus, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Discoid meniscus is a spectrum of congenital meniscal malformations.
Discoid meniscus is defined only by complete disc-like replacement of the normal meniscus.
A discoid meniscus has a portion extending to the central tibial plateau.
The lateral meniscus is more commonly affected.
On standard 4 mm sagittal slices, an oval or bow-tie meniscus on three or more contiguous slices supports the diagnosis.
options_after: Discoid meniscus is a spectrum of congenital meniscal malformations.
Discoid meniscus is defined primarily by complete disc-like replacement of the normal meniscus.
A discoid meniscus has a portion extending to the central tibial plateau.
The lateral meniscus is more commonly affected.
On standard 4 mm sagittal slices, an oval or bow-tie meniscus on three or more contiguous slices supports the diagnosis.
updates.explanation: The source defines discoid meniscus as a spectrum of congenital malformation ranging from increased meniscal thickness to a complete disc-like shape. It is defined by a portion of meniscus extending to the central tibial plateau, with the lateral meniscus more commonly affected. On standard 4 mm sagittal slices, a bow-tie or oval meniscus across three or more contiguous slices represents 12 mm medial-lateral thickness and supports the diagnosis.

updates.question_text: Which single next imaging step is most directly supported by the source after recognising a knee dislocation on radiography?
options_before: No further vascular imaging if distal pulses are palpable.
Delayed outpatient MRI only, because vascular injury is excluded by joint reduction.
CT angiography because popliteal artery injury may be present despite intact distal pulses.
Bone scan to evaluate occult patellar fracture.
Ultrasound assessment of meniscal roots as the first-line vascular test.
options_after: Further vascular imaging can be omitted if distal pulses are palpable.
Delayed outpatient MRI primarily, because vascular injury is excluded by joint reduction.
CT angiography because popliteal artery injury may be present despite intact distal pulses.
Bone scan to evaluate occult patellar fracture.
Ultrasound assessment of meniscal roots as the first-line vascular test.
updates.explanation: The source gives a clear imaging implication: vascular injury to the popliteal artery may be present even when distal pulses are intact. For that reason, CT angiography is typically recommended for all knee dislocations. MRI may be useful for ligamentous assessment later, but it does not replace urgent vascular evaluation in this context.

updates.question_text: Which single statement best explains why a central meniscal tear is less likely to heal than a peripheral tear?
options_before: The central meniscus is protected by the meniscofemoral ligaments.
The central meniscus has the same vascularity as the peripheral red zone.
The posterior horn of the lateral meniscus has no tibial root attachment.
Central tears always represent myxoid degeneration rather than true tear.
The central meniscus is considered avascular.
options_after: The central meniscus is protected by the meniscofemoral ligaments.
The central meniscus has the same vascularity as the peripheral red zone.
The posterior horn of the lateral meniscus lacks tibial root attachment.
Central tears characteristically represent myxoid degeneration rather than true tear.
The central meniscus is considered avascular.
updates.explanation: The source contrasts the vascular peripheral third, or red zone, with the central avascular portion of the meniscus. Injuries confined to the red zone may heal spontaneously or after repair, whereas central injuries generally do not heal. The reason is vascular supply, not meniscofemoral ligament protection or absence of root attachment.

updates.question_text: Regarding the clinical and imaging relevance of discoid meniscus, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Discoid meniscus commonly presents with joint-line pain, clicking or locking in a child or adolescent.
Discoid meniscus is asymptomatic unless there is a frank tear.
Discoid meniscus more commonly affects the medial meniscus.
Discoid meniscus is prone to cystic degeneration and tear.
Discoid meniscus is diagnosed only when the meniscus is absent on sagittal MRI.
options_after: Discoid meniscus commonly presents with joint-line pain, clicking or locking in a child or adolescent.
Discoid meniscus is asymptomatic unless there is a frank tear.
Discoid meniscus more commonly affects the medial meniscus.
Discoid meniscus is prone to cystic degeneration and tear.
Discoid meniscus is diagnosed primarily when the meniscus is absent on sagittal MRI.
updates.explanation: Discoid meniscus is described as a common cause of joint-line pain, clicking or locking in a child or adolescent. It is prone to cystic degeneration and tear, and may be symptomatic even without a tear. The lateral meniscus is more commonly affected. MRI diagnosis is based on excessive meniscal width or bow-tie persistence, not absence of the meniscus.

updates.question_text: Regarding PCL anatomy and injury, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The PCL is normally high signal on all MRI sequences.
The PCL is stronger and thicker than the ACL.
PCL injury is more common than ACL injury.
The PCL inserts on the posterior tibial plateau.
The PCL arises from the femoral intercondylar notch more anteriorly than the ACL.
options_after: The PCL is normally high signal on routine MRI sequences.
The PCL is stronger and thicker than the ACL.
PCL injury is more common than ACL injury.
The PCL inserts on the posterior tibial plateau.
The PCL arises from the femoral intercondylar notch more anteriorly than the ACL.
updates.explanation: The PCL is described as stronger and thicker than the ACL, arising from the femoral intercondylar notch more anteriorly than the ACL and inserting on the posterior tibial plateau. A normal PCL is low signal on all sequences. PCL injury is less common than ACL injury.

updates.question_text: Regarding mechanisms and pitfalls in MCL injury, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Periligamentous oedema around the MCL in an older patient with osteoarthritis should automatically be called MCL sprain.
MCL injuries are caused by a tensile pulling force.
MCL sprains most commonly occur in young athletes.
The Pellegrini-Stieda lesion is post-traumatic calcification medial to the medial femoral condyle.
Valgus stress, often from impact on the lateral knee, is a common mechanism.
options_after: Periligamentous oedema around the MCL in an older patient with osteoarthritis should ordinarily be called MCL sprain.
MCL injuries are caused by a tensile pulling force.
MCL sprains most commonly occur in young athletes.
The Pellegrini-Stieda lesion is post-traumatic calcification medial to the medial femoral condyle.
Valgus stress, often from impact on the lateral knee, is a common mechanism.
updates.explanation: The source describes MCL injuries as tensile injuries, most commonly from valgus stress due to lateral knee impact. MCL sprains are most common in young athletes. It also warns that MCL-region oedema is common with osteoarthritis and should not be mistaken for sprain in older patients. Pellegrini-Stieda lesion is post-traumatic calcification medial to the medial femoral condyle, potentially from MCL avulsion.

updates.question_text: Regarding the lateral collateral ligament complex, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The routinely evaluated LCL complex structures from posterior to anterior are biceps femoris tendon, LCL and iliotibial band.
The LCL complex is composed only of the popliteus tendon and arcuate ligament.
The biceps femoris tendon and LCL both attach to the lateral fibular head.
The iliotibial band is the most posterior routinely evaluated structure of the LCL complex.
The iliotibial band attaches to Gerdy's tubercle on the proximal lateral tibia.
options_after: The routinely evaluated LCL complex structures from posterior to anterior are biceps femoris tendon, LCL and iliotibial band.
The LCL complex is composed primarily of the popliteus tendon and arcuate ligament.
The biceps femoris tendon and LCL both attach to the lateral fibular head.
The iliotibial band is the most posterior routinely evaluated structure of the LCL complex.
The iliotibial band attaches to Gerdy's tubercle on the proximal lateral tibia.
updates.explanation: The source organises the routinely evaluated lateral complex from posterior to anterior as biceps femoris tendon, LCL and iliotibial band. The biceps femoris tendon and LCL both attach to the lateral fibular head and may share a conjoined tendon. The iliotibial band is anterior and attaches to Gerdy's tubercle. Popliteus and arcuate structures belong to the broader posterolateral corner rather than replacing the LCL complex.

updates.question_text: Regarding the extensor mechanism and quadriceps anatomy, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The extensor mechanism consists of the conjoined quadriceps tendon, patella and patellar tendon.
The patella is a sesamoid bone enclosed within the quadriceps tendon.
The patellar tendon attaches to the tibial tuberosity.
All four quadriceps muscles arise from the femur.
The rectus femoris arises from the anterior inferior iliac spine.
options_after: The extensor mechanism consists of the conjoined quadriceps tendon, patella and patellar tendon.
The patella is a sesamoid bone enclosed within the quadriceps tendon.
The patellar tendon attaches to the tibial tuberosity.
Most four quadriceps muscles arise from the femur.
The rectus femoris arises from the anterior inferior iliac spine.
updates.explanation: The source defines the extensor mechanism as the conjoined quadriceps tendon, patella and patellar tendon, with the patellar tendon attaching to the tibial tuberosity. The patella is a sesamoid within the quadriceps tendon. Vastus intermedius, medialis and lateralis arise from the femur, while rectus femoris arises from the anterior inferior iliac spine.

updates.question_text: Regarding Outerbridge grading of cartilage degeneration, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The knee has three compartments and six chondral surfaces.
The patellofemoral compartment consists of patellar and trochlear cartilage.
The medial and lateral tibiofemoral compartments each contain only one shared chondral surface.
A cartilage defect should be described by location, severity and size.
Delamination is a superficial surface scrape that never parallels subchondral bone.
options_after: The knee has three compartments and six chondral surfaces.
The patellofemoral compartment consists of patellar and trochlear cartilage.
The medial and lateral tibiofemoral compartments each contain a single shared chondral surface.
A cartilage defect should be described by location, severity and size.
Delamination is a superficial surface scrape that will not parallel subchondral bone.
updates.explanation: The knee has three compartments and six chondral surfaces. The patellofemoral compartment includes patellar and trochlear cartilage, and each tibiofemoral compartment contains femoral condyle and tibial plateau surfaces. A cartilage defect should be described by location, severity and size. Delamination is a dissecting detachment of the cartilage undersurface from bone, paralleling the subchondral bone.

updates.question_text: Regarding reporting cartilage injury in the knee, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Osteochondral lesion, defect and injury are interchangeable generic terms rather than specific diagnoses.
They describe focal disorders of articular cartilage, subchondral bone plate and subchondral bone.
They are limited to meniscal root injuries and do not involve articular cartilage.
Advanced cases are always separable by imaging without overlap.
Fluid or cystic change deep to a lesion implies instability.
options_after: Osteochondral lesion, defect and injury are interchangeable generic terms rather than specific diagnoses.
They describe focal disorders of articular cartilage, subchondral bone plate and subchondral bone.
They are limited to meniscal root injuries and do not involve articular cartilage.
Advanced cases are characteristically separable by imaging without overlap.
Fluid or cystic change deep to a lesion implies instability.
updates.explanation: Osteochondral lesion, defect and injury are generic interchangeable terms for focal disorders involving cartilage, subchondral bone plate and subchondral bone. Fluid or cystic change deep to the lesion implies instability, as does displacement. The source notes a wide range of causes and that advanced cases can overlap on imaging.

updates.question_text: Regarding subchondral insufficiency fracture and avascular necrosis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The key imaging finding of avascular necrosis is serpiginous signal abnormality of subchondral bone.
Subchondral insufficiency fracture often shows thickening and irregularity of the subchondral bone plate with exuberant surrounding oedema.
Subchondral insufficiency fracture often has concomitant meniscal tearing.
Avascular necrosis is primary osteonecrosis of the subchondral bone.
Avascular necrosis never causes subchondral collapse, even in advanced cases.
options_after: The key imaging finding of avascular necrosis is serpiginous signal abnormality of subchondral bone.
Subchondral insufficiency fracture often shows thickening and irregularity of the subchondral bone plate with exuberant surrounding oedema.
Subchondral insufficiency fracture often has concomitant meniscal tearing.
Avascular necrosis is primary osteonecrosis of the subchondral bone.
Avascular necrosis will not cause subchondral collapse, even in advanced cases.
updates.explanation: The source describes subchondral insufficiency fracture as subchondral-bone collapse in older patients, with irregular subchondral bone-plate thickening and exuberant oedema, often with meniscal tearing. Avascular necrosis is primary osteonecrosis of subchondral bone with serpiginous signal abnormality. Advanced avascular necrosis may cause subchondral collapse.

updates.question_text: Regarding MRI appearance of PVNS, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Recurrent haemorrhage produces residual intra-articular haemosiderin.
Haemosiderin is paramagnetic.
Paramagnetic effects cause T1 prolongation and T2 shortening.
PVNS masses are bright on all MRI sequences and do not bloom on gradient-echo imaging.
Blooming on gradient-echo sequences is expected.
options_after: Recurrent haemorrhage produces residual intra-articular haemosiderin.
Haemosiderin is paramagnetic.
Paramagnetic effects cause T1 prolongation and T2 shortening.
PVNS masses are bright on routine MRI sequences and do not bloom on gradient-echo imaging.
Blooming on gradient-echo sequences is expected.
updates.explanation: Recurrent haemorrhage in PVNS leaves intra-articular haemosiderin, which is paramagnetic. Its paramagnetic effect causes T1 prolongation and T2 shortening, producing dark signal on both T1- and T2-weighted images. Susceptibility blooming on gradient-echo imaging is therefore a key clue, as shown by the very dark masses in the source example.

updates.question_text: Regarding focal PVNS, which single statement is supported by the source?
options_before: PVNS is always diffuse and never focal.
Focal PVNS is synonymous with Baker's cyst.
Focal PVNS is defined by fat-signal frond-like synovial proliferation.
Focal PVNS can clinically mimic internal derangement.
Focal PVNS is primarily a popliteal aneurysm mimic.
options_after: PVNS is recognised as a diffuse process rather than a focal lesion.
Focal PVNS is synonymous with Baker's cyst.
Focal PVNS is defined by fat-signal frond-like synovial proliferation.
Focal PVNS can clinically mimic internal derangement.
Focal PVNS is primarily a popliteal aneurysm mimic.
updates.explanation: The source states that PVNS most commonly diffusely affects a joint, but may also be focal. Focal PVNS can clinically mimic internal derangement. Fatty frond-like synovial proliferation describes lipoma arborescens, while Baker's cyst and popliteal aneurysm are discussed separately as popliteal fossa entities.

updates.question_text: Regarding treatment implications of femoral neck fracture alignment, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Nondisplaced or valgus-impacted fractures can be treated with ORIF.
Young patients with femoral neck fracture preferentially undergo arthroplasty because joint preservation is not a goal.
Displaced or varus-angulated fractures in older active community ambulators are typically treated with arthroplasty.
All displaced femoral neck fractures are treated with dynamic hip screw because they are extracapsular.
Less active or debilitated older patients with displaced femoral neck fracture must undergo ORIF rather than hemiarthroplasty.
options_after: Nondisplaced or valgus-impacted fractures can be treated with ORIF.
Young patients with femoral neck fracture preferentially undergo arthroplasty because joint preservation is not a goal.
Displaced or varus-angulated fractures in older active community ambulators are typically treated with arthroplasty.
Most displaced femoral neck fractures are treated with dynamic hip screw because they are extracapsular.
Less active or debilitated older patients with displaced femoral neck fracture must undergo ORIF rather than hemiarthroplasty.
updates.explanation: Nondisplaced or valgus-impacted femoral neck fractures can be treated with ORIF, whereas displaced or varus-angulated fractures in older active community ambulators generally go to arthroplasty. Less active or debilitated older patients may be treated with hemiarthroplasty, not mandatory ORIF. In younger patients, ORIF is preferred to preserve the joint.

updates.question_text: Regarding greater trochanter fractures, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: They can be a tip-of-the-iceberg fracture, with true fracture extent beyond the visible greater trochanter.
A small isolated greater trochanter fragment on CT always excludes intertrochanteric extension.
Greater trochanter fractures are always managed as femoral neck fractures with arthroplasty.
The majority may actually be intertrochanteric fractures with the intertrochanteric component occult on radiography.
MRI is not useful after a small greater trochanter fracture is seen because oedema cannot show intertrochanteric extension.
options_after: They can be a tip-of-the-iceberg fracture, with true fracture extent beyond the visible greater trochanter.
A small isolated greater trochanter fragment on CT characteristically excludes intertrochanteric extension.
Greater trochanter fractures are characteristically managed as femoral neck fractures with arthroplasty.
The majority may actually be intertrochanteric fractures with the intertrochanteric component occult on radiography.
MRI is not useful after a small greater trochanter fracture is seen because oedema will not show intertrochanteric extension.
updates.explanation: Greater trochanter fractures can be tip-of-the-iceberg injuries, with occult intertrochanteric extension. Many are likely intertrochanteric fractures with the intertrochanteric component occult on radiography. MRI can show the true oedema and fracture extent, so a tiny CT-visible fragment does not exclude deeper extension.

updates.question_text: Regarding femoral neck stress fractures, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Medial cortical stress fractures are under tensile forces and require more aggressive treatment than lateral fractures.
They are typically seen in highly active patients.
Initial imaging always shows a discrete fracture line before marrow oedema appears.
The female athlete triad includes restrictive or disordered eating, menstrual dysfunction and low bone density.
Lateral cortical stress fractures are under compressive forces and usually need only cessation of activity.
options_after: Medial cortical stress fractures are under tensile forces and require more aggressive treatment than lateral fractures.
They are typically seen in highly active patients.
Initial imaging characteristically shows a discrete fracture line before marrow oedema appears.
The female athlete triad includes restrictive or disordered eating, menstrual dysfunction and low bone density.
Lateral cortical stress fractures are under compressive forces and usually need primarily cessation of activity.
updates.explanation: Femoral neck stress fractures are typically seen in highly active patients, and female athlete triad patients are at increased risk. Medial cortical fractures are compressive and tend to heal with cessation of activity. Lateral cortical fractures are tensile and therefore treated more aggressively. Imaging initially shows oedema, with fracture line in more advanced cases.

updates.question_text: Regarding atypical femoral fractures, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: They are associated only with denosumab and are not described with bisphosphonate use.
They characteristically begin in the medial femoral cortex and are usually highly comminuted.
They are caused by excessive osteoclast-induced remodelling, resulting in soft osteopenic bone.
They are insufficiency fractures of the proximal lateral femoral diaphyseal cortex, typically subtrochanteric.
Contralateral femur radiographs should be performed when one is identified.
options_after: They are associated primarily with denosumab and are not described with bisphosphonate use.
They characteristically begin in the medial femoral cortex and are usually highly comminuted.
They are caused by excessive osteoclast-induced remodelling, resulting in soft osteopenic bone.
They are insufficiency fractures of the proximal lateral femoral diaphyseal cortex, typically subtrochanteric.
Contralateral femur radiographs should be performed when one is identified.
updates.explanation: Atypical femoral fractures occur in the proximal lateral femoral diaphyseal cortex, typically subtrochanteric. Contralateral femur radiographs are recommended because bilateral disease occurs in a substantial minority. The mechanism is insufficient osteoclast-induced remodelling causing brittle bone, and these fractures are best known with bisphosphonates but also occur with denosumab or without these medications.

updates.question_text: Regarding practical AVN reporting and treatment implications, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Early AVN can be managed with medication or lifestyle changes and/or core decompression.
Bone marrow oedema is present in all AVN cases and has no clinical correlation with pain.
It is optimal to diagnose AVN before subchondral collapse and secondary osteoarthritis.
Once subchondral collapse and secondary osteoarthritis are present, treatment is generally arthroplasty.
Practical imaging descriptors include lesion size, subchondral bone-plate status and secondary osteoarthritis.
options_after: Early AVN can be managed with medication or lifestyle changes and/or core decompression.
Bone marrow oedema is present in most AVN cases and lacks clinical correlation with pain.
It is optimal to diagnose AVN before subchondral collapse and secondary osteoarthritis.
Once subchondral collapse and secondary osteoarthritis are present, treatment is generally arthroplasty.
Practical imaging descriptors include lesion size, subchondral bone-plate status and secondary osteoarthritis.
updates.explanation: The source stresses diagnosing AVN before collapse and osteoarthritis. Early disease can be treated with medication or lifestyle change and/or core decompression, while collapse with secondary osteoarthritis generally leads to arthroplasty. Practical reporting should include relative lesion size, subchondral bone-plate status and osteoarthritis. Bone marrow oedema is present in 50% and correlates with pain.

updates.question_text: Regarding cam-type and pincer-type FAI, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Cam-type FAI is characterised by osseous convexity of the femoral head-neck junction.
Pincer-type FAI is caused by acetabular undercoverage and is most common in adolescent males.
The crossover sign represents posterior acetabular wall crossing behind the anterior wall at the inferior acetabulum only.
Cam-type FAI is most common in young athletic males.
An alpha angle greater than 55 degrees is said to be abnormal, especially with symptoms.
options_after: Cam-type FAI is characterised by osseous convexity of the femoral head-neck junction.
Pincer-type FAI is caused by acetabular undercoverage and is most common in adolescent males.
The crossover sign represents posterior acetabular wall crossing behind the anterior wall at the inferior acetabulum in typical cases.
Cam-type FAI is most common in young athletic males.
An alpha angle greater than 55 degrees is said to be abnormal, especially with symptoms.
updates.explanation: Cam-type FAI is an osseous convexity at the femoral head-neck junction, most common in young athletic males. The alpha angle is measured on oblique axial MRI or CT, and greater than 55 degrees is considered abnormal, particularly when symptoms are present. Pincer-type FAI is acetabular overcoverage, more common in middle-aged females, with the superior anterior wall crossing over the posterior wall on frontal radiography.

updates.question_text: Which single reporting statement is most appropriate when imaging morphology suggests FAI in a young adult but the clinical syndrome is not established?
options_before: Diagnose definitive femoroacetabular impingement solely from morphology.
Do not mention the morphology because asymptomatic patients can have abnormal measurements.
Report only osteoarthritis and ignore labral or chondral associations.
State that the findings may predispose to impingement in the presence of pain.
Recommend arthroplasty because impingement is treated like advanced AVN.
options_after: Diagnose definitive femoroacetabular impingement solely from morphology.
Do not mention the morphology because asymptomatic patients can have abnormal measurements.
Report primarily osteoarthritis and ignore labral or chondral associations.
State that the findings may predispose to impingement in the presence of pain.
Recommend arthroplasty because impingement is treated like advanced AVN.
updates.explanation: The source emphasises that impingement is primarily a clinical diagnosis and that abnormal morphology can occur in asymptomatic patients. A general consensus is to describe imaging findings suggestive of FAI with the disclaimer that they may predispose to impingement in the presence of pain. This avoids overcalling a purely imaging-based diagnosis while still communicating relevant morphology.

updates.question_text: Regarding normal acromioclavicular joint measurements and stress radiography, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The normal acromioclavicular joint space should be greater than 10 mm
The coracoclavicular distance is abnormal only when it exceeds 25 mm on both sides
Passive traction with the patient holding a weight may be required to unmask an acromioclavicular injury
Side-to-side asymmetry is expected and is not useful in acromioclavicular assessment
The coracoclavicular interspace is used primarily to assess the acromioclavicular joint capsule
options_after: The normal acromioclavicular joint space should be greater than 10 mm
The coracoclavicular distance is abnormal primarily when it exceeds 25 mm on both sides
Passive traction with the patient holding a weight may be required to unmask an acromioclavicular injury
Side-to-side asymmetry is expected and is not useful in acromioclavicular assessment
The coracoclavicular interspace is used primarily to assess the acromioclavicular joint capsule
updates.explanation: The source states that passive traction with the patient holding a weight may be necessary to unmask an acromioclavicular injury. The normal acromioclavicular joint space should be less than 5 mm, and the normal coracoclavicular distance is less than 11-13 mm. Side-to-side asymmetry greater than 50% is abnormal. The coracoclavicular interspace evaluates the coracoclavicular ligaments rather than the acromioclavicular capsule.

updates.question_text: Regarding chronic full-thickness rotator cuff tears and rotator cuff atrophy, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Isolated infraspinatus tears are never related to posterior instability
Fatty degeneration may occur within 4 weeks of injury and is usually irreversible
The degree of fatty infiltration should be routinely assessed on sagittal images
The extent of muscle degeneration correlates with outcome after surgical repair
Chronic full-thickness rotator cuff tear due to rheumatoid arthritis may show superior migration of the humeral head
options_after: Isolated infraspinatus tears are not related to posterior instability
Fatty degeneration may occur within 4 weeks of injury and is usually irreversible
The degree of fatty infiltration should be routinely assessed on sagittal images
The extent of muscle degeneration correlates with outcome after surgical repair
Chronic full-thickness rotator cuff tear due to rheumatoid arthritis may show superior migration of the humeral head
updates.explanation: Rotator cuff atrophy is most commonly due to chronic rotator cuff tear. Fatty degeneration may occur within 4 weeks and is usually irreversible, and the extent of degeneration correlates with surgical outcome. The source emphasises sagittal assessment of fatty infiltration. Chronic full-thickness cuff tear from rheumatoid arthritis has a classic appearance with superior humeral head migration. Isolated infraspinatus tears can be seen with posterior instability.

updates.question_text: Regarding the Goutallier classification described in the source, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Grade 4 means fatty infiltration with more fat than muscle
Grade 0 means equal muscle and fat
Grade 1 means more fat than muscle
Grade 2 means a few fatty streaks only
Grade 3 means normal muscle with no fat
options_after: Grade 4 means fatty infiltration with more fat than muscle
Grade 0 means equal muscle and fat
Grade 1 means more fat than muscle
Grade 2 means a few fatty streaks in typical cases
Grade 3 means normal muscle without fat
updates.explanation: The source lists Goutallier grade 4 as fatty infiltration with more fat than muscle. Grade 0 is normal muscle with no fat, grade 1 is a few fatty streaks, grade 2 is more muscle than fat and grade 3 is equal muscle and fat. This grading is used for fatty replacement of rotator cuff muscles.

updates.question_text: Regarding the coracohumeral, superior glenohumeral and middle glenohumeral ligaments, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The coracohumeral ligament is located external to the joint capsule
The middle glenohumeral ligament is always present
The superior glenohumeral ligament connects the lesser tuberosity to the supraglenoid tubercle
The coracohumeral ligament attaches medially to the inferior glenoid labrum
Middle glenohumeral ligament tears are unrelated to SLAP lesions
options_after: The coracohumeral ligament is located external to the joint capsule
The middle glenohumeral ligament is characteristically present
The superior glenohumeral ligament connects the lesser tuberosity to the supraglenoid tubercle
The coracohumeral ligament attaches medially to the inferior glenoid labrum
Middle glenohumeral ligament tears are unrelated to SLAP lesions
updates.explanation: The coracohumeral ligament lies external to the joint capsule and contributes to the biceps pulley with the superior glenohumeral ligament. The superior glenohumeral ligament connects the lesser tuberosity to the supraglenoid tubercle. The middle glenohumeral ligament may be congenitally absent in up to one-third of patients, and its tears are associated with SLAP lesions. The coracohumeral ligament connects the coracoid process to the greater tubercle.

updates.question_text: Regarding long head of biceps tendon anatomy, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It originates at the inferior labrum
It courses posterior to the glenoid without entering the intertubercular groove
The biceps tendon sheath does not communicate with the glenohumeral joint
Fluid in the biceps tendon sheath may be normal
The tendon is stabilised only by the inferior glenohumeral ligament
options_after: It originates at the inferior labrum
It courses posterior to the glenoid without entering the intertubercular groove
The biceps tendon sheath does not communicate with the glenohumeral joint
Fluid in the biceps tendon sheath may be normal
The tendon is stabilised primarily by the inferior glenohumeral ligament
updates.explanation: The long head of the biceps tendon originates at the superior labrum and courses in the intertubercular groove. The biceps tendon sheath communicates with the glenohumeral joint, so fluid in the tendon sheath may be normal. Stabilisation of the tendon involves the biceps pulley, not the inferior glenohumeral ligament alone.

updates.question_text: Regarding biceps tendon tears, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Approximately 33% of supraspinatus tendon tears are associated with biceps tendon injury
Biceps tendon injury is never associated with rotator cuff tears
The biceps tendon is protected from impingement because it lies outside the coracoacromial arch
An acute tear always causes proximal retraction of the biceps muscle
An empty intertubercular groove may signify complete tear with retraction or biceps tendon dislocation
options_after: Approximately 33% of supraspinatus tendon tears are associated with biceps tendon injury
Biceps tendon injury is not associated with rotator cuff tears
The biceps tendon is protected from impingement because it lies outside the coracoacromial arch
An acute tear characteristically causes proximal retraction of the biceps muscle
An empty intertubercular groove may signify complete tear with retraction or biceps tendon dislocation
updates.explanation: The source states that approximately 33% of supraspinatus tendon tears are associated with biceps tendon injury, including complete tear, partial tear or degeneration. The biceps tendon is at risk for impingement because it is partly under the supraspinatus tendon in the coracoacromial arch. In acute tear, the biceps muscle may retract distally. An empty intertubercular groove can indicate complete tear with retraction or biceps tendon dislocation.

updates.question_text: Regarding direction-based classification of shoulder instability, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Radiologists usually classify instability by the degree of fatty infiltration of rotator cuff muscles
Anterior instability accounts for the vast majority of cases, approximately 95%
Posterior instability accounts for the vast majority of cases
Superior instability is the only recognised direction-based category
Multidirectional instability is excluded from radiological classification
options_after: Radiologists usually classify instability by the degree of fatty infiltration of rotator cuff muscles
Anterior instability accounts for the vast majority of cases, approximately 95%
Posterior instability accounts for the vast majority of cases
Superior instability is the principal recognised direction-based category
Multidirectional instability is excluded from radiological classification
updates.explanation: Radiologists usually classify instability according to the direction of joint subluxation: anterior, posterior, multidirectional or superior. The source states that anterior instability accounts for the vast majority, approximately 95%, of cases. Fatty infiltration grading belongs to rotator cuff atrophy assessment rather than instability direction.

updates.question_text: MRI shows complete discontinuity of the supraspinatus tendon with proximal tendon retraction and a large effusion continuous between the glenohumeral joint and subacromial/subdeltoid bursa. Which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: These findings support a full-thickness rotator cuff tear
The most likely lesion is an isolated biceps pulley injury with a preserved supraspinatus tendon
A full-thickness tear can be diagnosed when abnormal signal extends through the tendon fibres
The source states that full-thickness cuff tears are classified only by the presence or absence of marrow oedema
Full-thickness rotator cuff tears are classified by the length of affected tendon or muscle, from small to massive
options_after: These findings support a full-thickness rotator cuff tear
The most likely lesion is an isolated biceps pulley injury with a preserved supraspinatus tendon
A full-thickness tear can be diagnosed when abnormal signal extends through the tendon fibres
The source states that full-thickness cuff tears are classified primarily by the presence or absence of marrow oedema
Full-thickness rotator cuff tears are classified by the length of affected tendon or muscle, from small to massive
updates.explanation: Complete discontinuity of supraspinatus with retraction and communication between the glenohumeral joint and subacromial/subdeltoid bursa is the source example of a full-thickness rotator cuff tear. In non-arthrographic imaging, abnormal signal through the tendon fibres supports full-thickness tear. The source classifies full-thickness tears by length of affected tendon or muscle, ranging from small under 1 cm to massive over 5 cm.

updates.question_text: Regarding the glenoid labrum and its normal variants, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The glenoid labrum replaces the glenoid hyaline cartilage rather than resting on it
The labrum increases the surface area and depth of the glenoid cavity
The labrum has no stabilising relationship with the humeral head during motion
The glenohumeral ligaments, biceps tendon and joint capsule attach directly to the labrum
Labral injury location may be described by sextants or by a clock face
options_after: The glenoid labrum replaces the glenoid hyaline cartilage rather than resting on it
The labrum increases the surface area and depth of the glenoid cavity
The labrum lacks stabilising relationship with the humeral head during motion
The glenohumeral ligaments, biceps tendon and joint capsule attach directly to the labrum
Labral injury location may be described by sextants or by a clock face
updates.explanation: The glenoid labrum is a fibrocartilaginous ring resting on the glenoid hyaline cartilage. It increases the surface area and depth of the glenoid cavity and provides a suction effect that helps the humeral head adhere to the glenoid during motion. Important stabilisers attach directly to it, including glenohumeral ligaments, the biceps tendon and the joint capsule. The source describes labral location by sextants or by a clock face.

updates.question_text: Regarding anterior glenohumeral dislocation, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: It represents only 2-3% of shoulder dislocations
It is usually caused by severe muscle spasm after seizure or electrocution
It is by far the most common shoulder dislocation and usually displaces the humeral head anteroinferiorly
It is defined by inferior dislocation of the humerus with a superiorly projecting humerus
It is usually best diagnosed only on an axillary view because frontal radiographs appear normal
options_after: This injury accounts for approximately 2-3% of shoulder dislocations.
It is usually caused by severe muscle spasm after seizure or electrocution
It is by far the most common shoulder dislocation and usually displaces the humeral head anteroinferiorly
It is defined by inferior dislocation of the humerus with a superiorly projecting humerus
It is usually best diagnosed primarily on an axillary view because frontal radiographs appear normal
updates.explanation: Anterior dislocation of the humerus with respect to the glenoid is by far the most common shoulder dislocation. The humeral head usually dislocates in an anteroinferior direction and is typically caused by direct force on the arm. Severe muscle spasm after seizure or electrocution is the source's mechanism for posterior dislocation. Luxatio erecta describes inferior dislocation.

updates.question_text: Regarding Hill-Sachs detection on cross-sectional imaging, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: A Hill-Sachs lesion is excluded if no displaced glenoid fracture is visible
A Hill-Sachs lesion is defined as an anteromedial humeral head compression fracture
The normal humeral head should appear notched in three consecutive superior slices
A posterolateral notch in the humeral head on sequential axial images supports Hill-Sachs
Bone marrow oedema without fracture cannot indicate a subtle Hill-Sachs lesion
options_after: A Hill-Sachs lesion is excluded if displaced glenoid fracture is absent
A Hill-Sachs lesion is defined as an anteromedial humeral head compression fracture
The normal humeral head should appear notched in three consecutive superior slices
A posterolateral notch in the humeral head on sequential axial images supports Hill-Sachs
Bone marrow oedema without fracture will not indicate a subtle Hill-Sachs lesion
updates.explanation: The source describes scrolling through sequential axial images: with standard 5 mm slices, the normal humeral head should appear round in three consecutive slices starting superiorly. A posterolateral notch supports Hill-Sachs. Subtle Hill-Sachs can also be detected as bone marrow oedema in this location without a visible fracture. The anteromedial compression fracture is the trough sign or reverse Hill-Sachs lesion.

updates.question_text: Regarding posterior instability and associated lesions, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Posterior instability accounts for most instability cases
Posterior instability has no recognised relationship to reverse Bankart or reverse Hill-Sachs lesions
Teres minor and infraspinatus tears are unrelated to posterior instability because they insert anteriorly
Hypoplastic posterior glenoid may be a congenital cause of posterior instability
A Bennett lesion is extra-articular posterior ossification associated with posterior labral injury
options_after: Posterior instability accounts for most instability cases
Posterior instability lacks recognised relationship to reverse Bankart or reverse Hill-Sachs lesions
Teres minor and infraspinatus tears are unrelated to posterior instability because they insert anteriorly
Hypoplastic posterior glenoid may be a congenital cause of posterior instability
A Bennett lesion is extra-articular posterior ossification associated with posterior labral injury
updates.explanation: Posterior instability is uncommon, accounting for less than 5% of instability. Associated injuries include posterior variants of anterior lesions, such as posterior HAGL, reverse Bankart and reverse Hill-Sachs/trough sign. Infraspinatus and teres minor tears are associated because these muscles insert on the posterior aspect of the greater tuberosity. Hypoplastic posterior glenoid may be congenital, and Bennett lesion is extra-articular posterior ossification associated with posterior labral injury.

updates.question_text: Regarding SLAP tears, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: A SLAP tear is a posterior-inferior glenoid fracture associated with posterior dislocation
A SLAP tear is an anterior-posterior tear of the superior labrum centred at the biceps tendon attachment
A SLAP tear is synonymous with GLAD and does not involve the superior labrum
The biceps tendon inserts onto the posterior-inferior labrum in the source description
Only two types of SLAP lesions are recognised in current usage according to the source
options_after: A SLAP tear is a posterior-inferior glenoid fracture associated with posterior dislocation
A SLAP tear is an anterior-posterior tear of the superior labrum centred at the biceps tendon attachment
A SLAP tear is synonymous with GLAD and does not involve the superior labrum
The biceps tendon inserts onto the posterior-inferior labrum in the source description
Current SLAP classification is limited to the four originally described lesion types.
updates.explanation: SLAP means superior labrum anterior posterior tear: an anterior-posterior oriented tear of the superior labrum centred at the biceps tendon attachment. The source states that the biceps tendon inserts onto the anterior-superior labrum. It also notes that four types were originally described, with up to 10 subcategories now recognised. GLAD is a separate anterior-inferior labral and cartilage injury.

updates.question_text: Regarding GLAD lesions, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: GLAD is a superior labral tear centred on the biceps tendon attachment
GLAD occurs at the anterior-inferior labrum
GLAD includes adjacent glenoid articular cartilage injury
GLAD is usually not caused by or associated with instability
GLAD cannot lead to post-traumatic arthritis or intra-articular bodies
options_after: GLAD is a superior labral tear centred on the biceps tendon attachment
GLAD occurs at the anterior-inferior labrum
GLAD includes adjacent glenoid articular cartilage injury
GLAD is usually not caused by or associated with instability
GLAD will not lead to post-traumatic arthritis or intra-articular bodies
updates.explanation: Glenoid labral articular disruption is a superficial tear of the anterior-inferior labrum with adjacent glenoid articular cartilage injury. Although it occurs at the same labral site as Bankart, ALPSA and Perthes lesions, it is usually not caused by or associated with instability. The source notes that GLAD lesions may lead to post-traumatic arthritis and intra-articular bodies.

updates.question_text: Regarding paralabral cysts, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Paralabral cysts form adjacent to labral tears, analogous to parameniscal cysts adjacent to meniscal tears
A paralabral cyst excludes a labral tear if abnormal labral signal is not visible
Paralabral cysts are always intraosseous and not soft-tissue lesions
A paralabral cyst is a specific finding for labral tear even when abnormal labral signal is not seen
Paralabral cysts may compress a nerve and cause entrapment neuropathy
options_after: Paralabral cysts form adjacent to labral tears, analogous to parameniscal cysts adjacent to meniscal tears
A paralabral cyst excludes a labral tear if abnormal labral signal is not visible
Paralabral cysts are characteristically intraosseous and not soft-tissue lesions
A paralabral cyst is a specific finding for labral tear even when abnormal labral signal is not seen
Paralabral cysts may compress a nerve and cause entrapment neuropathy
updates.explanation: Paralabral cysts form adjacent to labral tears, analogous to parameniscal cysts near meniscal tears. They are usually seen in soft tissues adjacent to the labrum but may extend into bone. The source emphasises that a paralabral cyst is a specific finding for labral tear even if abnormal labral signal is not visible. Such cysts may compress adjacent nerves and cause entrapment neuropathy.

updates.question_text: Regarding MR arthrography with ABER positioning, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It is the standard method for confirming all posterior dislocations in patients unable to abduct
It is mainly used in the source to diagnose inferior luxatio erecta
It may be necessary to diagnose a Perthes lesion
It helps because the labrum in a Perthes lesion may remain attached to periosteum and in anatomic position
ABER stands for abduction-external rotation in this context
options_after: It is the standard method for confirming most posterior dislocations in patients unable to abduct
It is mainly used in the source to diagnose inferior luxatio erecta
It may be necessary to diagnose a Perthes lesion
It helps because the labrum in a Perthes lesion may remain attached to periosteum and in anatomic position
ABER stands for abduction-external rotation in this context
updates.explanation: The source states that a Perthes lesion can be difficult to visualise because the labrum remains attached to periosteum and may remain in its anatomic position. MR arthrography with ABER, meaning abduction-external rotation, is often necessary for diagnosis. Posterior dislocation is best shown with transscapular Y or axillary views rather than ABER arthrography.

updates.question_text: Regarding the relationship between instability direction and rotator cuff muscle findings, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Posterior instability is associated with supraspinatus and subscapularis tears because they insert on the lesser tuberosity
Tears of infraspinatus and teres minor are associated with posterior instability
The source links these posterior cuff tears to insertion on the posterior aspect of the greater tuberosity
Anterior instability always produces isolated teres minor atrophy
Posterior instability excludes congenital posterior glenoid hypoplasia
options_after: Posterior instability is associated with supraspinatus and subscapularis tears because they insert on the lesser tuberosity
Tears of infraspinatus and teres minor are associated with posterior instability
The source links these posterior cuff tears to insertion on the posterior aspect of the greater tuberosity
Anterior instability characteristically produces isolated teres minor atrophy
Posterior instability excludes congenital posterior glenoid hypoplasia
updates.explanation: The source associates posterior instability with tears of infraspinatus and teres minor because these rotator cuff muscles insert on the posterior aspect of the greater tuberosity. It also states that a hypoplastic posterior glenoid may be a congenital cause of posterior instability. Isolated teres minor atrophy is related to axillary nerve entrapment in the quadrilateral space, not anterior instability.

updates.question_text: Regarding distal radius fracture patterns, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Colles fracture is a distal radius fracture with volar angulation
Barton fracture is an extra-articular transverse fracture with no radiocarpal subluxation
Smith type I is a reverse Colles fracture and is extra-articular transverse
Hutchinson fracture involves the radial styloid and extends into the radiocarpal joint
Smith type II is a dorsal Barton fracture with dorsal displacement
options_after: Colles fracture is a distal radius fracture with volar angulation
Barton fracture is an extra-articular transverse fracture without radiocarpal subluxation
Smith type I is a reverse Colles fracture and is extra-articular transverse
Hutchinson fracture involves the radial styloid and extends into the radiocarpal joint
Smith type II is a dorsal Barton fracture with dorsal displacement
updates.explanation: Colles fracture is a distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation and commonly follows a fall on an outstretched hand. Smith type I is the common reverse Colles pattern: an extra-articular transverse fracture. Hutchinson, or chauffeur's, fracture involves the radial lateral distal radius, extending into the radial styloid and radiocarpal joint. Barton fracture is an intra-articular oblique dorsal distal radius fracture with dorsal radiocarpal subluxation or dislocation, while Smith type II is a reverse Barton pattern with volar displacement.

updates.question_text: Regarding medial collateral ligament injury of the elbow, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The medial collateral ligament is also known as the ulnar collateral ligament
It is the ligamentous stabiliser against valgus stress
Elbow MCL injuries are usually related to chronic stress from the late cocking phase of throwing
Valgus stress views are not useful because they cannot demonstrate medial joint space widening
Undersurface stripping of the sublime tubercle attachment creates the T-sign
options_after: The medial collateral ligament is also known as the ulnar collateral ligament
It is the ligamentous stabiliser against valgus stress
Elbow MCL injuries are usually related to chronic stress from the late cocking phase of throwing
Valgus stress views are not useful because they will not demonstrate medial joint space widening
Undersurface stripping of the sublime tubercle attachment creates the T-sign
updates.explanation: The elbow medial collateral ligament is also called the ulnar collateral ligament and stabilises against valgus stress. Unlike the knee, elbow MCL injury is usually due to chronic throwing-related stress, especially the late cocking phase. Valgus stress radiographs can demonstrate medial compartment widening. A common injury pattern is undersurface stripping at the sublime tubercle attachment, producing the T-sign on arthrographic MRI.

updates.question_text: Regarding triceps and distal biceps tendon tears at the elbow, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Triceps tears are relatively rare
Non-athletic triceps tears have no described association with olecranon bursitis or steroid use
Triceps tears never involve olecranon avulsion
An intact lacertus fibrosus helps prevent proximal retraction of the distal biceps
Proximal retraction of a torn distal biceps implies that the lacertus fibrosus is presumably torn
options_after: Triceps tears are relatively rare
Non-athletic triceps tears lack described association with olecranon bursitis or steroid use
Triceps tears will not involve olecranon avulsion
An intact lacertus fibrosus helps prevent proximal retraction of the distal biceps
Proximal retraction of a torn distal biceps implies that the lacertus fibrosus is presumably torn
updates.explanation: Triceps tears are relatively rare and commonly involve bony avulsion of the olecranon. Non-athletic traumatic triceps injuries often have a predisposing factor such as olecranon bursitis or steroid use. The distal biceps inserts on the radial tuberosity, and the lacertus fibrosus is located at the myotendinous junction. When intact, it limits proximal retraction; if proximal retraction is present, the lacertus fibrosus is presumably torn.

updates.question_text: Regarding triquetral fracture and Kienbock disease, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Triquetral fracture is best seen on lateral wrist radiograph as an avulsion fragment dorsal to the triquetrum
Triquetral fracture is always obvious on the frontal radiograph
Kienbock disease is avascular necrosis of the lunate
Kienbock disease is associated with positive ulnar variance, where the ulna is longer than the radius
Negative ulnar variance is thought to increase load on the lunate
options_after: Triquetral fracture is best seen on lateral wrist radiograph as an avulsion fragment dorsal to the triquetrum
Triquetral fracture is characteristically obvious on the frontal radiograph
Kienbock disease is avascular necrosis of the lunate
Kienbock disease is associated with positive ulnar variance, where the ulna is longer than the radius
Negative ulnar variance is thought to increase load on the lunate
updates.explanation: Triquetral fracture can be subtle or invisible on frontal radiography and is best seen on the lateral view as a dorsal avulsion fragment. Kienbock disease is avascular necrosis of the lunate. It is associated with negative ulnar variance, meaning the ulna is shorter than the radius, and is thought to result from increased load on the lunate.

updates.question_text: Regarding gamekeeper's thumb and Stener lesion, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Gamekeeper's thumb is also known as skier's thumb
It is injury to the ulnar collateral ligament at the base of the thumb proximal phalanx
It may be associated with an avulsion fragment at the base of the proximal phalanx
A Stener lesion is complete UCL disruption with interposition of the adductor aponeurosis and requires surgery
Incomplete UCL tears must always be treated surgically
options_after: Gamekeeper's thumb is also known as skier's thumb
It is injury to the ulnar collateral ligament at the base of the thumb proximal phalanx
It may be associated with an avulsion fragment at the base of the proximal phalanx
A Stener lesion is complete UCL disruption with interposition of the adductor aponeurosis and requires surgery
Incomplete UCL tears must characteristically be treated surgically
updates.explanation: Gamekeeper's or skier's thumb is ulnar collateral ligament injury at the base of the thumb proximal phalanx, caused by forced thumb abduction. It may have an avulsion fragment at the base of the proximal phalanx. Incomplete UCL tears may be treated conservatively, but complete tears require surgery. Stener lesion is complete UCL disruption with interposed adductor aponeurosis and also requires surgery.

updates.question_text: Regarding diagnostic arthrography, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: It is performed only for therapeutic steroid delivery
It is used only to assess extra-articular masses
Post-arthrogram MR or CT is rarely performed
It should avoid assessment of labra, menisci and ligaments
Contrast is injected into the joint to assess intra-articular structures and bodies
options_after: It is performed primarily for therapeutic steroid delivery
It is used primarily to assess extra-articular masses
Post-arthrogram MR or CT is rarely performed
It should avoid assessment of labra, menisci and ligaments
Contrast is injected into the joint to assess intra-articular structures and bodies
updates.explanation: Diagnostic arthrography injects contrast into a joint to assess intra-articular structures such as cartilage, menisci, labra and ligaments, and to evaluate for intra-articular bodies. Post-arthrogram MR or CT is almost always performed. Arthrography can also be therapeutic, but that is a separate indication involving steroid and anaesthetic injection under imaging guidance.

updates.question_text: Regarding dose reduction in fluoroscopic musculoskeletal procedures, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The ALARA principle should be maintained
The image intensifier should be kept as far from the patient as possible
Pulse mode should never be used during musculoskeletal procedures
Coning-in the image after the basic anatomy is seen reduces unnecessary irradiation
Reducing the number of images, pedal time and frames per second can reduce dose
options_after: The ALARA principle should be maintained
The image intensifier should be kept as far from the patient as possible
Pulse mode should not be used during musculoskeletal procedures
Coning-in the image after the basic anatomy is seen reduces unnecessary irradiation
Reducing the number of images, pedal time and frames per second can reduce dose
updates.explanation: The source emphasises ALARA for fluoroscopic procedures. Dose can be reduced by lowering imaging parameters, using low-dose mode when appropriate, reducing the number of images, pressing the pedal briefly and reducing frames per second with pulse mode. The image intensifier should be as close to the patient as feasible, and the image should be coned in once the relevant anatomy has been established.

updates.question_text: Regarding abnormal communication seen during wrist arthrography, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Communication between radiocarpal and distal radioulnar joints indicates scapholunate tear
Communication between radiocarpal and distal radioulnar joints indicates a TFC tear
Communication between radiocarpal and midcarpal spaces is a normal finding
Real-time fluoroscopy is unnecessary because abnormal communication cannot be detected during injection
Communication between the radiocarpal compartment and midcarpal space demonstrates scapholunate or lunotriquetral ligament tears
options_after: Communication between radiocarpal and distal radioulnar joints indicates scapholunate tear
Communication between radiocarpal and distal radioulnar joints indicates a TFC tear
Communication between radiocarpal and midcarpal spaces is a normal finding
Real-time fluoroscopy is unnecessary because abnormal communication will not be detected during injection
Communication between the radiocarpal compartment and midcarpal space demonstrates scapholunate or lunotriquetral ligament tears
updates.explanation: During wrist arthrography, contrast is injected into the radiocarpal compartment and real-time fluoroscopy is used to identify abnormal communication. Communication with the distal radioulnar joint indicates a TFC tear. Communication with the midcarpal space demonstrates tears of either the scapholunate or lunotriquetral ligaments.

updates.question_text: Regarding soft tissue mass biopsy, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Soft tissue mass biopsy is generally performed using a fine needle aspiration device only
A coaxial spring-loaded biopsy device is generally used
The least enhancing portion of the mass should be targeted even if an avidly enhancing component is safely accessible
Musculoskeletal soft tissue biopsies cannot be performed with ultrasound guidance
The most avidly enhancing portion or highest FDG uptake focus should be targeted if safe
options_after: Soft tissue mass biopsy is generally performed using a fine needle aspiration device in typical cases
A coaxial spring-loaded biopsy device is generally used
The least enhancing portion of the mass should be targeted even if an avidly enhancing component is safely accessible
Musculoskeletal soft tissue biopsies will not be performed with ultrasound guidance
The most avidly enhancing portion or highest FDG uptake focus should be targeted if safe
updates.explanation: Soft tissue mass biopsies are generally performed with a coaxial spring-loaded biopsy device. For highest diagnostic yield, the most avidly enhancing portion, or the most avid focus of FDG uptake if PET was performed, should be targeted provided it is safe. Most musculoskeletal soft tissue biopsies can be performed with ultrasound, although CT is often reasonable as well.

updates.question_text: Regarding bone biopsy targeting and CT guidance, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Most bone biopsies are performed with CT guidance
Lesions occult on CT but visible on MR cannot generally be targeted using CT landmarks
Sclerotic lesions generally have higher diagnostic yield than lucent lesions
Lucent lesions generally have higher diagnostic yield than sclerotic lesions
The most avidly enhancing or highest FDG uptake region should be avoided even if safe
options_after: Most bone biopsies are performed with CT guidance
A lesion visible on MRI but occult on CT is unsuitable for CT-guided targeting even when anatomic landmarks are available.
Sclerotic lesions generally have higher diagnostic yield than lucent lesions
Lucent lesions generally have higher diagnostic yield than sclerotic lesions
The most avidly enhancing or highest FDG uptake region should be avoided even if safe
updates.explanation: Most bone biopsies are performed with CT guidance. Lesions that are occult on CT but visible on MR can generally be targeted with CT using landmarks, and MR-guided biopsy can be performed in selected cases. Lucent lesions generally have higher diagnostic yield than sclerotic lesions. As in soft tissue biopsy, the most avidly enhancing or highest FDG uptake region should be targeted when safe.

updates.question_text: Regarding ventricular anatomy, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The foramina of Monro connect the third ventricle with the fourth ventricle.
The foramina of Monro connect the lateral ventricles with the third ventricle.
The cerebral aqueduct connects the third ventricle with the fourth ventricle.
The fourth ventricle drains into the basal cisterns through two foramina only.
The fourth ventricle continues inferiorly at the obex as the central canal of the spinal cord.
options_after: The foramina of Monro connect the third ventricle with the fourth ventricle.
The foramina of Monro connect the lateral ventricles with the third ventricle.
The cerebral aqueduct connects the third ventricle with the fourth ventricle.
The fourth ventricle drains into the basal cisterns through two foramina in typical cases.
The fourth ventricle continues inferiorly at the obex as the central canal of the spinal cord.
updates.explanation: The lateral ventricles drain into the third ventricle through the foramina of Monro. The cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius connects the third and fourth ventricles. The fourth ventricle continues inferiorly at its tip, the obex, as the central canal of the spinal cord. It also drains into the basal cisterns through three foramina: paired foramina of Luschka and the single foramen of Magendie.

updates.question_text: Regarding spin-echo T1- and T2-weighted imaging, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: T1 hyperintensity can be a clue to fat, proteinaceous material, methemoglobin or melanin.
Minerals can never contribute to T1 shortening.
T2 hypointensity can be a clue to most stages of blood, calcification, fibrous tissue or highly cellular tumours.
Fast-moving blood appears hypointense on T2-weighted spin-echo sequences as a flow void.
FLAIR is a T1-only sequence that cannot be applied to T2-weighted imaging.
options_after: T1 hyperintensity can be a clue to fat, proteinaceous material, methemoglobin or melanin.
Minerals will not contribute to T1 shortening.
T2 hypointensity can be a clue to most stages of blood, calcification, fibrous tissue or highly cellular tumours.
Fast-moving blood appears hypointense on T2-weighted spin-echo sequences as a flow void.
FLAIR is a T1-predominant sequence that will not be applied to T2-weighted imaging.
updates.explanation: The source lists fat, proteinaceous material, methemoglobin, melanin and several minerals as causes of T1 shortening. T2 shortening can occur with most stages of blood, calcification, fibrous tissue, highly cellular tumours and desiccated secretions. Fast-moving blood appears hypointense on long-TE T2-weighted spin-echo sequences as a flow void. FLAIR is the addition of an inversion pulse that nulls fluid signal and is most commonly used as a T2-FLAIR sequence.

updates.question_text: Regarding diffusion-weighted imaging and ADC maps, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: DWI depicts Brownian motion of water protons.
Free water experiences the least signal attenuation on DWI.
The ADC map retains T2 weighting and therefore cannot separate diffusion from T2 signal.
Reduced diffusivity is hyperintense on trace DWI and hypointense on the ADC map.
Higher b-values increase contrast for detecting reduced diffusivity but reduce signal-to-noise ratio unless scan time is increased.
options_after: DWI depicts Brownian motion of water protons.
Free water experiences the least signal attenuation on DWI.
The ADC map retains T2 weighting and therefore will not separate diffusion from T2 signal.
Reduced diffusivity is hyperintense on trace DWI and hypointense on the ADC map.
Higher b-values increase contrast for detecting reduced diffusivity but reduce signal-to-noise ratio unless scan time is increased.
updates.explanation: DWI depicts Brownian motion of water protons, with signal lost as diffusion increases. Free water, such as CSF, experiences the most signal attenuation. Trace DWI is sensitive to reduced diffusivity, which appears hyperintense, while the ADC map provides diffusion information without T2 weighting and shows reduced diffusivity as hypointense. Increasing the b-value increases diffusion contrast but reduces signal-to-noise ratio unless additional acquisitions increase scan time.

updates.question_text: Regarding MR spectroscopy methods and metabolites, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Single-voxel spectroscopy provides high signal-to-noise ratio with short scan time but only single-voxel coverage.
Chemical shift imaging provides only single-voxel coverage and is best for small homogeneous lesions.
Choline is a marker of cell membrane turnover that increases in most abnormalities.
N-acetylaspartate is a marker of neuronal viability that decreases in most abnormalities.
Lipids and lactate reflect abnormal tissue damage and anaerobic glycolysis, respectively.
