options_after: T2 hypointensity may reflect hypercellularity, haemorrhage, calcification or proteinaceous fluid.
Marked CT hyperattenuation may be caused by cystic or necrotic components or fat.
T1 hyperintensity is specific for calcification and does not occur with fat, haemorrhage or melanin.
Most high-grade gliomas enhance, without low-grade neoplasm enhances.
Contrast enhancement occurs in the vast majority of extra-axial and non-glial intra-axial neoplasms.
updates.explanation: The source states that T2 hypointensity can result from hypercellularity, haemorrhage, calcification or proteinaceous fluid. More marked CT hyperattenuation may reflect haemorrhage or calcification, whereas hypoattenuation may reflect cystic or necrotic components or fat. T1 hyperintensity can be due to fat, haemorrhage, melanin or proteinaceous fluid, so it is not specific for calcification. Enhancement is common in extra-axial and non-glial intra-axial neoplasms, but glioma grade does not perfectly correlate with enhancement.

updates.question_text: Regarding molecular diagnosis of diffuse gliomas, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Since 2016, molecular data have been ignored in favour of histological phenotype alone.
1p/19q co-deletion status is described as relevant only to metastatic disease and not diffuse glioma classification.
IDH-wildtype diffuse gliomas are most commonly diagnosed as glioblastoma, WHO grade 4.
Most glioblastomas are IDH-wildtype, which confers a worse prognosis.
Grade 2 or 3 IDH-wildtype diffuse gliomas are treated as indolent low-grade tumours because transformation to grade 4 is rare.
options_after: Since 2016, molecular data have been ignored in favour of histological phenotype alone.
1p/19q co-deletion status is described as relevant primarily to metastatic disease and not diffuse glioma classification.
IDH-wildtype diffuse gliomas are most commonly diagnosed as glioblastoma, WHO grade 4.
Most glioblastomas are IDH-wildtype, which confers a worse prognosis.
Grade 2 or 3 IDH-wildtype diffuse gliomas are treated as indolent low-grade tumours because transformation to grade 4 is rare.
updates.explanation: Since 2016, molecular data including IDH1/2 mutation and 1p/19q co-deletion status are considered with, and usually supersede, histological phenotype in integrated diffuse glioma diagnoses. IDH-wildtype diffuse gliomas are most commonly diagnosed as glioblastoma, WHO grade 4, and most glioblastomas are IDH-wildtype with worse prognosis. Rare grade 2 or 3 IDH-wildtype diffuse gliomas are treated as early glioblastoma because they rapidly transform to grade 4, not as indolent low-grade tumours.

updates.question_text: Regarding tumour spread routes described for IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Tumour spread is limited to direct cortical surface extension and cannot use white matter tracts.
Tumour can spread through white matter tracts.
The source excludes CSF and leptomeningeal pathways as routes of tumour spread.
Tumour can spread along ependymal and subependymal routes.
The source illustrates subependymal extension and transcallosal spread on post-contrast T1-weighted MRI.
options_after: Tumour spread is limited to direct cortical surface extension and will not use white matter tracts.
Tumour can spread through white matter tracts.
The source excludes CSF and leptomeningeal pathways as routes of tumour spread.
Tumour can spread along ependymal and subependymal routes.
The source illustrates subependymal extension and transcallosal spread on post-contrast T1-weighted MRI.
updates.explanation: The source states that tumour can spread through white matter tracts, through CSF, and along leptomeningeal, ependymal and subependymal routes. The illustrated post-contrast T1-weighted MRI shows extensive enhancement extending via the subependymal surface and crossing the midline through the corpus callosum. The claims excluding white matter, CSF and leptomeningeal spread are incompatible with the described routes.

updates.question_text: Regarding typical age and presentation patterns for IDH-mutant astrocytoma and oligodendroglioma, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: 1p/19q non-co-deleted astrocytomas usually present between 30 and 40 years with seizures.
1p/19q non-co-deleted astrocytomas usually present younger, typically between 20 and 30 years.
1p/19q co-deleted oligodendrogliomas usually present between 20 and 30 years without seizures.
1p/19q co-deleted oligodendrogliomas usually present only in elderly adults with haemorrhage.
IDH-mutant diffuse gliomas occur mostly in young to middle-aged adults.
options_after: 1p/19q non-co-deleted astrocytomas usually present between 30 and 40 years with seizures.
1p/19q non-co-deleted astrocytomas usually present younger, typically between 20 and 30 years.
1p/19q co-deleted oligodendrogliomas usually present between 20 and 30 years without seizures.
1p/19q co-deleted oligodendrogliomas usually present primarily in elderly adults with haemorrhage.
IDH-mutant diffuse gliomas occur mostly in young to middle-aged adults.
updates.explanation: The source states that IDH-mutant diffuse gliomas occur mostly in young to middle-aged adults. Non-co-deleted astrocytomas usually present younger, typically between 20 and 30 years. Co-deleted oligodendrogliomas usually present between 30 and 40 years with seizures, not between 20 and 30 years without seizures.

updates.question_text: Regarding pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It is a WHO grade 4 embryonal tumour of the posterior fossa.
It usually presents in children or young adults.
It is most commonly located in the temporal lobe and involves cortex and leptomeninges.
The main cortical solid-and-cystic differential in this age group is medulloblastoma.
It is usually non-enhancing and never associated with cyst formation.
options_after: It is a WHO grade 4 embryonal tumour of the posterior fossa.
It usually presents in children or young adults.
It is most commonly located in the temporal lobe and involves cortex and leptomeninges.
The main cortical solid-and-cystic differential in this age group is medulloblastoma.
Associated cyst formation argues against this diagnosis.
updates.explanation: PXA is a WHO grade 2 astrocytic tumour, with an anaplastic grade 3 variant, and usually presents in children or young adults. It is most commonly temporal and involves cortex and leptomeninges. On MRI it is often avidly enhancing, associated with cyst formation and a thickened or enhancing pial tail. The main cortical solid-and-cystic differential in this age group is ganglioglioma, not medulloblastoma.

updates.question_text: Regarding posterior fossa ependymoma imaging, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It appears as an enhancing mass with heterogeneity from cystic or necrotic change, calcification or haemorrhage.
It has been called the toothpaste or plastic tumour because it remains confined to the fourth ventricle and never squeezes through foramina.
Unlike ependymoma, medulloblastoma can fill the fourth ventricle but does not typically squeeze through the foramina.
It never causes obstructive hydrocephalus because it is extra-ventricular.
Anaplastic ependymoma is a more aggressive grade 3 variant.
options_after: It appears as an enhancing mass with heterogeneity from cystic or necrotic change, calcification or haemorrhage.
Extension through the fourth ventricular foramina argues against ependymoma.
Unlike ependymoma, medulloblastoma can fill the fourth ventricle but does not typically squeeze through the foramina.
It will not cause obstructive hydrocephalus because it is extra-ventricular.
Anaplastic ependymoma is a more aggressive grade 3 variant.
updates.explanation: Ependymoma appears as an enhancing heterogeneous mass due to cystic or necrotic change, calcification or haemorrhage. The posterior fossa form is called toothpaste or plastic tumour because it fills the fourth ventricle and squeezes through foramina; confinement to the ventricle is therefore incorrect. Medulloblastoma can fill the fourth ventricle but does not typically squeeze through foramina. Anaplastic ependymoma is grade 3.

updates.question_text: Regarding medulloblastoma imaging and dissemination, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It is slightly hyperattenuating on CT because of densely packed cells.
It is typically hyperintense on T2-weighted images and has high ADC values.
Low ADC cannot help distinguish medulloblastoma from ependymoma or pilocytic astrocytoma.
Leptomeningeal metastatic disease is present in up to one-third of patients.
It is the most common cause of drop metastases to the spine in children.
options_after: It is slightly hyperattenuating on CT because of densely packed cells.
It is typically hyperintense on T2-weighted images and has high ADC values.
Low ADC will not help distinguish medulloblastoma from ependymoma or pilocytic astrocytoma.
Leptomeningeal metastatic disease is present in up to one-third of patients.
It is the most common cause of drop metastases to the spine in children.
updates.explanation: Medulloblastoma is slightly hyperattenuating on CT because of densely packed cells and therefore tends to be T2 hypointense with low ADC. Low ADC can be useful for differentiating medulloblastoma from ependymoma and pilocytic astrocytoma, so the claim that it cannot help is incorrect. Leptomeningeal metastatic disease is present in up to one-third of patients, and medulloblastoma is the most common cause of spinal drop metastases in children.

updates.question_text: Regarding atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumour, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It is a WHO grade 1 tumour with a corduroy appearance of thickened cerebellar folia.
It is more common than medulloblastoma and occurs in older children.
It is an uncommon WHO grade 4 embryonal tumour characterised molecularly by loss of SMARCB1/INI1 or SMARCA4/BRG1 expression.
It should be considered for a large brain tumour in children younger than three years.
Almost all cases are supratentorial and cerebellar involvement is rare.
options_after: It is a WHO grade 1 tumour with a corduroy appearance of thickened cerebellar folia.
It is more common than medulloblastoma and occurs in older children.
It is an uncommon WHO grade 4 embryonal tumour characterised molecularly by loss of SMARCB1/INI1 or SMARCA4/BRG1 expression.
It should be considered for a large brain tumour in children younger than three years.
More than 90% arise supratentorially, with cerebellar involvement being uncommon.
updates.explanation: AT/RT is an uncommon WHO grade 4 embryonal tumour characterised by loss of SMARCB1/INI1 or SMARCA4/BRG1 expression. It resembles medulloblastoma but is less common and occurs in slightly younger patients, so it should be considered in children younger than three years. The majority are cerebellar, while about one-third are supratentorial; cerebellar involvement is therefore not rare. Corduroy cerebellar folia describe Lhermitte-Duclos disease.

updates.question_text: Regarding intraventricular tumours at the start of this section, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Ependymoma, subependymoma and medulloblastoma are excluded from the intraventricular mass differential because they never protrude into ventricles.
Other sites of origin include the septum pellucidum and choroid plexus.
Developmental or degenerative cysts that do not enhance are excluded from the intraventricular mass differential.
Intraventricular tumours can cause obstructive hydrocephalus.
Central neurocytoma is illustrated as a lobulated lateral ventricular mass attached to the septum pellucidum with enhancement and cystic foci.
options_after: Ependymoma, subependymoma and medulloblastoma are excluded from the intraventricular mass differential because they will not protrude into ventricles.
Other sites of origin include the septum pellucidum and choroid plexus.
Developmental or degenerative cysts that do not enhance are excluded from the intraventricular mass differential.
Intraventricular tumours can cause obstructive hydrocephalus.
Central neurocytoma is illustrated as a lobulated lateral ventricular mass attached to the septum pellucidum with enhancement and cystic foci.
updates.explanation: The source states that posterior fossa intra-axial tumours such as ependymoma, subependymoma and medulloblastoma can protrude into ventricles and should be considered in intraventricular mass differential diagnosis. Other sites of origin include the septum pellucidum and choroid plexus. Non-neoplastic developmental or degenerative cysts that do not enhance remain in the differential, and intraventricular tumours can cause obstructive hydrocephalus. The illustrated central neurocytoma is a lobulated enhancing mass attached to the septum pellucidum with cystic foci.

updates.question_text: Regarding secondary CNS lymphoma, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It is defined as lymphoma isolated to the CNS with no systemic disease.
It is more commonly an isolated intraventricular mass with no extra-axial involvement.
It is always restricted to the lateral ventricles.
It less commonly presents as a parenchymal mass.
It represents CNS involvement in a patient with known systemic lymphoma.
options_after: It is defined as lymphoma isolated to the CNS without systemic disease.
It is more commonly an isolated intraventricular mass without extra-axial involvement.
It is characteristically restricted to the lateral ventricles.
It less commonly presents as a parenchymal mass.
It represents CNS involvement in a patient with known systemic lymphoma.
updates.explanation: Secondary CNS lymphoma means CNS involvement in a patient with known systemic lymphoma. It is more commonly extra-axial, involving leptomeninges, dura and/or skull, not usually an isolated intraventricular mass. It less commonly appears as a parenchymal mass. Lymphoma isolated to the CNS is primary CNS lymphoma, not secondary CNS lymphoma.

updates.question_text: Regarding conspicuity and haemorrhage in intra-axial metastases, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Larger metastases often have marked oedema.
Small metastases may be visible only as tiny enhancing foci on post-contrast images.
Higher contrast dose, delayed imaging and higher field strength can increase lesion conspicuity.
Melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, choriocarcinoma and thyroid cancer are common haemorrhagic metastases.
A haemorrhagic neoplasm is excluded if the initial haemorrhage resembles hypertension or amyloid angiopathy.
options_after: Larger metastases often have marked oedema.
Small metastases may be visible primarily as tiny enhancing foci on post-contrast images.
Higher contrast dose, delayed imaging and higher field strength can increase lesion conspicuity.
Melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, choriocarcinoma and thyroid cancer are common haemorrhagic metastases.
A haemorrhagic neoplasm is excluded if the initial haemorrhage resembles hypertension or amyloid angiopathy.
updates.explanation: Larger metastases often show marked oedema, while small metastases may present as tiny enhancing foci only on post-contrast images. Conspicuity increases with factors such as higher contrast dose, higher-relaxivity gadolinium agent, delayed post-contrast imaging and higher field strength. The common haemorrhagic metastases listed are melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, choriocarcinoma and thyroid cancer. Tumorous haemorrhage can initially mimic primary intracerebral haemorrhage but should be suspected with enhancement or failure to resolve.

updates.question_text: Regarding extra-axial metastatic disease, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Multiple dural masses are caused only by metastases and never meningiomatosis.
FLAIR should remain normal in leptomeningeal metastases because only the dura is involved.
Nonenhancing sulcal FLAIR hyperintensity can also be caused by subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Dural metastases usually appear as nonenhancing intra-axial cysts.
Leptomeningeal metastases can appear as serpentine enhancement at the pial surface.
options_after: Multiple dural masses favour metastases and exclude meningiomatosis.
Leptomeningeal metastases involve the dura without altering CSF signal on FLAIR.
Nonenhancing sulcal FLAIR hyperintensity can also be caused by subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Dural metastases usually appear as nonenhancing intra-axial cysts.
Leptomeningeal metastases can appear as serpentine enhancement at the pial surface.
updates.explanation: Leptomeningeal metastases, or carcinomatous meningitis, appear as serpentine pial surface enhancement and can cause sulcal FLAIR hyperintensity. Similar enhancement and FLAIR changes can also be seen with infectious or inflammatory meningitis, and nonenhancing sulcal FLAIR hyperintensity can occur with subarachnoid haemorrhage. Dural metastases are focal enhancing extra-axial masses, not nonenhancing intra-axial cysts. Multiple dural masses are caused by multiple meningiomatosis or metastases.

updates.question_text: Regarding meningioma imaging, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: On noncontrast CT, meningiomas are usually hyperattenuating relative to brain.
Approximately 25% calcify.
They avidly enhance, and a dural tail is thought to reflect vasoactive substances rather than tumour spread.
On angiography, the mother-in-law sign means early arterial enhancement and venous-phase contrast retention.
Severe oedema excludes meningioma because extra-axial tumours cannot produce white matter oedema.
options_after: On noncontrast CT, meningiomas are usually hyperattenuating relative to brain.
Approximately 25% calcify.
They avidly enhance, and a dural tail is thought to reflect vasoactive substances rather than tumour spread.
On angiography, the mother-in-law sign means early arterial enhancement and venous-phase contrast retention.
Severe oedema excludes meningioma because extra-axial tumours will not produce white matter oedema.
updates.explanation: Meningiomas are usually hyperattenuating on noncontrast CT, and approximately 25% calcify. They avidly enhance; the dural tail is attributed to vasoactive substances released by the tumour rather than direct tumour spread. On angiography, early arterial enhancement with venous retention is termed the mother-in-law sign. Despite the extra-axial location, marked white matter oedema can occur and may be disproportionate to tumour size.

updates.question_text: Regarding pineal teratoma and pineal parenchymal tumours, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Teratoma is the most common pineal region tumour and has a homogeneous imaging appearance.
Intralesional fat suggests teratoma.
Pineal parenchymal tumours are limited to pineoblastoma and have no lower-grade spectrum.
Pineoblastomas affect young children, while other pineal parenchymal tumours are mostly seen in adults.
Pineal parenchymal tumours engulf pineal calcification, whereas germ cell tumours explode it peripherally.
options_after: Teratoma is the most common pineal region tumour and has a homogeneous imaging appearance.
Intralesional fat suggests teratoma.
Pineal parenchymal tumours are limited to pineoblastoma and lack lower-grade spectrum.
Pineoblastomas affect young children, while other pineal parenchymal tumours are mostly seen in adults.
Pineal parenchymal tumours engulf pineal calcification, whereas germ cell tumours explode it peripherally.
updates.explanation: Teratoma is the second most common pineal region tumour and has a heterogeneous imaging appearance; intralesional fat suggests teratoma, and teratoma is prone to haemorrhage and coarse calcification. Pineal parenchymal tumours span pineocytoma, intermediate/papillary tumours and pineoblastoma, not pineoblastoma alone. Pineoblastomas affect young children while the others are mostly adult tumours. Germ cell tumours engulf pineal calcification, whereas pineal parenchymal tumours explode or peripherally displace existing calcification.

updates.question_text: Regarding pineal cysts and other pineal-region masses, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Pineal cysts are common on MRI and most are less than 1 cm and asymptomatic.
Small pineal cysts routinely require follow-up because most grow.
Pineal cysts may show thin smooth peripheral enhancement but should not show thick irregular or nodular enhancement.
Tentorial meningioma tends to depress the internal cerebral veins, unlike pineal gland origin tumours which lift them.
Quadrigeminal plate lipoma is T1 hypointense and is never associated with corpus callosum abnormality.
options_after: Pineal cysts are common on MRI and most are less than 1 cm and asymptomatic.
Small pineal cysts routinely require follow-up because most grow.
Pineal cysts may show thin smooth peripheral enhancement but should not show thick irregular or nodular enhancement.
Tentorial meningioma tends to depress the internal cerebral veins, unlike pineal gland origin tumours which lift them.
Quadrigeminal plate lipoma is T1 hypointense and is not associated with corpus callosum abnormality.
updates.explanation: Pineal cysts are common, usually less than 1 cm and asymptomatic, and very few grow; follow-up of small cysts is not routinely recommended. They may show thin smooth peripheral enhancement but not thick, irregular or nodular enhancement, so contrast is needed when the differential includes pineal parenchymal tumour. Tentorial meningioma tends to depress internal cerebral veins, while pineal gland origin tumours lift them. Quadrigeminal plate lipoma is T1 hyperintense and may be associated with corpus callosum agenesis or hypoplasia.

updates.question_text: Regarding multiple sclerosis clinical context and diagnostic framework, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: MS is idiopathic inflammatory destruction of CNS axons in the brain and spinal cord.
It is the most common chronic demyelinating disease.
It is more common in middle-aged Caucasian females from northern latitudes.
Relapsing-remitting MS is the most common clinical presentation.
McDonald criteria are based only on CSF findings and not MRI dissemination in space or time.
options_after: MS is idiopathic inflammatory destruction of CNS axons in the brain and spinal cord.
It is the most common chronic demyelinating disease.
It is more common in middle-aged Caucasian females from northern latitudes.
Relapsing-remitting MS is the most common clinical presentation.
McDonald criteria are based primarily on CSF findings and not MRI dissemination in space or time.
updates.explanation: MS is described as idiopathic inflammatory destruction of CNS axons in the brain and spinal cord, likely autoimmune, and the most common chronic demyelinating disease. It is more common in middle-aged Caucasian females from northern latitudes. Relapsing-remitting disease is the most common presentation, while progressive forms have incomplete or absent resolution. Diagnosis is based on focal neurological disease disseminated in space and time using clinical symptoms and MRI findings within the McDonald framework.

updates.question_text: Regarding NMO spectrum disease and ADEM, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: NMOSD is identical to MS and characteristically spares optic nerves and spinal cord.
NMO-IgG is an aquaporin-4 antibody that is highly specific for NMOSD.
NMOSD confers a better prognosis than MS according to the source.
ADEM is a monophasic demyelinating disorder seen primarily in children, often after viral infection or vaccination.
ADEM is confined to the pineal region and cannot resemble MS on imaging.
options_after: NMOSD is closely comparable to MS and characteristically spares optic nerves and spinal cord.
NMO-IgG is an aquaporin-4 antibody that is highly specific for NMOSD.
NMOSD confers a better prognosis than MS according to the source.
ADEM is a monophasic demyelinating disorder seen primarily in children, often after viral infection or vaccination.
ADEM is confined to the pineal region and will not resemble MS on imaging.
updates.explanation: NMOSD is distinct from MS and involves optic nerves and spinal cord; it has a worse prognosis than MS. NMO-IgG is an aquaporin-4 antibody and is highly specific for NMOSD. ADEM is a monophasic demyelinating disorder seen mainly in children after viral infection or vaccination, and imaging can be identical to MS with involvement of brain, brainstem or spinal cord. It is not confined to the pineal region.

updates.question_text: Regarding whole brain radiation injury, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The acute phase may occur during or immediately after radiotherapy
The early delayed phase occurs years after treatment and is usually due to vascular coagulative necrosis
The acute phase is thought to reflect oedema due to endothelial injury
The early delayed phase may occur from several weeks up to 6 months and is thought to reflect demyelination
Late delayed effects are always self-limited and usually resolve without treatment
options_after: The acute phase may occur during or immediately after radiotherapy
The early delayed phase occurs years after treatment and is usually due to vascular coagulative necrosis
The acute phase is thought to reflect oedema due to endothelial injury
The early delayed phase may occur from several weeks up to 6 months and is thought to reflect demyelination
Late delayed effects are characteristically self-limited and usually resolve without treatment
updates.explanation: The source separates radiation injury into acute, early delayed and late delayed patterns. The acute phase occurs during or immediately after treatment and is thought to reflect endothelial injury with oedema. The early delayed phase occurs from several weeks up to 6 months and is attributed to demyelination. Late delayed effects are typically irreversible and include vascular changes, radionecrosis and white matter injury.

updates.question_text: Regarding late radiation effects, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Radiation necrosis always occurs within the first week of radiotherapy
Mineralising microangiopathy presents as unilateral striatal T1 hyperintensity with CT hyperdensity
Late delayed radiation injury is most commonly seen with stereotactic radiosurgery
Radiation vasculitis cannot affect large vessels
Distal internal carotid artery involvement may produce a moyamoya phenomenon
options_after: Radiation necrosis characteristically occurs within the first week of radiotherapy
Mineralising microangiopathy presents as unilateral striatal T1 hyperintensity with CT hyperdensity
Late delayed radiation injury is most commonly seen with stereotactic radiosurgery
Radiation vasculitis will not affect large vessels
Distal internal carotid artery involvement may produce a moyamoya phenomenon
updates.explanation: Late delayed radiation injury is described as most commonly associated with stereotactic radiosurgery and may begin as early as 6 months, most often between 9 and 15 months. Radiation vasculitis can involve large vessels, and distal internal carotid artery involvement may produce a moyamoya phenomenon. Unilateral striatal T1 hyperintensity with CT hyperdensity belongs to diabetic striatopathy, not mineralising microangiopathy. Radiation necrosis is not an immediate first-week complication in the source.

updates.question_text: Regarding imaging methods for pseudoprogression versus early progressive disease, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: FDG-PET is the source's preferred definitive discriminator
Diffusion and perfusion MRI reliably separate all cases
Higher relative cerebral blood volume favours radiation necrosis rather than progression
No imaging technique is currently described as reliably differentiating pseudoprogression from early progressive disease
Lower mean ADC values and ADC ratios are associated with pseudoprogression
options_after: FDG-PET is the source's preferred definitive discriminator
Diffusion and perfusion MRI reliably separate more than 90% of cases
Higher relative cerebral blood volume favours radiation necrosis rather than progression
No imaging technique is currently described as reliably differentiating pseudoprogression from early progressive disease
Lower mean ADC values and ADC ratios are associated with pseudoprogression
updates.explanation: The source states that no imaging technique can currently reliably differentiate pseudoprogression from early progressive disease. Investigated techniques include diffusion MRI, perfusion MRI and PET tracers, but all have limitations. Lower mean ADC values and higher relative cerebral blood volume are associated with progressive disease rather than pseudoprogression. FDG-PET is widely available but is described as having unacceptably low sensitivity and specificity.

updates.question_text: Regarding autoimmune encephalitis classification, which of the following statements is correct?
options_before: Group I antibodies target cell-surface antigens and are usually non-paraneoplastic
Group II antibodies target intracellular antigens and are usually associated with worse outcomes
The disorder is classified only by whether MRI is normal or abnormal at presentation
Group I antibodies target intracellular antigens and are more closely associated with paraneoplastic syndromes
NMDAr encephalitis is defined as a group I paraneoplastic syndrome of elderly men
options_after: Group I antibodies target cell-surface antigens and are usually non-paraneoplastic
Group II antibodies target intracellular antigens and are usually associated with worse outcomes
The disorder is classified primarily by whether MRI is normal or abnormal at presentation
Group I antibodies target intracellular antigens and are more closely associated with paraneoplastic syndromes
NMDAr encephalitis is defined as a group I paraneoplastic syndrome of elderly men
updates.explanation: The source classifies autoimmune encephalitis by paraneoplastic versus non-paraneoplastic context and by antibody target location. Group I antibodies target intracellular antigens, are more closely associated with paraneoplastic syndromes and have worse clinical outcomes. Group II antibodies target cell-surface antigens, are more often non-paraneoplastic and have better outcomes. NMDAr encephalitis is described as the most common group II form, classically seen in young women and children.

updates.question_text: Regarding differentiating abscess from necrotic tumour or metastasis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Abscess typically has a thick irregular T2-hyperintense rim
Necrotic tumour is distinguished from abscess because it always has no enhancement
A thin, smooth, T2-hypointense rim supports abscess rather than glioma or metastasis
Restricted diffusion of the lesion contents strongly supports abscess in the source's description
Abscess contents are expected to be bright on ADC due to free diffusion
options_after: Abscess typically has a thick irregular T2-hyperintense rim
Necrotic tumour is distinguished from abscess because it characteristically lacks enhancement
A thin, smooth, T2-hypointense rim supports abscess rather than glioma or metastasis
Restricted diffusion of the lesion contents strongly supports abscess in the source's description
Abscess contents are expected to be bright on ADC due to free diffusion
updates.explanation: The source contrasts the abscess rim with that of glioma or metastasis: an abscess rim is thin and smooth and hypointense on T2-weighted images. A brain abscess almost always demonstrates restricted diffusion, with bright DWI signal and dark ADC. Necrotic tumours and metastases can enhance, so absence of enhancement is not a reliable separator. Free diffusion with bright ADC would conflict with the abscess pattern described.

updates.question_text: Regarding tuberculoma and pyogenic abscess, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: A tuberculoma is a localised tuberculosis granuloma
Tuberculoma can always be reliably distinguished from pyogenic abscess on MRI
Tuberculoma tends to show central T2 hypointensity, unlike a pyogenic abscess which is usually T2 hyperintense centrally
Tuberculomas do not restrict diffusion
A cystic tuberculoma may mimic a pyogenic abscess
options_after: A tuberculoma is a localised tuberculosis granuloma
Tuberculoma can characteristically be reliably distinguished from pyogenic abscess on MRI
Tuberculoma tends to show central T2 hypointensity, unlike a pyogenic abscess which is usually T2 hyperintense centrally
Tuberculomas do not restrict diffusion
A cystic tuberculoma may mimic a pyogenic abscess
updates.explanation: The source defines tuberculoma as a localised tuberculosis granuloma and notes that it is not always possible to distinguish it from pyogenic abscess. Central T2 hypointensity favours tuberculoma, whereas pyogenic abscess is typically centrally T2 hyperintense. Cystic tuberculomas may mimic pyogenic abscess. Restricted diffusion can be seen in tuberculomas, so diffusion restriction alone is not a reliable separator.

updates.question_text: Regarding intracranial fungal infection, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Radiological manifestations are always specific for the organism
Fungal infection may present as abscess, granuloma, cerebritis, meningitis, vasculitis or mycotic aneurysm
A crenated or lobulated abscess border may help distinguish fungal from bacterial abscess
Non-enhancing intracavitary projections with restricted diffusion may represent fungal hyphae
Skull base involvement with basilar meningitis can cause multiple cranial nerve palsies
options_after: Radiological manifestations are characteristically specific for the organism
Fungal infection may present as abscess, granuloma, cerebritis, meningitis, vasculitis or mycotic aneurysm
A crenated or lobulated abscess border may help distinguish fungal from bacterial abscess
Non-enhancing intracavitary projections with restricted diffusion may represent fungal hyphae
Skull base involvement with basilar meningitis can cause multiple cranial nerve palsies
updates.explanation: The source emphasises that CNS fungal infection is often non-specific radiologically and can manifest as abscesses, granulomas, cerebritis, meningitis, vasculitis or mycotic aneurysms. Features favouring fungal abscess over bacterial abscess include crenated or lobulated borders and non-enhancing intracavitary projections that restrict diffusion, thought to represent hyphae. Skull base basilar meningitis is a common feature and can produce multiple cranial nerve palsies. The organism is not always identifiable from imaging alone.

updates.question_text: Regarding cryptococcosis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It is caused by Aspergillus and primarily produces frontal lobe infarcts from sinus invasion
It is the most common CNS fungal infection in patients with AIDS
It is caused by Candida species
AIDS patients become susceptible only when CD4 cells are less than 50 cells per microlitre
The most common clinical presentation is chronic basilar meningitis
options_after: It is caused by Aspergillus and primarily produces frontal lobe infarcts from sinus invasion
It is the most common CNS fungal infection in patients with AIDS
It is caused by Candida species
AIDS patients become susceptible primarily when CD4 cells are less than 50 cells per microlitre
The most common clinical presentation is chronic basilar meningitis
updates.explanation: Cryptococcosis is described as the most common CNS fungal infection in AIDS and is caused by Cryptococcus neoformans. AIDS patients become susceptible with CD4 counts below 100 cells per microlitre, not the lower CMV threshold. The most common clinical presentation is chronic basilar meningitis and the most common imaging finding is nonspecific hydrocephalus. Aspergillus is angioinvasive and can lead to infarction and mycotic aneurysm formation, while Candida is discussed separately as a cause of multiple brain microabscesses.

updates.question_text: Regarding Aspergillus CNS infection, which of the following statement is correct?
options_before: It is non-angioinvasive and therefore rarely causes infarction or haemorrhage
It primarily occurs in immunocompetent patients and has no relationship to lung or sinus disease
Its abscesses always show central unrestricted diffusion without peripheral abnormality
Aspergillus is angioinvasive and may cause vasculitis with thrombosis, infarction and mycotic aneurysm formation
Voriconazole is ineffective and is specifically avoided in all cases
options_after: It is non-angioinvasive and therefore rarely causes infarction or haemorrhage
It primarily occurs in immunocompetent patients and lacks relationship to lung or sinus disease
Its abscesses characteristically show central unrestricted diffusion without peripheral abnormality
Aspergillus is angioinvasive and may cause vasculitis with thrombosis, infarction and mycotic aneurysm formation
Voriconazole is ineffective and is specifically avoided in more than 90% of cases
updates.explanation: Aspergillus species are described as ubiquitous angioinvasive moulds that can disseminate in immunocompromised patients. Routes include haematogenous spread from lung, extension from paranasal sinuses, or direct trauma inoculation. Vascular invasion can lead to vasculitis, thrombosis, infarction and mycotic aneurysm formation, often with haemorrhage. Treatment includes voriconazole or amphotericin B.

updates.question_text: Regarding mucormycosis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It infects a similar patient population to aspergillosis
Intracranial extension from invasive sinusitis is the primary aetiology, particularly in poorly controlled diabetes mellitus
It is less aggressive than aspergillosis and responds well to voriconazole
Unlike aspergillosis, it has no propensity for angioinvasion, infarction or necrosis
Treatment includes aggressive surgical debridement, high-dose amphotericin B and supportive therapies
options_after: It infects a similar patient population to aspergillosis
Intracranial extension from invasive sinusitis is the primary aetiology, particularly in poorly controlled diabetes mellitus
It is less aggressive than aspergillosis and responds well to voriconazole
Unlike aspergillosis, it lacks propensity for angioinvasion, infarction or necrosis
Treatment includes aggressive surgical debridement, high-dose amphotericin B and supportive therapies
updates.explanation: Mucormycosis affects a similar population to aspergillosis but is more aggressive, has higher mortality and responds poorly to voriconazole. The primary aetiology is intracranial extension from invasive sinusitis, particularly in poorly controlled diabetes mellitus. Like aspergillosis, it can be angioinvasive with infarction, necrosis and haemorrhage, so absence of angioinvasion is incorrect. Treatment requires aggressive surgical debridement, high-dose amphotericin B and supportive care.

updates.question_text: Regarding other CNS fungal infections, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: CNS candidiasis most commonly presents as chronic basilar meningitis with hydrocephalus
CNS candidiasis most commonly presents as multiple brain microabscesses
Blastomycosis is restricted to the ventricles and never causes abscesses
Histoplasmosis always produces basal ganglia calcification
Disseminated coccidioidomycosis may cause meningitis or chronic basilar meningitis complicated by hydrocephalus or ischaemic vasculitis
options_after: CNS candidiasis most commonly presents as chronic basilar meningitis with hydrocephalus
CNS candidiasis most commonly presents as multiple brain microabscesses
Blastomycosis is restricted to the ventricles and will not cause abscesses
Histoplasmosis characteristically produces basal ganglia calcification
Disseminated coccidioidomycosis may cause meningitis or chronic basilar meningitis complicated by hydrocephalus or ischaemic vasculitis
updates.explanation: The source states that CNS candidiasis most commonly presents as multiple brain microabscesses, with meningitis or vascular involvement being less common. Disseminated coccidioidomycosis often causes meningitis or chronic basilar meningitis similar to cryptococcosis, which may be complicated by hydrocephalus or ischaemic vasculitis. Histoplasmosis tends to cause isolated meningitis but may also produce granuloma or abscess. Blastomycosis can cause meningitis, cerebral abscesses preferentially involving basal ganglia or cerebellum, or vertebral osteomyelitis.

updates.question_text: Regarding stages of neurocysticercosis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The colloidal stage is specific because it always demonstrates a visible scolex
The colloidal stage may appear as ring-enhancing lesions
In contrast to pyogenic abscess, colloidal lesions have increased diffusivity
The calcified stage shows only leptomeningeal enhancement and no CT abnormality
The nodular/granular stage shows decreasing oedema as the cyst involutes and the wall thickens
options_after: The colloidal stage is specific because it characteristically demonstrates a visible scolex
The colloidal stage may appear as ring-enhancing lesions
In contrast to pyogenic abscess, colloidal lesions have increased diffusivity
The calcified stage shows primarily leptomeningeal enhancement without CT abnormality
The nodular/granular stage shows decreasing oedema as the cyst involutes and the wall thickens
updates.explanation: The colloidal stage is described as the least specific, presenting as ring-enhancing lesions, but with increased diffusivity compared with pyogenic abscess. In the nodular/granular stage, oedema decreases as the cyst involutes and the cyst wall thickens. The calcified stage shows small parenchymal calcifications on CT and susceptibility foci on GRE. A visible scolex is associated with many viable/vesicular cysts, not a required colloidal-stage feature.

updates.question_text: Regarding intraventricular and racemose neurocysticercosis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Intraventricular neurocysticercosis can occur in up to 20% of cases
It typically occurs in the aqueduct of Sylvius or fourth ventricle
Hydrocephalus may be the initial presentation
The obstructing cyst may be most apparent on FLAIR because protein-rich intracystic fluid is not nulled
The racemose form is defined by numerous visible scolices in every cyst
options_after: Intraventricular neurocysticercosis can occur in up to 20% of cases
It typically occurs in the aqueduct of Sylvius or fourth ventricle
Hydrocephalus may be the initial presentation
The obstructing cyst may be most apparent on FLAIR because protein-rich intracystic fluid is not nulled
The racemose form is defined by numerous cysts, each containing a visible scolex.
updates.explanation: The source states that intraventricular neurocysticercosis can occur in up to 20% of cases, typically in the aqueduct of Sylvius or fourth ventricle. Hydrocephalus may be the initial presentation, and the obstructing cyst may be most apparent on FLAIR because protein-rich fluid is not nulled. The racemose form is an older term for a variant without a visible scolex, now thought to represent degeneration of the scolex.

updates.question_text: Regarding spinal ependymoma, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It is the most common intramedullary tumour in children
It is the most common intramedullary tumour in adults
It is associated with neurofibromatosis type 2
Haemorrhage is common and may produce a haemosiderin cap sign
It typically has infiltrative ill-defined margins with only wispy enhancement
options_after: It is the most common intramedullary tumour in children
It is the most common intramedullary tumour in adults
It is associated with neurofibromatosis type 2
Haemorrhage is common and may produce a haemosiderin cap sign
It typically has infiltrative ill-defined margins with wispy enhancement.
updates.explanation: Ependymomas are described as the most common intramedullary tumour in adults and the second most common in children. They are associated with neurofibromatosis type 2, along with schwannomas and meningiomas. Typical imaging includes well-defined margins, intense heterogeneous enhancement, cystic components in up to half of cases, and haemorrhage causing a haemosiderin cap sign. Infiltrative margins and patchy enhancement better fit astrocytoma.

updates.question_text: Regarding sagittal cord involvement in non-neoplastic intramedullary disease, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Long-segment involvement can be seen with NMOSD, transverse myelitis, cord infarction, vascular malformation, chronic infection and sarcoidosis
Multiple sclerosis is never short segment in the spinal cord
Short-segment involvement is typical for multiple sclerosis
Anti-MOG associated myelitis is not included among long-segment causes
Sarcoidosis is restricted to short-segment cord lesions
options_after: Long-segment involvement can be seen with NMOSD, transverse myelitis, cord infarction, vascular malformation, chronic infection and sarcoidosis
Multiple sclerosis is not short segment in the spinal cord
Short-segment involvement is typical for multiple sclerosis
Anti-MOG associated myelitis is not included among long-segment causes
Sarcoidosis is restricted to short-segment cord lesions
updates.explanation: The source table lists transverse myelitis, NMOSD, cord infarction, vascular malformation, chronic infection, sarcoidosis and anti-MOG associated myelitis among long-segment non-neoplastic cord processes. Multiple sclerosis is listed as an uncommon long-segment cause but as a typical short-segment cause. Sarcoidosis appears in both long- and short-segment categories. Segment length therefore helps narrow the differential but does not work as an absolute rule.

updates.question_text: Regarding ADEM, NMOSD and anti-MOG antibody-associated disease, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: ADEM usually has an acute monophasic course after viral infection or vaccination and usually occurs in children
NMOSD is associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies
Anti-MOG antibody-associated disease requires aquaporin-4 seropositivity
Anti-MOG disease overlaps clinically with NMOSD and can present with optic neuritis or myelitis
ADEM spinal cord involvement always lacks enhancement and cord swelling
options_after: ADEM usually has an acute monophasic course after viral infection or vaccination and usually occurs in children
NMOSD is associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies
Anti-MOG antibody-associated disease requires aquaporin-4 seropositivity
Anti-MOG disease overlaps clinically with NMOSD and can present with optic neuritis or myelitis
ADEM spinal cord involvement characteristically lacks enhancement and cord swelling
updates.explanation: ADEM is described as an uncommon acute monophasic demyelinating disorder, typically following viral infection or vaccination and usually occurring in children. NMOSD is associated with antibodies against aquaporin-4. Anti-MOG antibody-associated disease overlaps clinically with NMOSD but patients are seronegative for aquaporin-4 antibodies. ADEM spinal involvement may show multifocal or large confluent T2-hyperintense intramedullary lesions with cord swelling and variable enhancement.

updates.question_text: Regarding clinical and imaging features of spinal cord infarction, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Clinical features may include bowel and bladder dysfunction, impaired perineal sensation and motor/sensory impairment of the legs
Risk factors include aortic surgery, aortic aneurysm, arteritis, sickle cell anaemia, vascular malformation and disc herniation
MRI usually shows no T2 abnormality because infarction is only visible on CT
The affected cord may be enlarged and typically restricts diffusion
Concomitant vertebral body infarction is more common in sickle cell disease and chronic steroid use
options_after: Clinical features may include bowel and bladder dysfunction, impaired perineal sensation and motor/sensory impairment of the legs
Risk factors include aortic surgery, aortic aneurysm, arteritis, sickle cell anaemia, vascular malformation and disc herniation
MRI usually fails to show T2 abnormality because infarction is primarily visible on CT
The affected cord may be enlarged and typically restricts diffusion
Concomitant vertebral body infarction is more common in sickle cell disease and chronic steroid use
updates.explanation: Spinal cord infarction may present with loss of bowel and bladder control, loss of perineal sensation and impairment of motor and sensory function in the legs. The source lists aortic surgery, aortic aneurysm, arteritis, sickle cell anaemia, vascular malformation and disc herniation as risk factors. Imaging shows T2 hyperintensity of affected cord regions, possible cord enlargement and typical diffusion restriction. Vertebral body infarction may coexist, especially in sickle cell disease and chronic steroid use.

updates.question_text: Regarding imaging and diagnosis of spinal dural AVF, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: MRI often shows long-segment cord oedema with surrounding intradural extramedullary flow voids
CTA and MRA always exclude the diagnosis when negative
CT myelography confirms dural AVF only by demonstrating vertebral body collapse
Diagnosis may require catheter angiography despite occult CTA or MRA
The typical patient is a young child with a monophasic post-viral illness
options_after: MRI often shows long-segment cord oedema with surrounding intradural extramedullary flow voids
CTA and MRA characteristically exclude the diagnosis when negative
CT myelography confirms dural AVF primarily by demonstrating vertebral body collapse
Diagnosis may require catheter angiography despite occult CTA or MRA
The typical patient is a young child with a monophasic post-viral illness
updates.explanation: MRI of dural AVF often shows long-segment cord oedema with or without mild expansion and surrounding intradural extramedullary vascular flow voids from dilated perimedullary veins. CTA and MRA can miss the lesion, so catheter angiography may be needed when the clinical and imaging pattern is suspicious. CT myelography may show serpentine intradural filling defects, not vertebral body collapse. The typical presentation is in older males with progressive congestive myelopathy, not a paediatric monophasic demyelinating syndrome.

updates.question_text: Regarding spinal cavernous malformation, which of the following statement is correct?
options_before: It is the most common spinal vascular malformation
It is a high-flow lesion with a radiculomeningeal feeder and no nidus
It is typically small, often involving only one vertebral level, and most often occurs in the thoracic cord
It characteristically produces serpentine intradural filling defects on CT myelography
It is defined by longitudinally extensive bright spotty lesions more hyperintense than CSF
options_after: It is the most common spinal vascular malformation
It is a high-flow lesion with a radiculomeningeal feeder without nidus
It is typically small, often involving only one vertebral level, and most often occurs in the thoracic cord
It characteristically produces serpentine intradural filling defects on CT myelography
It is defined by longitudinally extensive bright spotty lesions more hyperintense than CSF
updates.explanation: Spinal cavernous malformations are rare low-flow vascular malformations with imaging findings identical to intracranial cavernous malformations. The source states that they are typically small, often involving only one vertebral level, and are most commonly thoracic followed by cervical. Dural AVF is the most common spinal vascular malformation and is the high-flow lesion with radiculomeningeal feeding artery and no nidus. Bright spotty longitudinal myelitis is an NMOSD pattern.

updates.question_text: Regarding subacute combined degeneration, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It involves the dorsal and lateral columns and is caused by vitamin B12 deficiency
Causes include malabsorption, inadequate intake and interfering drugs such as nitrous oxide, proton pump inhibitors and metformin
MRI shows longitudinal symmetric T2 hyperintensity primarily in the dorsal columns with an inverted V configuration on axial images
It primarily affects the ventral horns after aortic surgery
It is irreversible in all cases and never regresses with treatment
options_after: It involves the dorsal and lateral columns and is caused by vitamin B12 deficiency
Causes include malabsorption, inadequate intake and interfering drugs such as nitrous oxide, proton pump inhibitors and metformin
MRI shows longitudinal symmetric T2 hyperintensity primarily in the dorsal columns with an inverted V configuration on axial images
It primarily affects the ventral horns after aortic surgery
It is irreversible in more than 90% of cases and will not regress with treatment
updates.explanation: Subacute combined degeneration is a vitamin B12 deficiency myelopathy involving the dorsal and lateral columns. The source lists malabsorption, inadequate intake and interfering drugs such as nitrous oxide, proton pump inhibitors and metformin among causes. MRI shows longitudinal symmetric dorsal column T2 hyperintensity with an inverted V configuration in the axial plane, involving cervical and/or thoracic cord. Findings can regress with treatment, although chronic disease can lead to permanent axonal loss and gliosis.

updates.question_text: Regarding compressive and traumatic spinal cord injury, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Compressive myelopathy most commonly results from degenerative cervical spondylosis
MRI in compressive myelopathy shows no signal abnormality within the compressed cord segment
Cord concussion is defined by a large T2-hypointense haematoma
Cord haematoma greater than 4 mm has the best prognosis among traumatic cord injury patterns
MRI can help evaluate severity and prognosis after traumatic cord injury
options_after: Compressive myelopathy most commonly results from degenerative cervical spondylosis
MRI in compressive myelopathy fails to show signal abnormality within the compressed cord segment
Cord concussion is defined by a large T2-hypointense haematoma
Cord haematoma greater than 4 mm has the best prognosis among traumatic cord injury patterns
MRI can help evaluate severity and prognosis after traumatic cord injury
updates.explanation: Compressive myelopathy is described as neurological deficit from cord compression, most commonly due to degenerative cervical spondylosis, with T2 prolongation in the compressed segment. MRI is useful in traumatic cord injury for severity assessment and functional prognosis. Concussion can have a normal MRI appearance, while cord haematoma is a larger focus of T2 hypointensity surrounded by hyperintensity and carries the poorest prognosis. The claim that compressive myelopathy has no cord signal abnormality conflicts with the source.

updates.question_text: Regarding classic incomplete spinal cord syndromes, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Central cord syndrome usually results from penetrating trauma affecting half the cord
Central cord syndrome is the most common incomplete cord syndrome and often follows hyperextension in a stenotic cervical canal
Brown-Sequard syndrome is due to hemicord injury and usually results from penetrating trauma
Ventral/anterior cord syndrome involves the anterior two-thirds of the cord with dorsal column sparing
Conus medullaris and cauda equina syndromes are always caused by Chiari I malformation
options_after: Central cord syndrome usually results from penetrating trauma affecting half the cord
Central cord syndrome is the most common incomplete cord syndrome and often follows hyperextension in a stenotic cervical canal
Brown-Sequard syndrome is due to hemicord injury and usually results from penetrating trauma
Ventral/anterior cord syndrome involves the anterior two-thirds of the cord with dorsal column sparing
Conus medullaris and cauda equina syndromes are characteristically caused by Chiari I malformation
updates.explanation: Central cord syndrome is the most common incomplete cord syndrome and usually follows hyperextension trauma in patients with degenerative cervical canal stenosis. Brown-Sequard syndrome is a hemicord injury, usually from penetrating trauma. Ventral or anterior cord syndrome involves the anterior two-thirds of the cord while sparing dorsal columns, and may be due to anterior spinal artery infarction or trauma. Conus and cauda equina syndromes have multiple causes, including trauma, disc herniation, tumour and epidural abscess.

updates.question_text: Regarding intradural extramedullary lesions, which of the following statement is correct?
options_before: They are outside the dura and cannot displace the spinal cord
They are within the dura but outside the cord and may show CSF above and below the lesion or as a cleft between lesion and cord
They are defined by originating inside the spinal cord parenchyma
They are always vertebral body lesions
They exclude lesions of the conus medullaris and cauda equina
options_after: They are outside the dura and will not displace the spinal cord
They are within the dura but outside the cord and may show CSF above and below the lesion or as a cleft between lesion and cord
They are defined by originating inside the spinal cord parenchyma
They are characteristically vertebral body lesions
They exclude lesions of the conus medullaris and cauda equina
updates.explanation: Intradural extramedullary lesions are located within the dura but outside the cord, usually involving nerve roots or meninges and projecting into the subarachnoid space. They may deviate or compress the cord, with CSF visible above and below the lesion and sometimes as a cleft between the lesion and the cord. The source also notes a subset of conus medullaris, cauda equina and filum terminale lesions with a distinct differential. Vertebral body lesions are extradural.

updates.question_text: Regarding distinguishing tumour from inflammatory demyelinating spinal cord disease, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Cord expansion favours neoplasm over many non-neoplastic signal abnormalities
Absence of cord expansion, multifocal brain/spine disease and CSF oligoclonal bands help distinguish MS from neoplasm
Active MS can enhance and mimic a spinal tumour
All enhancing intramedullary lesions should be reported as neoplasm
Typical MS lesions occupy a majority of the cord cross-section
options_after: Cord expansion favours neoplasm over many non-neoplastic signal abnormalities
Absence of cord expansion, multifocal brain/spine disease and CSF oligoclonal bands help distinguish MS from neoplasm
Active MS can enhance and mimic a spinal tumour
Most enhancing intramedullary lesions should be reported as neoplasm
Typical MS lesions occupy a majority of the cord cross-section
updates.explanation: Neoplasms frequently expand the spinal cord, whereas many non-neoplastic aetiologies more often cause nonexpansile signal change. The source states that active MS may enhance and mimic a spinal tumour, but MS is often distinguished by absence of cord expansion, multifocal brain and spine involvement and CSF oligoclonal bands. Reporting every enhancing intramedullary lesion as neoplasm would ignore that demyelination may enhance. Typical MS lesions occupy a minority, not a majority, of the cord cross-section.

updates.question_text: Regarding transverse extent and axial localisation of spinal cord lesions, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: NMOSD lesions are not transversally extensive and occupy only a minority of the cord cross-section
Typical spinal MS lesions occupy the majority of the cord cross-section
Subacute combined degeneration primarily involves the dorsal columns and has an inverted V pattern on axial images
Anterior spinal artery infarction maps to ventral cord involvement
Ventral/anterior cord syndrome primarily damages the dorsal columns while sparing the anterior two-thirds of the cord
options_after: NMOSD lesions are not transversally extensive and occupy primarily a minority of the cord cross-section
Typical spinal MS lesions occupy the majority of the cord cross-section
Subacute combined degeneration primarily involves the dorsal columns and has an inverted V pattern on axial images
Anterior spinal artery infarction maps to ventral cord involvement
Ventral/anterior cord syndrome primarily damages the dorsal columns while sparing the anterior two-thirds of the cord
updates.explanation: The source describes subacute combined degeneration as longitudinal symmetric dorsal column T2 hyperintensity with an inverted V configuration on axial images. Anterior spinal artery infarction is mapped to ventral cord involvement. NMOSD is transversally extensive and involves a majority of the cord cross-section, while ventral/anterior cord syndrome involves the anterior two-thirds of the cord and spares the dorsal columns. Typical MS involves a minority of the cord cross-section.

updates.question_text: Regarding genetic associations and operative implications of spinal schwannoma and neurofibroma, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Multiple schwannomas in younger patients are typical of neurofibromatosis type 1 only
Multiple neurofibromas in younger patients are seen with neurofibromatosis type 1
Neurofibromas are encapsulated and separable from the parent nerve
Schwannomas are encapsulated and separable from the parent nerve, allowing nerve-sparing resection
Schwannomatosis is unrelated to multiple schwannomas
options_after: Multiple schwannomas in younger patients are typical of neurofibromatosis type 1 in typical cases
Multiple neurofibromas in younger patients are seen with neurofibromatosis type 1
Neurofibromas are encapsulated and separable from the parent nerve
Schwannomas are encapsulated and separable from the parent nerve, allowing nerve-sparing resection
Schwannomatosis is unrelated to multiple schwannomas
updates.explanation: The source links multiple neurofibromas in younger patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 and multiple schwannomas with neurofibromatosis type 2 or schwannomatosis. Schwannomas are encapsulated and separable from the parent nerve, so nerve-sparing resection is possible. Neurofibromas are unencapsulated and infiltrate between nerve fascicles, so complete resection requires nerve sacrifice. Schwannomatosis is specifically mentioned as a genetic disorder with multiple schwannomas.

updates.question_text: Regarding myxopapillary ependymoma, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It is usually an intramedullary WHO grade IV tumour of the cervical cord
It is the most common tumour of the cauda equina region
It arises from ependymal glia within the conus medullaris and filum terminale
It is a benign WHO grade I variant of ependymoma
It never haemorrhages
options_after: It is usually an intramedullary WHO grade IV tumour of the cervical cord
It is the most common tumour of the cauda equina region
It arises from ependymal glia within the conus medullaris and filum terminale
It is a benign WHO grade I variant of ependymoma
It will not haemorrhage
updates.explanation: Myxopapillary ependymoma is described as the most common tumour of the cauda equina region. It arises from ependymal glia within the conus medullaris and filum terminale and is a benign WHO grade I ependymoma variant. It grows slowly and often presents when larger and sausage-shaped, with vertebral scalloping and canal enlargement. Haemorrhage is frequent and may produce peripheral haemosiderin deposits.

updates.question_text: Regarding open and closed spinal dysraphism, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The spectrum of closed dysraphism includes split cord malformations and caudal regression syndrome
Open spinal dysraphism is always clinically insignificant
The most common open spinal dysraphism is myelomeningocele
Closed dysraphism may include dorsal dermal sinus, neurenteric cyst and spinal lipoma variants
Myelocystocele is herniation of a syrinx outside the spinal canal
options_after: The spectrum of closed dysraphism includes split cord malformations and caudal regression syndrome
Open spinal dysraphism is characteristically clinically insignificant
The most common open spinal dysraphism is myelomeningocele
Closed dysraphism may include dorsal dermal sinus, neurenteric cyst and spinal lipoma variants
Myelocystocele is herniation of a syrinx outside the spinal canal
updates.explanation: The source lists split cord malformations, caudal regression syndrome, persistent ventriculus terminalis, dorsal dermal sinus, neurenteric cyst, spinal lipoma variants, meningocele and myelocystocele among closed spinal dysraphisms. Myelomeningocele is the most common open spinal dysraphism. Myelocystocele is defined as herniation of a syrinx outside the spinal canal. Open dysraphism is not clinically insignificant; myelomeningocele requires early repair and is associated with neurological deficits.

updates.question_text: Regarding historical split cord terminology, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Diastematomyelia refers to sagittal bifurcation of the spinal cord into left and right hemicords
Diplomyelia is an accessory spinal cord without roots located dorsal or ventral to the main cord
Dimyelia is rare duplication of the cord with each cord having a complete set of roots
Dimyelia cords are separated into two dural sacs
Diplomyelia cords always contain two complete sets of roots
options_after: Diastematomyelia refers to sagittal bifurcation of the spinal cord into left and right hemicords
Diplomyelia is an accessory spinal cord without roots located dorsal or ventral to the main cord
Dimyelia is rare duplication of the cord with each cord having a complete set of roots
Dimyelia cords are separated into two dural sacs
Diplomyelia cords characteristically contain two complete sets of roots
updates.explanation: The source notes that historical terminology is inconsistently applied, then defines diastematomyelia as sagittal bifurcation into hemicords, each with a single set of dorsal and ventral horns and roots. Diplomelia is an accessory spinal cord without roots, dorsal or ventral to the main cord, within a single dural sac. Dimyelia is rare duplication with each cord having a complete set of roots, separated into two dural sacs. The claim that diplomyelia has two complete root sets contradicts the definition.

updates.question_text: Regarding spinal lipomas and fatty filum, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Spinal lipomas are acquired malignant fatty lesions of the ventral extradural canal
Spinal lipomas are congenital non-neoplastic fatty lesions along the dorsal midline spinal canal
Filar lipoma is linear or tubular fibrofatty thickening of the filum terminale
Fatty filum is visible only after gadolinium and not on noncontrast sequences
Filar lipoma may be associated with tethered cord syndrome
options_after: Spinal lipomas are acquired malignant fatty lesions of the ventral extradural canal
Spinal lipomas are congenital non-neoplastic fatty lesions along the dorsal midline spinal canal
Filar lipoma is linear or tubular fibrofatty thickening of the filum terminale
Fatty filum is visible primarily after gadolinium and not on noncontrast sequences
Filar lipoma may be associated with tethered cord syndrome
updates.explanation: Spinal lipomas are congenital, non-neoplastic fatty lesions along the dorsal midline spinal canal, usually intradural but sometimes with extradural components. Filar lipoma is linear or tubular fibrofatty thickening of the filum terminale and is T1 hyperintense. A fatty filum is visible on noncontrast sequences, which helps avoid mistaking an enhancing vessel for fat. It is often clinically insignificant but may be associated with tethered cord syndrome.

updates.question_text: Regarding dorsal dermal sinus and dermoid cyst, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Dorsal dermal sinuses are encapsulated nerve root tumours without any skin connection
They predominantly occur in the lumbosacral region
They are often associated with intradural dermoid or epidermoid cysts
Dermoid cysts contain only CSF and are characteristically T1 hypointense
Dermoid rupture may cause potentially fatal chemical meningitis
options_after: Dorsal dermal sinuses are encapsulated nerve root tumours without any skin connection
They predominantly occur in the lumbosacral region
They are often associated with intradural dermoid or epidermoid cysts
Dermoid cysts contain primarily CSF and are characteristically T1 hypointense
Dermoid rupture may cause potentially fatal chemical meningitis
updates.explanation: Dorsal dermal sinuses are epithelial-lined tracts from neural tissue to the dorsal skin, usually presenting as a midline dimple or ostium and predominantly occurring in the lumbosacral region. They are often associated with intradural dermoid, more commonly, or epidermoid cyst. Dermoid cysts contain macroscopic fat and are T1 hyperintense. Dermoid rupture may cause potentially fatal chemical meningitis.

updates.question_text: Regarding spinal epidermoid cysts, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Acquired epidermoids may result from implantation of skin elements during spinal puncture
They are always extradural vertebral body lesions
They most commonly appear identical to fat on all MR sequences
They usually restrict diffusion
They may be intradural extramedullary and rarely intramedullary
options_after: Acquired epidermoids may result from implantation of skin elements during spinal puncture
They are characteristically extradural vertebral body lesions
They most commonly appear closely comparable to fat on most MR sequences
They usually restrict diffusion
They may be intradural extramedullary and rarely intramedullary
updates.explanation: Spinal epidermoids are more often acquired than congenital, with acquired lesions caused by implantation of skin elements in the subarachnoid space during spinal puncture. They are usually intradural extramedullary but can rarely be intramedullary. On conventional sequences they often resemble a simple cyst, with low T1 and high T2 signal, although proteinaceous content may cause T1 shortening. As with epidermoids elsewhere, diffusivity is restricted.

updates.question_text: Regarding spinal arachnoid cyst, which of the following statement is correct?
options_before: It is a solid enhancing tumour arising from ependymal glia
It is defined by restricted diffusion and implantation of skin elements after puncture
It follows CSF on all MRI sequences and may be difficult to distinguish from surrounding CSF
It is always intramedullary
It is the classic cause of an enhancing cauda equina mass with vascular flow voids
options_after: It is a solid enhancing tumour arising from ependymal glia
It is defined by restricted diffusion and implantation of skin elements after puncture
It follows CSF on all MRI sequences and may be difficult to distinguish from surrounding CSF
It is characteristically intramedullary
It is the classic cause of an enhancing cauda equina mass with vascular flow voids
updates.explanation: An arachnoid cyst is a CSF collection, usually intradural but occasionally extradural, that may be congenital or related to trauma, postoperative scarring or inflammation. It follows CSF on all MRI sequences, making it hard to distinguish from surrounding CSF. Cord displacement or a broad cord impression should prompt careful scrutiny for cyst walls. Restricted diffusion and skin-element implantation describe epidermoid cyst, not arachnoid cyst.

updates.question_text: Regarding Guillain-Barre syndrome and CIDP, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Guillain-Barre syndrome most commonly has descending proximal-to-distal progression over years
Guillain-Barre syndrome is most commonly an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy
Campylobacter jejuni is the most common preceding infection listed for Guillain-Barre syndrome
Spinal MRI in Guillain-Barre syndrome may show enhancement and thickening of cauda equina nerve roots
CIDP is an acute monophasic illness lasting only a few days
options_after: Guillain-Barre syndrome most commonly has descending proximal-to-distal progression over years
Guillain-Barre syndrome is most commonly an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy
Campylobacter jejuni is the most common preceding infection listed for Guillain-Barre syndrome
Spinal MRI in Guillain-Barre syndrome may show enhancement and thickening of cauda equina nerve roots
CIDP is an acute monophasic illness lasting primarily a few days
updates.explanation: Guillain-Barre syndrome is described as most commonly acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, with symmetric weakness and diminished reflexes and classically ascending distal-to-proximal progression over several weeks. Campylobacter jejuni is the most common preceding infection. Spinal MRI may show enhancement and thickening of cauda equina roots. CIDP has a progressive or recurrent course lasting at least several months, so a few-day monophasic course is incorrect.

updates.question_text: Regarding common spinal extradural malignancies and primary tumours, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Breast, lung and prostate are the most common primary tumours to metastasise to the spinal column
The most common extradural neoplasms causing epidural spinal cord compression include carcinoma metastases, plasmacytoma/multiple myeloma and lymphomas
Chordoma occurs most commonly in vertebral bodies and only rarely in the sacrococcygeal region
Chondrosarcoma never contains chondroid rings-and-arcs calcification
Chordoma is a benign tumour of young adults arising from annular fibrosus remnants
options_after: Breast, lung and prostate are the most common primary tumours to metastasise to the spinal column
The most common extradural neoplasms causing epidural spinal cord compression include carcinoma metastases, plasmacytoma/multiple myeloma and lymphomas
Chordoma occurs most commonly in vertebral bodies and primarily rarely in the sacrococcygeal region
Chondrosarcoma will not contain chondroid rings-and-arcs calcification
Chordoma is a benign tumour of young adults arising from annular fibrosus remnants
updates.explanation: The source lists breast, lung and prostate as the most common primary tumours metastasising to the spinal column. Extradural neoplasms that commonly cause epidural spinal cord compression include carcinoma metastases, plasmacytoma or multiple myeloma, and lymphomas. Chordoma is a malignant notochord-remnant tumour of older adults, most common in the sacrococcygeal region and second in the clivus, with up to 15% in vertebral bodies. Chondrosarcoma can show chondroid rings-and-arcs calcification.

updates.question_text: Regarding lumbar degenerative spine reporting, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The major anterior anatomic units are the disc-endplate complexes
Symptoms from neural compression typically produce painless systemic symptoms rather than radicular pain
Neural compression may occur in the spinal canal, lateral recess or neural foramen
Axial back pain may arise from the disc-endplate complex or facet arthropathy
There is no interobserver variability in reporting degenerative spinal lesions
options_after: The major anterior anatomic units are the disc-endplate complexes
Symptoms from neural compression typically produce painless systemic symptoms rather than radicular pain
Neural compression may occur in the spinal canal, lateral recess or neural foramen
Axial back pain may arise from the disc-endplate complex or facet arthropathy
There is an absence of interobserver variability in reporting degenerative spinal lesions
updates.explanation: The source identifies the disc-endplate complex as the anterior degenerative unit and the facet joints/ligamentum flavum posteriorly. Neural compression may occur in the canal, lateral recess or neural foramen, while axial pain may arise from the disc-endplate complex or facet arthropathy. Neural compression typically produces radicular pain, so describing it as painless systemic symptoms is incorrect. The text explicitly notes substantial interobserver variability despite attempts at standardisation.

updates.question_text: Regarding disc herniation location and nerve root compression, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Central or subarticular disc herniations may compress the descending/traversing nerve root
Foraminal or extra-foraminal lesions may compress the exiting nerve root
A sequestered disc fragment remains attached to the parent disc and cannot migrate
A Schmorl node is an intravertebral herniation through the cartilaginous endplate
Right central, right paracentral and right subarticular terms must never be used interchangeably, even if neural compression is described
options_after: Central or subarticular disc herniations may compress the descending/traversing nerve root
Foraminal or extra-foraminal lesions may compress the exiting nerve root
A sequestered disc fragment remains attached to the parent disc and will not migrate
A Schmorl node is an intravertebral herniation through the cartilaginous endplate
Right central, right paracentral and right subarticular terms must will not be used interchangeably, even if neural compression is described
updates.explanation: The source states that central and subarticular lateral recess lesions may compress the descending or traversing nerve root, while foraminal and extra-foraminal lesions may compress the exiting root. Disc material can separate from the parent disc to form a sequestered fragment that migrates superiorly or inferiorly, so immobility while attached is incorrect. An intravertebral herniation through the endplate is a Schmorl node. The text accepts some heterogeneity among off-midline terms as long as relevant neural compression is discussed.

updates.question_text: Which Modic change is specifically described as potentially associated with active back pain?
options_before: Modic type 2 fatty metaplasia.
Modic type 3 fibrosis.
Chronic hypointensity on all sequences.
Modic type 1 oedema.
Normal fatty marrow conversion.
options_after: Modic type 2 fatty metaplasia.
Modic type 3 fibrosis.
Chronic hypointensity on most sequences.
Modic type 1 oedema.
Normal fatty marrow conversion.
updates.explanation: The source specifically links Modic type 1 oedematous change with active back pain. Modic type 2 is less likely to be associated with active symptoms, while the clinical significance of type 3 fibrosis is unclear and chronic in timecourse.
